units.title: Dolor abdominal en el infante
units.body:
# Dolor abdominal en el infante

## 0. One-line exam model

Dolor abdominal en el infante is an age-and-vomit router:

`age + vomit type + pain rhythm + obstruction sign -> diagnosis -> first move`

Take-home point: in infants, bilious vomiting and intermittent colicky distress
are surgical signals until proven otherwise.

## 1. Why it happens

This topic groups several pediatric surgical entities that present with crying,
vomiting, distension or poor feeding rather than precise adult-style pain
localization.

| Mechanism | Entity | Why the child looks sick |
|---|---|---|
| Bowel telescopes into distal bowel | Intussusception | Venous congestion, edema, bleeding, obstruction and possible ischemia. |
| Narrow mesenteric base twists around vessels | Malrotation with volvulus | Midgut ischemia can progress fast. |
| Distal bowel lacks ganglion cells | Hirschsprung disease | The aganglionic segment cannot relax, causing functional obstruction. |
| Pyloric muscle hypertrophies | Hypertrophic pyloric stenosis | Gastric outlet obstruction causes projectile nonbilious vomiting and alkalosis. |
| Congenital luminal block | Atresias, meconium ileus | Neonatal obstruction from birth. |

Take-home point: the common final pathway is obstruction, but the first move
depends on age, vomit type and stability.

## 2. Who gets it

### Age map

| Age | Most exam-relevant diagnoses |
|---|---|
| Birth to 48 h | Atresia duodenal, atresia pyloric, Hirschsprung disease, meconium ileus, malrotation/volvulus. |
| Newborn to early infancy | Volvulus by malrotation, Hirschsprung disease, necrotizing enterocolitis if premature/sick. |
| 2-8 weeks | Hypertrophic pyloric stenosis, especially male infant and firstborn in classic teaching. |
| 3 months to 2 years | Intussusception peak. |
| 2-6 years | Intussusception still possible; lead point becomes more important. |

### Risk and association clues

- Intussusception: often idiopathic; may follow viral illness; older children
  suggest pathologic lead point such as Meckel diverticulum, polyp, lymphoma,
  IgA vasculitis or foreign body.
- Hirschsprung: male predominance; associated with trisomy 21 and RET pathway in
  classic teaching.
- Pyloric stenosis: early infancy; local card emphasizes male, firstborn,
  macrolide exposure and formula feeding as risk clues.
- Volvulus/malrotation: can present early, but malrotation can present later.

Take-home point: the same symptom means different things at different ages.

## 3. How it presents

### High-yield pattern table

| Entity | Canonical presentation |
|---|---|
| Intussusception | Intermittent severe crying/colic, drawing up legs, pallor, vomiting, lethargy between episodes; late blood/mucus stool. |
| Volvulus/malrotation | Abrupt bilious vomiting in newborn/infant, distension, possible bloody stool and rapid deterioration. |
| Hirschsprung | Delayed meconium beyond 24-48 h, distension, bilious vomiting, poor feeding; later severe constipation from birth. |
| Pyloric stenosis | Progressive projectile nonbilious vomiting after feeds at 3-6 weeks, hungry after vomiting, dehydration/weight loss. |
| Atresia duodenal | Bilious vomiting from birth with double bubble pattern; Down association in exams. |
| Atresia pyloric | Nonbilious vomiting from birth with single bubble pattern. |

### Red flags

- Bilious vomiting.
- Peritonism, guarding or rigidity.
- Shock, toxic appearance, poor perfusion.
- Distension with absent stool/meconium.
- Bloody stool with lethargy.
- Severe dehydration or electrolyte disturbance.
- Irreducible hernia.
- Scrotal pain/swelling, because testicular torsion can mimic abdominal pain.

Take-home point: "dolor abdominal" in an infant may be crying, pallor, lethargy,
vomiting or refusal to feed.

## 4. Diagnosis

### Intussusception

Best first imaging when suspected: abdominal ultrasound.

Classic findings:

- Target/donut sign on ultrasound.
- Sausage-shaped mass or filling defect on contrast/air enema.
- Empty right lower quadrant and elongated mass can appear in local exam stems.

Do not wait for currant jelly stool; it is a late sign.

### Malrotation with volvulus

Bilious vomiting in an infant is a surgical warning.

If stable, upper GI series is the classic test to evaluate malrotation. Ultrasound
can support the diagnosis with a whirlpool sign or abnormal vessel relationship,
but local exam language often emphasizes contrast study/seriada alta.

If unstable or ischemic, do not delay surgical consultation for perfect imaging.

### Hirschsprung disease

Definitive diagnosis: rectal biopsy showing absence of ganglion cells.

Supportive tests:

- Abdominal X-ray: distended bowel, little/no rectal gas.
- Contrast enema: transition zone or narrow distal segment with proximal
  dilation.
- Anorectal manometry: absent rectoanal inhibitory reflex.

Local exam contrast:

| Feature | Functional constipation | Hirschsprung |
|---|---|---|
| Start | Usually after infancy | Neonatal or from birth |
| Rectal ampulla | Stool present | Empty ampulla |
| Encopresis | Common | Rare |
| Biopsy | Normal | Aganglionosis |

### Hypertrophic pyloric stenosis

Best initial imaging: ultrasound.

Local ENAM thresholds from card:

- Pyloric muscle thickness > 3 mm.
- Pyloric canal length > 15 mm.

Lab clue:

- Hypochloremic hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis.

Take-home point: ultrasound for intussusception and pylorus; upper GI series for
stable bilious vomiting suspicious for malrotation; rectal biopsy for
Hirschsprung.

## 5. Management

### Initial management for suspected surgical infant abdomen

Do this while refining diagnosis:

- Assess airway, breathing, circulation and perfusion.
- IV access, fluids if dehydrated/shock.
- Analgesia; appropriate analgesia does not erase dangerous disease.
- NPO.
- Early pediatric surgery/pediatric team discussion if surgical cause possible.
- Nasogastric decompression if bowel obstruction suspected.
- Transfer if care exceeds local capacity.

### Intussusception

If stable and no signs of perforation, peritonitis, shock or instability:

1. Fluid resuscitation/analgesia as needed.
2. Ultrasound confirmation.
3. Pneumatic or hydrostatic enema reduction with surgical backup.

Residentado exact anchor: 2-year-old with episodic abdominal pain, vomiting,
sausage sign and mass; correct conduct was air enema.

Go to surgery if:

- Peritonitis.
- Shock/instability.
- Perforation.
- Failed reduction.
- Necrosis.
- Strong suspicion of lead point requiring resection.

### Malrotation with volvulus

Bilious vomiting in a neonate or infant requires urgent surgical evaluation.

- Stable: image quickly, classically upper GI series.
- Unstable, peritonitic or ischemic: surgical route; do not wait for extensive
  studies.
- Treatment: Ladd procedure in classic exam framing.

### Hirschsprung disease

Initial logic:

- Decompress/support.
- Treat enterocolitis aggressively if fever, diarrhea, toxic appearance or
  distension.
- Confirm with rectal biopsy.
- Definitive treatment is surgical: resection/pull-through; staged ostomy if
  severe or unstable.

### Pyloric stenosis

Do not operate first.

1. Correct dehydration, chloride and potassium/electrolyte abnormalities.
2. Confirm with ultrasound.
3. Definitive treatment: pyloromyotomy of Ramstedt.

Take-home point: in intussusception, stable child gets reduction by enema; in
volvulus, bilious vomiting is time-critical; in pylorus, fix electrolytes before
surgery.

## 6. Complications

| Entity | Complications |
|---|---|
| Intussusception | Bowel ischemia, necrosis, perforation, peritonitis, shock, recurrence after reduction. |
| Volvulus | Midgut ischemia, short bowel syndrome, perforation, sepsis, death. |
| Hirschsprung | Hirschsprung-associated enterocolitis, perforation, failure to thrive, postoperative bowel dysfunction. |
| Pyloric stenosis | Severe dehydration, hypochloremic hypokalemic alkalosis, preoperative anesthesia risk if not corrected. |

Take-home point: the dangerous endpoint is ischemia/perforation/shock, except
pylorus where the immediate danger is dehydration and alkalosis.

## 7. Follow-up and prognosis

### Intussusception

Observe after successful reduction according to local protocol. Recurrence is
most common early, especially within the first 24-48 h in guideline framing.
Older children or recurrent cases need evaluation for a lead point.

### Hirschsprung

Long-term follow-up is needed after pull-through/ostomy closure because
constipation, enterocolitis, obstruction and continence problems can occur.

### Pyloric stenosis

After pyloromyotomy, feeding is gradually resumed. Some postoperative vomiting
can occur from edema, but persistent deterioration requires reassessment.

### Volvulus

Outcome depends on speed of recognition before bowel ischemia. Bilious vomiting
is therefore treated as a time-critical clue.

Take-home point: the faster the obstructive/ischemic entities are recognized,
the less bowel is lost.

## 8. Local exam blueprints

### P01 - What does the child have?

- 4-12 month infant with episodic colicky crying, leg flexion, pallor/lethargy,
  vomiting and late blood/mucus stool: intussusception.
- Newborn with no meconium, distension, bilious vomiting and empty rectal
  ampulla: Hirschsprung.
- Neonate/infant with abrupt bilious vomiting and distension: malrotation with
  volvulus until proven otherwise.
- 3-6 week infant with projectile nonbilious vomiting and hunger after vomiting:
  pyloric stenosis.

### P03 - Next step

- Suspected intussusception: ultrasound first, then enema reduction if stable.
- Confirmed/stable intussusception without peritonitis: air or hydrostatic enema
  reduction.
- Intussusception with shock/perforation/peritonitis: surgery.
- Suspected Hirschsprung: rectal biopsy.
- Suspected volvulus with instability: urgent surgery/surgical consultation.
- Pyloric stenosis: correct electrolytes and dehydration before pyloromyotomy.

### P06 - Mechanism

- Hirschsprung: failed cranio-caudal neural crest migration -> aganglionosis.
- Intussusception: bowel telescoping -> venous congestion -> edema/bleeding ->
  ischemia/necrosis.
- Volvulus: malrotation -> narrow mesenteric base -> twist around superior
  mesenteric vessels.
- Pyloric stenosis: pyloric muscle hypertrophy -> gastric outlet obstruction ->
  loss of HCl -> metabolic alkalosis.

## 9. Must-not-confuse list

- Currant jelly stool is not required for intussusception.
- Air/hydrostatic enema is not for an unstable child with peritonitis.
- Bilious vomiting in a neonate is not reflux.
- Pyloric stenosis causes nonbilious vomiting; bilious vomiting points distal to
  the ampulla.
- Hirschsprung has delayed meconium and empty rectum; functional constipation
  usually has stool in the rectum.
- Pyloromyotomy is not the first move before resuscitation/electrolyte
  correction.
- A pediatric infant abdomen is not the same as the adult obstruction package.

## 10. Product caution

This package is ready for internal classes and qbank development. It remains
`fail_to_publish` because local ENAM/Residentado wording, imaging preferences,
enema modality, exact ultrasound thresholds, Ladd/Ramstedt details and local
transfer/surgical availability need final source-lock before public manual use.

This topic groups several pediatric surgical entities that present with crying, vomiting, distension or poor feeding rather than precise adult-style pain localization. | Mechanism | Entity | Why the child looks sick | |---|---|---| | Bowel telescopes into distal bowel | Intussusception | Venous congestion, edema, bleeding, obstruction a

units.title: Trastornos de la coagulacion
units.body:
# Trastornos de la coagulacion

## 0. One-line anchor

Trastornos de la coagulacion is an exam-first cluster where the safe diagnosis comes from matching bleeding phenotype with platelet count, TP/TTPa, fibrinogen, D-dimer and smear.

Take-home: do not memorize the disease first; route the bleeding pattern.

## 1. Guion: why it happens

Hemostasis has three practical layers.

| Layer | Function | Failure looks like |
|---|---|---|
| Primary hemostasis | platelet adhesion/activation/aggregation and VWF bridge | petechiae, purpura, epistaxis, gingival bleeding, menorrhagia |
| Secondary hemostasis | coagulation factors generate fibrin to stabilize clot | hemarthrosis, deep hematoma, delayed bleeding after trauma/procedure |
| Fibrinolysis/control | prevents clot from spreading and later dissolves clot | high D-dimer, consumption, thrombosis plus bleeding in CID |

The core mechanism is not "bleeding equals low platelets." It can be:

- platelet destruction: PTI
- platelet-rich microthrombi: PTT/TTP or HUS
- factor deficiency: hemophilia A/B
- VWF defect: von Willebrand disease
- systemic consumption of factors and platelets: CID
- reduced synthesis or medication effect: hepatopathy, vitamin K deficit, anticoagulants

Take-home: mucosal bleeding suggests primary hemostasis; hemarthrosis suggests factor defect; bleeding plus systemic illness suggests consumption or TMA.

## 2. Guion: who gets it

| Entity | Typical exam patient |
|---|---|
| Acute PTI | child after viral illness; often self-limited |
| Chronic PTI | young adult woman with isolated thrombocytopenia |
| PTT/TTP | adult, often woman, with MAHA, thrombocytopenia, neuro/renal signs |
| Typical HUS/SHU | child under 5 after bloody diarrhea, usually STEC |
| CID acute | sepsis, trauma, obstetric catastrophe, acute promyelocytic leukemia |
| CID chronic | cancer, especially mucin-producing tumors; thrombosis may dominate |
| Hemophilia A/B | male, X-linked pattern, family history, hemarthrosis |
| VWD | most common inherited bleeding disorder; mucosal bleeding, menorrhagia/dental bleeding |
| Post-splenectomy PTI | risk for encapsulated organisms, especially pneumococcus |

Take-home: the patient profile narrows the branch, but the lab pattern confirms it.

## 3. Guion: how it presents

### Bleeding phenotype router

| Stem clue | Most useful branch |
|---|---|
| Petechiae, purpura, epistaxis, gingivorrhagia | platelet/VWF problem |
| Menorrhagia, dental bleeding, mucosal bleeding | VWD or platelet disorder |
| Hemarthrosis, muscle hematoma, deep bleeding | hemophilia/factor defect |
| Bleeding from puncture sites in sepsis/trauma/obstetric emergency | acute CID |
| Confusion, fever, anemia, schistocytes, thrombocytopenia | PTT/TTP |
| Bloody diarrhea followed by oliguria/anuria and anemia | HUS/SHU |
| Palpable purpura lower limbs/buttocks + abdominal pain/arthralgia | IgA vasculitis, not platelet failure |

### Frequent clinical packages

- PTI: isolated mucocutaneous bleeding with low platelets and otherwise normal blood counts.
- PTT/TTP: thrombocytopenia + microangiopathic hemolytic anemia; neuro changes are high-yield.
- HUS/SHU: similar TMA, but renal failure dominates after diarrhea.
- CID: bleeding and thrombosis in a very sick patient; labs show consumption.
- Hemophilia: recurrent hemarthrosis or deep hematomas with prolonged TTPa.
- VWD: mucocutaneous bleeding, often family history, variable TTPa.

Take-home: deep bleeding belongs to factors; superficial mucosal bleeding belongs to platelets/VWF until proven otherwise.

## 4. Manejo: diagnosis

### First lab panel

Order or interpret:

- CBC with platelet count
- peripheral smear
- TP/INR
- TTPa
- fibrinogen
- D-dimer
- hemolysis markers if TMA suspected: LDH, bilirubin indirect, haptoglobin, reticulocytes, Coombs
- disease-specific tests if needed: factor VIII/IX, VWF antigen/activity/FVIII, ADAMTS13, stool/STEC testing, liver tests

### Lab interpretation matrix

| Pattern | Diagnosis to prioritize |
|---|---|
| Platelets low, TP normal, TTPa normal, no schistocytes | PTI |
| Platelets low, TP normal, TTPa normal, schistocytes | PTT/TTP or HUS/SHU |
| Platelets low, TP high, TTPa high, fibrinogen low, D-dimer high | acute CID |
| Platelets normal, TP normal, TTPa prolonged, deep bleeding | hemophilia A/B |
| Platelets normal, TP normal, TTPa normal/mild high, mucosal bleeding | VWD |
| TP prolonged first, TTPa normal/prolonged later | vitamin K deficit/warfarin |
| TP and TTPa prolonged with liver disease | hepatopathy or severe synthetic failure |

### Mixing study

If TTPa is prolonged:

- correction after mixing with normal plasma: factor deficiency likely
- no correction: inhibitor or anticoagulant effect likely

Take-home: the exam often hides the diagnosis in "TP normal, TTPa prolonged, platelets normal" or "TP/TTPa normal with schistocytes."

## 5. Manejo: classification

### By pathophysiology

| Group | Diseases |
|---|---|
| Primary hemostasis | PTI, VWD, platelet function disorders |
| Secondary hemostasis | hemophilia A, hemophilia B, vitamin K deficit, anticoagulant effects |
| Consumption | acute/chronic CID |
| Thrombotic microangiopathy | PTT/TTP, HUS/SHU |
| Vascular purpura | IgA vasculitis; normal platelets and coagulation tests |

### By urgency

| Urgency | Examples |
|---|---|
| Immediate action | suspected TTP, acute CID with bleeding, severe hemophilia bleed, critical PTI bleeding |
| Same-day specialist pathway | new severe thrombocytopenia, suspected VWD with procedure need, chronic/refractory PTI |
| Observation possible | child with PTI and no/minor bleeding; mild stable inherited disorder after risk assessment |

Take-home: classification should decide the first safe move, not just name the disease.

## 6. Manejo: treatment by syndrome

### Initial stabilization

1. Assess hemodynamic stability and bleeding site.
2. Stop anticoagulants/antiplatelets if clinically appropriate.
3. Draw labs before transfusion if possible, but do not delay emergency care.
4. Activate hematology/critical care for TTP, CID, severe hemophilia bleeding or life-threatening thrombocytopenia.
5. Transfuse/support according to syndrome, not just the platelet number.

### PTI

Mechanism: immune IgG against platelet glycoproteins, with splenic macrophage destruction.

Diagnosis:

- isolated thrombocytopenia, often below 100,000/mcL
- TP and TTPa normal
- no anemia/leukopenia unless bleeding or another diagnosis
- consider HIV/HCV and secondary causes

Treatment:

- child with no/minor bleeding: observation is often preferred
- adult/newly diagnosed or clinically relevant bleeding: corticosteroids; ASH allows prednisone 0.5-2 mg/kg/day or dexamethasone 40 mg/day for 4 days
- severe/non-life-threatening mucosal bleeding: steroids and/or IVIG depending context
- critical bleeding: IVIG + steroids + platelet transfusion as rescue, not platelet monotherapy
- second line: splenectomy, thrombopoietin receptor agonists, rituximab; individualize
- post-splenectomy: vaccinate/counsel against encapsulated organisms; pneumococcus is exam-high-yield

Local exam lock:

- ENAM card uses prednisone 1 mg/kg/day as first-line adult exam framing.
- Residentado asks pneumococcus after splenectomy in refractory PTI.

Take-home: isolated thrombocytopenia with normal TP/TTPa is PTI until red flags appear, but platelets alone are not a durable treatment for critical PTI bleeding.

### PTT/TTP

Mechanism: severe ADAMTS13 deficiency or inhibitor causes ultra-large VWF multimers and platelet-rich microthrombi.

Diagnosis:

- thrombocytopenia
- microangiopathic hemolytic anemia: schistocytes, LDH high, bilirubin indirect high, haptoglobin low, Coombs negative
- fever and neurologic changes may appear
- renal injury can occur but is usually less dominant than in HUS
- TP and TTPa usually normal
- ADAMTS13 confirms, but treatment must not wait

Treatment:

- therapeutic plasma exchange/plasmaferesis + corticosteroids immediately
- rituximab can be added in selected immune TTP
- caplacizumab is a modern option in acute immune TTP where available
- avoid platelet transfusion unless life-threatening bleeding or critical procedure

Take-home: normal TP/TTPa does not make TTP benign; schistocytes plus thrombocytopenia is a hematologic emergency.

### HUS/SHU

Mechanism:

- typical STEC-HUS: shiga toxin endothelial injury after diarrheal illness
- atypical HUS: complement dysregulation

Diagnosis:

- microangiopathic hemolytic anemia
- thrombocytopenia
- acute kidney injury, often prominent
- child after bloody diarrhea is the classic local frame

Treatment:

- supportive care, hydration, renal support and dialysis if needed
- avoid routine antibiotics in suspected STEC because they can increase HUS risk
- atypical HUS: complement blockade such as eculizumab/ravulizumab in specialist care; vaccine/prophylaxis planning is required

Take-home: HUS is a TMA where kidneys dominate; typical STEC-HUS is not an antibiotic reflex.

### CID

Mechanism: systemic coagulation activation produces microthrombi, consumes platelets/factors, and activates fibrinolysis.

Causes:

- sepsis, especially gram-negative sepsis
- massive trauma
- obstetric catastrophe: abruptio, amniotic fluid embolism, retained dead fetus
- acute promyelocytic leukemia
- malignancy, especially chronic CID

Labs:

- platelets low
- TP prolonged
- TTPa prolonged
- fibrinogen low in acute CID
- D-dimer high
- TT can be prolonged

Treatment:

- treat the underlying cause; this is the cornerstone
- if bleeding or high-risk procedure: platelets, fresh frozen plasma, cryoprecipitate/fibrinogen support according to labs and local protocol
- chronic CID with thrombosis-dominant phenotype can require anticoagulation in selected cases
- do not give heparin by default in acute bleeding CID

Take-home: CID is consumption plus cause. Replace only when the clinical context needs support; curing the trigger is the real treatment.

### Hemophilia A/B

Mechanism:

- hemophilia A: factor VIII deficiency
- hemophilia B: factor IX deficiency
- X-linked recessive inheritance

Diagnosis:

- male with deep bleeding, hemarthrosis, muscle hematoma or post-procedure bleeding
- platelets normal
- TP normal
- TTPa prolonged
- factor VIII or IX activity low

Severity:

- mild: factor activity above 5%
- moderate: around 1-5%
- severe: below 1%

Treatment:

- factor VIII or IX concentrate for clinically significant bleeding
- DDAVP can be used in selected mild/moderate hemophilia A after documented response
- antifibrinolytics can help mucosal bleeding, but avoid unsafe combinations per specialist protocol
- emicizumab and bypassing agents are specialist therapies, especially inhibitor contexts

Local exam lock:

- Residentado factor VIII = hemophilia A.
- Young male + hemarthrosis + normal TP/platelets + prolonged TTPa = hemophilia A unless factor IX clue is explicit.

Take-home: hemarthrosis plus isolated prolonged TTPa is a factor VIII/IX problem.

### Von Willebrand disease

Mechanism: VWF defect impairs platelet adhesion and factor VIII stabilization.

Classification:

- type 1: partial quantitative deficiency
- type 2: qualitative defect
- type 3: severe/near-total deficiency

Diagnosis:

- mucosal bleeding, epistaxis, menorrhagia, dental/procedure bleeding
- platelets usually normal
- TP normal
- TTPa can be normal or mildly prolonged because FVIII may be low
- VWF antigen, VWF activity and FVIII are key tests

Treatment:

- DDAVP for many type 1 patients after response assessment
- tranexamic acid for mucosal bleeding and heavy menstrual bleeding contexts
- VWF concentrate for severe disease, type 3, many type 2 cases or major procedures
- avoid treating all VWD types as if cryoprecipitate were the modern universal option

Local exam lock:

- Older/local material may mention cryoprecipitate for types 2/3; keep this as source-locked and update with guideline context in class/manual products.

Take-home: VWD can look like platelet disease clinically but can prolong TTPa through FVIII.

## 7. Complications

| Disease | Complications |
|---|---|
| PTI | severe mucosal bleeding, intracranial bleeding rare, treatment toxicity, post-splenectomy infection |
| PTT/TTP | stroke, renal injury, cardiac ischemia, death if untreated |
| HUS/SHU | acute kidney failure, dialysis need, chronic kidney disease |
| CID | shock, organ failure, thrombosis, fatal bleeding |
| Hemophilia | recurrent hemarthrosis, arthropathy, inhibitors, procedure bleeding |
| VWD | severe menstrual bleeding, iron deficiency, surgical/dental bleeding |

Take-home: complications follow mechanism: TMA injures organs, hemophilia injures joints, CID injures everything.

## 8. Follow-up and prognosis

- PTI: monitor platelet count and bleeding; avoid prolonged steroid exposure; plan second-line therapy if persistent/refractory.
- Post-splenectomy: vaccination, fever action plan and infection counseling.
- PTT/TTP: monitor platelets, LDH, hemolysis, neurologic status; relapse risk requires specialist follow-up.
- HUS/SHU: monitor renal recovery, blood pressure, proteinuria and chronic kidney disease.
- CID: monitor trigger control, platelets, TP/TTPa, fibrinogen and D-dimer.
- Hemophilia: factor levels, bleed frequency, joint health, inhibitor screening, prophylaxis adherence.
- VWD: bleeding score/history, VWF/FVIII levels, menstrual/procedure planning and iron deficiency.

Take-home: follow-up is not generic; it tracks the organ or system threatened by the mechanism.

## 9. Local exam blueprints

| Stem | Expected move |
|---|---|
| Woman with petechiae, platelets 15,000/mcL, Hb/WBC normal, TP/TTPa normal | PTI |
| Severe thrombocytopenia, schistocytes, fever/confusion, TP/TTPa normal | PTT/TTP; plasma exchange + steroids |
| Child after bloody diarrhea with anemia, thrombocytopenia and renal failure | typical HUS; supportive care, avoid antibiotics |
| Sepsis/obstetric catastrophe with bleeding from puncture sites, TP/TTPa prolonged, fibrinogen low, D-dimer high | acute CID |
| Male with hemarthrosis, platelets normal, TP normal, TTPa prolonged | hemophilia A/B; check factor VIII/IX |
| X-linked bleeding disease, asks deficient factor | factor VIII if hemophilia A |
| Refractory PTI after splenectomy, asks frequent germ | Streptococcus pneumoniae |
| Mucosal bleeding with normal platelets and abnormal VWF tests | VWD |

Take-home: Residentado loves hemophilia A and pneumococcus; ENAM loves the lab matrix.

## 10. Must-not-confuse list

- Do not call every purpura PTI.
- Do not miss TTP because TP/TTPa are normal.
- Do not wait ADAMTS13 before treating suspected TTP.
- Do not transfuse platelets routinely in TTP.
- Do not give routine antibiotics in suspected STEC-HUS.
- Do not call hemophilia if TP and TTPa are both prolonged; think CID/liver/warfarin.
- Do not exclude VWD just because TTPa is normal.
- Do not give heparin by default in acute CID with bleeding.
- Do not universalize cryoprecipitate as modern first-line VWD therapy.

Take-home: the safest student is not the one who remembers the most names, but the one who avoids the dangerous reflex.

units.title: Patologia oido medio
units.body:
# Patologia oido medio

## 0. One-line anchor

Patologia oido medio is an otoscopy-first cluster: diagnose by tympanic membrane findings, symptoms, duration and complications before choosing antibiotics, observation, tubes or surgery.

Take-home: red tympanic membrane alone is not OMA; bulging/effusion plus acute inflammation is the exam hinge.

## 1. Guion: why it happens

The middle ear is connected to the nasopharynx through the eustachian tube. After viral URI, allergy, adenoid hypertrophy or immature tube function, ventilation fails.

This creates three routes:

| Route | Mechanism | Disease |
|---|---|---|
| Negative pressure + bacterial ascent | infected middle ear effusion/pus | otitis media aguda |
| Chronic tube dysfunction | sterile mucus/fluid persists | otitis media with effusion/serous OM |
| Chronic perforation or retraction | recurrent drainage, colonization or keratin invasion | chronic suppurative OM or colesteatoma |

Middle ear fluid blocks mechanical sound transmission, so many middle ear diseases produce conductive hearing loss.

Take-home: eustachian tube dysfunction is the shared doorway; infection, sterile effusion and destructive keratin disease are different endpoints.

## 2. Guion: who gets it

| Entity | Typical patient |
|---|---|
| OMA | child 6 months to 3 years, often after URI |
| OME/serous OM | child after OMA/URI or with chronic tube dysfunction; adult with fullness/autophony requires careful evaluation |
| OMC simple | patient with chronic/recurrent purulent otorrhea and tympanic membrane perforation |
| Colesteatoma | adult/older child with chronic fetid otorrhea, hearing loss and attic/marginal disease |
| Mastoiditis | child or adult after untreated/partially treated OMA |
| Facial palsy from OM | child with abrupt OMA-related palsy or slow palsy from colesteatoma |

Risk modifiers:

- younger age
- daycare/crowding
- smoke exposure
- no breastfeeding or shorter breastfeeding
- craniofacial abnormalities
- immunodeficiency or recurrent severe infections
- adenoid disease

Take-home: age and risk tell you where to look, but otoscopy decides the branch.

## 3. Guion: how it presents

### Otitis media aguda

Classic pattern:

- otalgia, irritability or ear tugging
- fever
- URI prodrome
- bulging, congestive/inflamed tympanic membrane
- middle ear effusion/pus
- conductive hearing symptoms
- otorrhea if spontaneous perforation occurs; pain may decrease after perforation

Local CTO/ENAM phases:

| Phase | Findings |
|---|---|
| Collection | bulging, red, purulent tympanic membrane; pulsatile otalgia, hearing loss, fever |
| Otorrhea | spontaneous perforation, classically posteroinferior pars tensa; pain improves |

### Otitis media with effusion / serous OM

Pattern:

- fluid behind tympanic membrane without acute infection
- fullness, autophony, popping/clicks
- conductive hearing loss
- little/no fever
- tympanic membrane can look amber, retracted or show air-fluid level

### Otitis media cronica simple

Pattern:

- chronic or recurrent purulent otorrhea
- usually painless
- variable conductive hearing loss
- central perforation
- no bony erosion

### Colesteatoma

Pattern:

- chronic fetid otorrhea that persists despite treatment
- hearing loss
- attic/marginal perforation, retraction pocket, white keratin debris or polyp
- CT can show soft-tissue mass and bony erosion
- can cause facial palsy, vertigo, labyrinthitis, abscess or intracranial infection

### Complications

| Complication | Stem clue |
|---|---|
| Mastoiditis | fever, persistent throbbing otalgia, postauricular swelling/redness, pinna displacement |
| Subperiosteal abscess | retroauricular swelling; lateral form may push pinna forward |
| Bezold abscess | neck pain/swelling/torticollis from mastoid tip extension |
| Petrositis | Gradenigo syndrome: otorrhea + retro-orbital pain + diplopia |
| Facial palsy | peripheral VII palsy ipsilateral to OM |
| Meningitis | fever/headache/meningism after OM; local card calls it the most frequent intracranial complication |
| Sigmoid sinus thrombophlebitis | septic spikes, headache, retroauricular pain/edema |

Take-home: otorrhea + hearing loss is not always benign; fetid chronic drainage or neurologic signs demand ENT escalation.

## 4. Manejo: diagnosis

### OMA diagnostic criteria

Use symptoms plus otoscopy:

- moderate/severe tympanic membrane bulging, or
- new otorrhea not explained by otitis externa, or
- mild bulging plus recent otalgia or intense erythema

Do not diagnose OMA without middle ear effusion.

Pain with tragus/pinna movement points more to otitis externa than OMA.

### OME diagnosis

- document middle ear effusion, ideally with pneumatic otoscopy
- tympanometry helps when diagnosis is uncertain
- hearing evaluation if effusion persists 3 months or if child is at risk

### Chronic disease diagnosis

| Suspected disease | Diagnostic move |
|---|---|
| OMC simple | otoscopy, culture if persistent/severe drainage, assess perforation |
| Colesteatoma | ENT otoscopy, CT temporal bone/penasco for erosion, diffusion MRI for specificity/recurrence |
| Mastoiditis | clinical diagnosis; CT when complication/coalescent disease suspected |
| Intracranial complication | urgent imaging and IV therapy pathway |

Take-home: OMA and OME are clinical/otoscopic diagnoses; imaging is for complications, erosion or surgical planning.

## 5. Manejo: classification

| Group | Diseases |
|---|---|
| Acute infectious | OMA, bullous myringitis spectrum |
| Noninfectious effusion | OME/serous OM |
| Chronic suppurative | OMC simple |
| Destructive chronic | colesteatoma |
| Intratemporal complications | mastoiditis, petrositis, facial palsy, labyrinthitis |
| Intracranial complications | meningitis, abscess, sigmoid sinus thrombosis |
| Sequelae | tympanosclerosis, conductive hearing loss |

Exam classification should answer one of four questions:

1. Does this need antibiotic now?
2. Does this need observation/hearing follow-up instead?
3. Does this need ENT surgery?
4. Does this need emergency IV antibiotics/imaging?

Take-home: classification is useful only if it changes treatment.

## 6. Manejo: treatment

### Universal first step

- analgesia matters in OMA
- assess severity, age, bilateral disease, otorrhea/perforation, follow-up reliability and immunocompromise
- do not use antibiotics to treat sterile OME
- escalate if complication signs appear

### OMA

Pathogens:

- S pneumoniae
- H influenzae
- Moraxella catarrhalis
- S pyogenes

Treatment:

- amoxicillin is first-line when antibiotic is indicated and no recent amoxicillin exposure
- local ENAM lock: high-dose amoxicillin 80-90 mg/kg/day
- use amoxicillin-clavulanate if amoxicillin was used in the last 30 days, purulent conjunctivitis is present, or recurrent OMA did not respond to amoxicillin
- non-type I penicillin allergy: cephalosporin options may be used depending protocol
- reassess if no improvement in 48-72 hours

Duration/source-lock:

- local Residentado asks 10 days minimum for a 2-year-old with fever/otalgia and tympanic membrane perforation
- many modern pathways use shorter courses in older nonsevere uncomplicated cases, but otorrhea/perforation and young age favor 10 days

Take-home: OMA treatment is not "always amox-clav"; ordinary first-line is amoxicillin, but conjunctivitis-otitis points to H influenzae and amox-clav logic.

### OME / serous OM

Current guideline-aligned management in children:

- watchful waiting for about 3 months if not at-risk
- educate family about natural history and follow-up
- hearing test if persistent 3 months or at-risk child
- reevaluate every 3-6 months if chronic and no tubes
- avoid routine systemic antibiotics
- avoid routine intranasal/systemic steroids
- avoid antihistamines/decongestants for treating OME

Local source conflict:

- ENAM/CTO local material lists vasoconstrictors, topical/systemic corticosteroids, lavados nasales and Valsalva.
- For class/manual ground truth, this needs source-lock because AAO-HNS pediatric OME guidance recommends against those routine drug strategies.

Take-home: OME is fluid without infection. The exam trap is treating it like OMA.

### Recurrent AOM and tympanostomy tubes

Definitions used in tube guidelines:

- recurrent AOM: 3 or more episodes in 6 months, or 4 or more in 12 months with at least 1 in the last 6 months
- chronic OME: effusion for 3 months or longer

Tube logic:

- recurrent AOM with middle ear effusion at assessment: offer/consider bilateral tympanostomy tubes
- recurrent AOM without effusion at assessment: do not place tubes just for recurrence
- bilateral chronic OME with documented hearing difficulty: offer bilateral tubes
- OME shorter than 3 months: do not place tubes

Take-home: tubes need persistent fluid or recurrent AOM with effusion at assessment, not just parental frustration.

### OMC simple

Treatment:

- dry ear precautions
- topical quinolone-style antibiotic drops are common modern therapy when active drainage is present
- avoid ototoxic drops when tympanic membrane is perforated unless specialist protocol permits
- systemic antibiotics for severe exacerbation or spread
- tympanoplasty can be considered in remission or for persistent perforation/hearing problems

Local ENAM lock:

- OMC simple = central perforation, no osteolysis, no otalgia, chronic otorrhea.

Take-home: chronic painless otorrhea with central perforation is OMC simple until destructive signs appear.

### Colesteatoma

Treatment:

- surgical removal is required
- tympanoplasty with mastoidectomy/open or closed technique depending case
- main goal is disease control and complication prevention; hearing rehabilitation can be staged
- follow-up is necessary because recurrence can occur

Take-home: colesteatoma is not a tumor by name, but behaves destructively. It is a surgical disease.

### Mastoiditis and complications

Management:

- urgent ENT evaluation
- IV antibiotics with CNS penetration, often ceftriaxone-based in references
- CT temporal bone if coalescent mastoiditis or complication suspected
- myringotomy/tube or mastoidectomy if coalescent disease, abscess, no response or complicated course

Local ENAM lock:

- mastoiditis is the most frequent intratemporal complication of OMA
- meningitis is the most frequent intracranial complication in local card
- petrositis = Gradenigo syndrome

Take-home: mastoid pain/swelling or neurologic signs convert otitis into an emergency pathway.

## 7. Complications

| Disease | Complications |
|---|---|
| OMA | perforation, recurrent AOM, mastoiditis, meningitis, hearing symptoms |
| OME | conductive hearing loss, speech/language risk if persistent in at-risk child |
| OMC simple | persistent drainage, conductive hearing loss, chronic perforation |
| Colesteatoma | ossicular erosion, labyrinthine fistula, vertigo, facial palsy, abscess, meningitis |
| Mastoiditis | subperiosteal abscess, Bezold abscess, sigmoid sinus thrombosis, meningitis, sepsis |
| Tympanosclerosis | conductive hearing loss from calcified plaques/ossicular fixation |

Take-home: complications follow anatomy: middle ear -> mastoid -> facial nerve/labyrinth -> intracranial space.

## 8. Follow-up and prognosis

- OMA: reassess if no improvement in 48-72 hours; verify resolution if recurrent, complicated or persistent symptoms.
- OME: observe up to 3 months if not at-risk; hearing test if persistent; follow every 3-6 months if chronic.
- Recurrent AOM: assess whether middle ear effusion is present before tube decision.
- OMC simple: ensure dry ear, response to topical therapy, hearing assessment and ENT planning if perforation persists.
- Colesteatoma: ENT surgical follow-up and recurrence surveillance.
- Mastoiditis/complications: inpatient/specialist follow-up, imaging/labs as clinically needed.

Take-home: follow-up protects hearing and catches destructive disease early.

## 9. Local exam blueprints

| Stem | Expected answer |
|---|---|
| 7-month infant, URI, fever/crying, bulging congestive tympanic membrane | otitis media aguda |
| 2-year-old, fever/otalgia 4 days, tympanic membrane perforation | 10 days antibiotic minimum in Residentado lock |
| purulent conjunctivitis plus ipsilateral OMA | H influenzae; amox-clav logic in treatment |
| middle ear infection followed by sudden hearing loss | conductive hearing loss |
| chronic fetid otorrhea, hipoacusia, attic/marginal perforation, white scales | colesteatoma |
| central perforation, chronic painless otorrhea, no osteolysis | OMC simple |
| OMA followed by retroauricular edema and pinna displacement | mastoiditis |
| otorrhea + retro-orbital pain + diplopia | petrositis/Gradenigo |
| chronic suppurative OM with ipsilateral hemiface palsy | VII cranial nerve |
| otitis followed by meningism/headache/fever | otogenic meningitis |

Take-home: ENAM tests the matrix; Residentado tests the one-line associations.

## 10. Must-not-confuse list

- Do not diagnose OMA from erythema alone.
- Do not treat OME as bacterial OMA.
- Do not use routine antibiotics/steroids/decongestants for pediatric OME as modern ground truth.
- Do not call otitis externa if the decisive finding is a bulging tympanic membrane.
- Do not miss otitis externa when pain increases with tragus/pinna movement.
- Do not treat colesteatoma as recurrent simple otitis.
- Do not call every mastoid opacification on imaging surgical mastoiditis; clinical coalescent disease matters.
- Do not ignore facial palsy, vertigo, diplopia or meningism in OM.
- Do not make amox-clav first-line for every ordinary OMA.

Take-home: middle ear pathology is a pattern-recognition topic, but safe management depends on resisting three reflexes: overdiagnose OMA, overtreat OME, and undertreat colesteatoma/complications.
units.example: Patologia oido medio is an otoscopy-first cluster: diagnose by tympanic membrane findings, symptoms, duration and complications before choosing antibiotics, observation, tubes or surgery. Take-home: red tympanic membrane alone is not OMA; bulging/effusion plus acute inflammation is the exam hinge. The middle ear is connected to the nasopharynx through the eustachian tube. After viral URI, allergy, adenoid hypertrophy or immature tube function, ventilation fails. This creates three routes: | Route | Mechanism | Disease | |---|---|---| | Negative pressure + bacterial ascent | infected middle ear

units.title: Hipertiroidismo
units.body:
# Hipertiroidismo

## 0. One-line anchor

Hipertiroidismo is the exam router where low TSH opens the door, but etiology and scenario decide treatment: Graves/nodules synthesize hormone; thyroiditis/factitious states do not.

Take-home: TSH baja tells you "thyrotoxicosis"; uptake/TSI/context tells you what to do.

## 1. Guion: why it happens

Two terms matter.

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Tirotoxicosis | excess action of thyroid hormone in peripheral tissues, from any source |
| Hipertiroidismo | excess thyroid secretion/synthesis; a subset of thyrotoxicosis |

Mechanistic buckets:

| Bucket | Mechanism | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| Autoimmune stimulation | antibody activates TSH receptor | Graves-Basedow |
| Autonomous nodular production | nodules produce hormone independent of TSH | toxic multinodular goiter, toxic adenoma |
| Destructive release | damaged follicles release stored hormone | subacute, painless, postpartum, amiodarone type 2 thyroiditis |
| Exogenous/iodine-related | hormone or iodine load creates thyrotoxicosis | factitious, Jod-Basedow, amiodarone type 1 |

Graves mechanism:

- TSI/TRAb are IgG antibodies that stimulate TSH receptor.
- This causes diffuse hyperplasia and hormone synthesis.
- Orbital and dermal fibroblast activation helps explain ophthalmopathy and pretibial myxedema.

Take-home: thionamides work when new hormone synthesis is the problem; they do not work when hormone is merely leaking from damaged follicles.

## 2. Guion: who gets it

| Entity | Typical exam patient |
|---|---|
| Graves | young or middle-aged woman, diffuse goiter, ophthalmopathy |
| Toxic multinodular goiter | older adult, atrial fibrillation or heart failure without clear cause |
| Toxic adenoma | adult with single autonomous nodule |
| Subacute thyroiditis | woman after viral respiratory illness with painful tender thyroid |
| Painless/postpartum thyroiditis | postpartum or autoimmune context, transient thyrotoxicosis |
| Factitious thyrotoxicosis | weight-loss treatment, psychiatric/iatrogenic exposure, no goiter |
| Thyroid storm | untreated Graves/toxic disease plus infection, surgery, delivery, iodine load or ATD withdrawal |
| Pediatric hyperthyroidism | school problems, tremor, insomnia, emotional lability, tachycardia; can mimic ADHD/anxiety |

Take-home: the elderly may present with atrial fibrillation, heart failure, weight loss or apathy rather than "classic nervous energy."

## 3. Guion: how it presents

General thyrotoxicosis:

- weight loss with preserved/increased appetite
- heat intolerance
- sweating
- palpitations, tachycardia, atrial fibrillation
- tremor fine
- anxiety, insomnia, irritability
- diarrhea or frequent stools
- proximal weakness
- oligomenorrhea
- warm moist skin

Graves-specific:

- diffuse goiter
- ophthalmopathy: proptosis/exophthalmos, diplopia, chemosis
- pretibial myxedema: nonpitting plaques, orange-peel texture
- thyroid acropachy, rare

Apatic hyperthyroidism in older adults:

- weight loss
- weakness
- depression/apathy
- slowed mental state
- atrial fibrillation or heart failure

Thyroid storm:

- fever, often high
- marked tachycardia, atrial fibrillation or heart failure
- agitation, delirium, confusion
- vomiting/diarrhea, dehydration
- jaundice can signal severe disease

Take-home: tachycardia plus weight loss plus tremor is the pattern; eye disease and diffuse goiter make Graves the answer.

## 4. Manejo: diagnosis

### Step 1: prove biochemical thyrotoxicosis

| Test | Interpretation |
|---|---|
| TSH | first test; suppressed in primary thyrotoxicosis |
| Free T4 | quantifies overt disease |
| T3 | useful if TSH low but free T4 normal; T3-toxicosis occurs |

Typical overt primary hyperthyroidism:

`TSH low + free T4 high and/or T3 high`

### Step 2: identify cause

| Test | Use |
|---|---|
| TSI/TRAb | positive supports Graves |
| Thyroid uptake/scintigraphy | diffuse high vs focal/multinodular high vs low/absent uptake |
| Thyroid ultrasound/Doppler | nodules and vascularity; useful if uptake contraindicated |
| Thyroglobulin | low suggests factitious/exogenous hormone |
| ESR/CRP | high supports painful subacute thyroiditis |

### Etiologic matrix

| Cause | Uptake | Antibody | Clue |
|---|---|---|---|
| Graves | diffuse increased | TSI/TRAb positive | diffuse goiter, ophthalmopathy |
| Toxic multinodular goiter | patchy/multinodular | negative | older adult, nodular gland |
| Toxic adenoma | single hot nodule, rest suppressed | negative | solitary autonomous nodule |
| Subacute thyroiditis | low/absent | usually negative | painful thyroid after viral illness, high ESR |
| Factitious | low/absent | negative | no goiter, low thyroglobulin, exogenous hormone |
| Jod-Basedow | variable/low if iodine saturated | negative | iodine contrast/amiodarone in autonomous gland |

Take-home: low uptake means the gland is not actively taking iodine to synthesize hormone; think leak, iodine saturation or exogenous source.

## 5. Manejo: classification

| Axis | Categories |
|---|---|
| By mechanism | synthesis excess, destructive release, exogenous hormone |
| By severity | subclinical, overt, storm |
| By population | adult, child/adolescent, pregnancy, older adult |
| By definitive therapy | antithyroid drug, radioiodine, surgery, observation/support |

Subclinical hyperthyroidism:

- low TSH with normal free T4/T3
- risk depends on age, TSH suppression depth, symptoms, atrial fibrillation/osteoporosis risk
- this package focuses on overt/storm because that is the local exam core

Take-home: classification must answer whether to block synthesis, ablate/remove tissue, or just treat symptoms while the leak resolves.

## 6. Manejo: treatment

### Symptomatic control

Beta-blockers reduce adrenergic symptoms:

- propranolol is classic and at high doses reduces T4-to-T3 conversion
- cardioselective options can be considered when bronchospasm/asthma risk matters

Take-home: beta-blocking buys control while the etiology-specific treatment works.

### Antithyroid drugs

| Drug | Mechanism | Best local use |
|---|---|---|
| Methimazole/tiamazol | blocks thyroid peroxidase organification/coupling | preferred in most nonpregnant adults |
| PTU | blocks thyroid peroxidase and peripheral T4-to-T3 conversion | first trimester pregnancy and thyroid storm |

Local dose locks from ENAM:

- methimazole 10-30 mg/day PO
- PTU 100-200 mg PO every 8h for routine use
- Graves course often 12-18 months

Adverse effects:

- rash, GI symptoms
- agranulocytosis: fever or odynophagia means stop and check CBC urgently
- hepatotoxicity, more concerning with PTU

Take-home: methimazole is the ordinary adult drug; PTU is special-scenario medicine.

### Graves adult nonpregnant

Options:

- antithyroid drugs
- radioactive iodine
- thyroidectomy

Choice depends on severity, goiter size, ophthalmopathy, patient preference, availability, pregnancy plans and comorbidities.

Local ENAM framing:

- methimazole first for adult nonpregnant Graves
- if relapse/failure: radioiodine or surgery depending context

Current guideline nuance:

- ATA accepts RAI, antithyroid drugs or thyroidectomy as effective options for overt Graves.
- NICE often frames RAI as first-line definitive for many adults, with exceptions.

Take-home: do not turn "methimazole is common first-line local exam" into "only valid treatment."

### Toxic multinodular goiter and toxic adenoma

Treatment logic:

- beta-blocker for symptoms
- methimazole can stabilize thyroid function
- definitive therapy is usually radioiodine or surgery
- adenoma toxic can be treated with radioiodine or hemitiroidectomy depending patient/nodule

Take-home: nodular autonomy rarely remits with a finite thionamide course; definitive therapy matters.

### Thyroiditis and factitious thyrotoxicosis

Thyroiditis:

- beta-blocker if symptomatic
- NSAIDs for pain in mild/moderate subacute thyroiditis
- glucocorticoids if severe pain or poor response
- no antithyroid drugs for destructive thyroiditis

Factitious:

- stop exogenous source
- beta-block symptoms
- look for low uptake and low thyroglobulin

Take-home: low uptake saves the patient from the wrong treatment.

### Radioiodine

Uses:

- Graves in selected adults
- toxic multinodular goiter
- toxic adenoma

Contraindications:

- pregnancy
- lactation
- active/important ophthalmopathy requires caution or alternative
- suspicion of malignancy requires different pathway

Main consequence:

- hypothyroidism requiring levothyroxine

Take-home: radioiodine is definitive, but pregnancy/lactation are hard stops.

### Surgery

Indications:

- compressive goiter
- suspicion of malignancy
- large goiter/nodule or patient preference
- active significant ophthalmopathy where RAI is less attractive
- medication/RAI unsuitable
- pregnancy refractory/intolerant to ATDs: safest in second trimester

Preparation:

- render euthyroid with antithyroid drug when possible
- Lugol/iodide can be used before Graves surgery to reduce vascularity, per protocol

Complications:

- recurrent laryngeal nerve injury: dysphonia
- hypoparathyroidism/hypocalcemia: paresthesias, tetany
- hypothyroidism

Take-home: surgery is not just "last resort"; it is the right route in compression, cancer concern and selected ophthalmopathy/pregnancy contexts.

## 7. Tormenta tiroidea

### Suspect it when

- known/untreated hyperthyroidism or Graves
- fever
- marked tachycardia, often over 140
- agitation/delirium
- diarrhea/vomiting/dehydration
- heart failure or atrial fibrillation
- trigger: infection, surgery, delivery, contrast iodine, trauma, medication withdrawal

### Treatment sequence

| Step | Intervention | Why |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | beta-blocker | controls adrenergic toxicity; propranolol also reduces T4-to-T3 conversion |
| 2 | PTU or methimazole | blocks new synthesis; local exam favors PTU |
| 3 | iodine after thionamide | blocks release of stored hormone; must come after synthesis blockade |
| 4 | hydrocortisone/dexamethasone | reduces T4-to-T3 conversion and supports stress physiology |
| 5 | supportive care | cooling, fluids, oxygen, treat trigger, ICU-level monitoring |

Local ENAM storm lock:

- PTU loading 600 mg then repeated dosing
- Lugol/iodide 1-2 hours after PTU
- propranolol for adrenergic control
- hydrocortisone or dexamethasone
- paracetamol for fever
- avoid aspirin

Take-home: iodine is not first. Fever drug in Residentado is paracetamol, not aspirin.

## 8. Pregnancy and special populations

### Pregnancy

Core rules:

- mild gestational thyrotoxicosis can be monitored if mother/fetus are well
- if antithyroid drug is needed early pregnancy, PTU is preferred
- use the lowest effective dose to keep maternal free T4 high-normal or mildly elevated
- radioiodine is contraindicated
- surgery, if needed, is safest in the second trimester
- beta-blockers can be used briefly for significant symptoms, not as long-term casual therapy

QA note:

- ATA has a 2026 updated pregnancy guideline. Before this package becomes official manual/class ground truth, pregnancy details must be reconciled with the 2026 document.

Take-home: pregnancy is not "untreated Graves"; it is controlled minimal-dose therapy with fetal protection.

### Older adult

Think hyperthyroidism in:

- new atrial fibrillation
- unexplained heart failure
- weight loss
- muscle weakness
- apathy/depression without classic hyperactivity

Take-home: in older adults, the heart may be the thyroid symptom.

### Children/adolescents

Pattern:

- hyperactivity, insomnia, irritability, school decline
- tremor, warm wet skin, tachycardia, hyperreflexia
- can be confused with ADHD/anxiety

Take-home: behavior-only diagnosis is unsafe when there is tachycardia and hypermetabolic physiology.

## 9. Follow-up and prognosis

- Monitor free T4/T3 early because TSH can remain suppressed after treatment starts.
- Monitor TSH/free T4/free T3 periodically during antithyroid therapy.
- Check baseline CBC and liver function before antithyroid drugs in many guideline pathways.
- Educate patient to report fever, sore throat, jaundice, severe abdominal pain or rash.
- After radioiodine or surgery, monitor for hypothyroidism and replace with levothyroxine.
- In Graves, monitor relapse risk, ophthalmopathy, smoking and TRAb/TSI where relevant.
- In thyroiditis, follow for hypothyroid phase and recovery.

Take-home: follow-up tracks both overtreatment and undertreatment; "feels better" is not enough.

## 10. Local exam blueprints

| Stem | Expected answer |
|---|---|
| young woman, weight loss, palpitations, warm wet skin, diffuse goiter, exophthalmos | Graves-Basedow |
| TSI stimulates TSH receptor | Graves-Basedow |
| older adult, atrial fibrillation, multinodular gland | toxic multinodular goiter |
| single hot nodule suppresses rest | toxic adenoma |
| no goiter, weight-loss medication, TSH low, T4L high | factitious/yatrogenic thyrotoxicosis |
| child referred for ADHD but has tremor, insomnia, tachycardia, warm wet skin | hyperthyroidism |
| thyroid storm, fever treatment | paracetamol |
| thyroid storm, block release of preformed hormone | potassium iodide/Lugol after thionamide |
| painful thyroid after infection, high ESR/leukocytosis | thyroiditis boundary |
| pregnancy first trimester with Graves requiring ATD | PTU |
| adult nonpregnant Graves | methimazole in local exam frame |

Take-home: Residentado tests associations; ENAM tests the scenario-specific algorithm.

## 11. Must-not-confuse list

- Do not call all thyrotoxicosis "Graves."
- Do not use methimazole for destructive thyroiditis just because TSH is low.
- Do not give iodine before thionamide in thyroid storm.
- Do not use aspirin as fever drug in thyroid storm exam framing.
- Do not use radioiodine in pregnancy or lactation.
- Do not forget PTU in first trimester and storm.
- Do not forget methimazole is preferred in most nonpregnant adults.
- Do not miss factitious thyrotoxicosis when there is no goiter and weight-loss/iatrogenic context.
- Do not use TSH alone to decide etiology.
- Do not dismiss hyperthyroidism in a child or older adult because presentation is behavioral or cardiac.

Take-home: the safe student separates syndrome, cause and scenario before choosing the drug.

units.title: Asma bronquial
units.body:
# Asma bronquial

## Status

- note_type: enfermedad-condicion + emergencia-decision + farmaco-terapeutica
- topic_code: MI-NEU-04
- products: ENAM, Residentado, EsSalud, class/manual
- qa_status: qa_pending
- publish_status: fail_to_publish
- source_inputs: ENAM card 057, Residentado direct items, CN-274, CN-801, CN-991, GINA 2025, NHLBI 2020

## Take-home point

Asthma is not "wheezing." Asthma is variable respiratory symptoms plus variable expiratory airflow limitation. Chronic care must treat inflammation, while acute care must detect the patient who is running out of airflow.

## 1. Guion de enfermedad

### 1A. Por que da

Asthma is a chronic inflammatory airway disease with bronchial hyperresponsiveness and variable airflow obstruction. The airway narrows because smooth muscle contracts, mucosa becomes edematous, and mucus increases. The classic phenotype is allergic/type 2 inflammation, but asthma is heterogeneous.

Mechanism to remember:

```text
trigger -> airway inflammation/hyperreactivity -> bronchoconstriction + edema + mucus
  -> episodic obstruction -> wheeze/dyspnea/cough
  -> reversibility/variability over time
```

High-yield triggers include viral infections, allergens, cold air, exercise, smoke/irritants, occupational exposures, AINE/aspirin in susceptible patients, and poor controller adherence.

Take-home: beta-2 agonists open the airway fast, but ICS reduces inflammatory risk.

### 1B. A quien le da

Exam stems favor young adults or children with atopy: allergic rhinitis, dermatitis/eczema, family history, recurrent obstructive episodes, or allergen exposure. Dermatophagoides is a classic local exam allergen. Adult-onset asthma, occupational asthma, aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease, obesity-associated asthma, pregnancy and asthma-COPD overlap modify the frame.

Take-home: atopy raises probability, but diagnosis still needs variable symptoms and objective support when possible.

### 1C. Como se presenta

Typical symptoms are recurrent wheeze, shortness of breath, chest tightness and/or cough. They vary in intensity, often worsen at night or on waking, and are triggered by exercise, allergens, cold air or viral infection.

Common exam pattern:

- episodic cough/sibilancias/disnea
- nocturnal or early-morning symptoms
- improvement with bronchodilator
- obstructive spirometry such as low FEV1/FVC
- bronchodilator response or PEF variability

Danger pattern:

- cannot finish sentences
- cyanosis, exhaustion, agitation/confusion
- SatO2 low
- PEF/FEV1 low
- normal/rising PaCO2 in a severe-looking patient
- silent chest

Take-home: silent chest is not improvement; it means too little airflow to wheeze.

## 2. Manejo

### 2A. Diagnostico

Use two axes:

| Axis | What you need |
|---|---|
| Clinical axis | variable respiratory symptoms: wheeze, dyspnea, cough, chest tightness |
| Physiologic axis | variable expiratory airflow limitation: bronchodilator reversibility, PEF variability, bronchoprovocation, or improvement after ICS when objective testing is limited |

Classic confirmation:

- Spirometry shows obstruction.
- Bronchodilator response supports diagnosis. ENAM/CTO card: FEV1 increase >=12% after SABA. Current adult guideline framing usually adds >200 mL in adults.
- If spirometry is normal between symptoms, repeat during symptoms or use PEF diary/bronchoprovocation.
- FeNO/eosinophils can support type 2 inflammation, but do not diagnose asthma alone.

Exam key: if a stem asks "what test confirms asthma?" after obstructive spirometry, choose bronchodilator response test.

Take-home: one normal exam between attacks does not rule out asthma.

### 2B. Clasificacion

Do not mix these:

| Concept | What it answers |
|---|---|
| Severity of disease | how much treatment is needed to control it |
| Symptom control | symptoms, night waking, activity limitation, reliever need |
| Future risk | exacerbations, low lung function, SABA overuse, poor adherence, comorbidities |
| Crisis severity | how close the patient is to respiratory failure now |

Classic crisis severity for exams:

| Feature | Mild | Moderate | Severe | Life-threatening |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Speech | sentences | phrases | words/rest dyspnea | unable, confused/drowsy |
| Respiratory effort | mild | accessory muscles | marked tirage | paradoxical/poor effort |
| PEF/FEV1 | >70% | 50-70% | <50% | very low/unmeasurable |
| SatO2 | often normal | may fall | low | very low |
| Auscultation | wheeze | wheeze | loud or reduced wheeze | silent chest |
| CO2 | low | low/normal | normal can be bad | high = failure |

Take-home: classify the crisis by speech, oxygenation, airflow and exhaustion, not only by the word "sibilancias."

### 2C. Manejo cronico

Modern official principle: do not leave asthma on SABA-only treatment. Use ICS-containing therapy to reduce exacerbation risk.

| Treatment frame | What it means | When to teach it |
|---|---|---|
| GINA Track 1 | low-dose ICS-formoterol is the preferred reliever; Steps 1-2 use as-needed ICS-formoterol; Steps 3-5 use MART | class/manual official frame |
| GINA Track 2 | SABA or ICS-SABA reliever, with ICS-containing controller strategy; if SABA is used, ICS must be taken with/around it as indicated | alternative when Track 1 unavailable or unsuitable |
| NHLBI 2020 | mild persistent: daily low-dose ICS + SABA or as-needed ICS with SABA; moderate-severe persistent: SMART ICS-formoterol | US support frame |
| ENAM legacy | intermittent asthma may appear with SABA-only answer | mark as historical exam framing, not official safety truth |

Step logic:

1. Confirm diagnosis and assess control/risk.
2. Check inhaler technique and adherence before escalating.
3. Start or step up ICS-containing therapy based on symptoms/risk.
4. Step down only after sustained control, with action plan and monitoring.
5. Refer severe/uncontrolled asthma for phenotype assessment and add-ons.

Take-home: a controller plan without inhaler-technique check is an incomplete plan.

### 2D. Manejo de exacerbacion

Start assessment and treatment together.

Immediate sequence:

1. Assess severity: speech, mental status, FR/FC, SatO2, PEF/FEV1 if feasible.
2. Give inhaled SABA repeatedly.
3. Give oxygen if hypoxemic; current GINA target is 93-95% in adults/adolescents and >=94% in children 6-12, adjusted by altitude/context. Local ENAM material often uses >=92%.
4. Add ipratropium for moderate/severe crisis.
5. Give systemic corticosteroid for all except mild exacerbations.
6. Consider IV magnesium sulfate when severe/refractory or poor response to intensive initial therapy.
7. Transfer/UCI if silent chest, altered sensorium, exhaustion, persistent hypoxemia, rising CO2 or poor response.

Avoid routine antibiotics, sedatives, routine chest X-ray or blood gases unless an alternative diagnosis/complication is suspected.

Take-home: acute asthma is a reassessment loop, not a one-dose treatment.

### 2E. Complicaciones

Asthma complications include severe exacerbation, respiratory failure, atelectasis, pneumothorax/pneumomediastinum, medication adverse effects, recurrent steroid toxicity and asthma death. Local residentado has tested atelectasis after persistent crisis with focal absent breath sounds.

Medication complications:

- repeated beta-2 agonists: tremor, tachycardia, hypokalemia, arrhythmias
- systemic corticosteroids: hyperglycemia, leukocytosis, glycosuria, mood/sleep effects
- montelukast: neuropsychiatric warning in modern guidance contexts
- theophylline: narrow therapeutic index; historical association, not preferred acute care

Take-home: complications can come from the disease and from rescue therapy.

### 2F. Seguimiento

At every visit:

- symptom control and night waking
- reliever use and SABA overuse
- exacerbations/ED visits/oral steroid courses
- inhaler technique
- adherence and access
- triggers and comorbidities: rhinitis, GERD, obesity, smoking, occupational exposure, anxiety/vocal cord dysfunction
- spirometry/PEF when indicated
- written action plan

After exacerbation:

- reassess soon
- ensure ICS-containing maintenance
- check technique/adherence
- identify trigger and risk factors
- plan step-up/step-down

Take-home: post-crisis discharge without controller optimization is a setup for recurrence.

### 2G. Pronostico

Prognosis is good when diagnosis is correct, ICS-containing therapy is used, technique/adherence are strong, and triggers/comorbidities are controlled. Risk rises with prior severe exacerbation, SABA overuse, low lung function, poor adherence, smoking, psychosocial barriers, pregnancy without controller continuity, and asthma-COPD overlap.

Take-home: "few symptoms" does not equal "low risk" if the patient has SABA overuse or prior severe crisis.

## 3. Cluster comparativo de sibilancias

| Row | Asma | EPOC | Bronquiolitis | Cuerpo extrano | Anafilaxia |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Usual age/context | child/young adult, atopy | older smoker/biomass | infant <2 years, viral URI | sudden onset, choking | minutes after food/drug/sting |
| Tempo | episodic/recurrent | chronic progressive | acute viral days | abrupt | abrupt systemic |
| Sound | diffuse wheeze, variable | wheeze/ronchi, chronic | wheeze/crackles | unilateral wheeze or decreased breath sounds | wheeze plus upper airway/skin/GI/shock |
| Key proof | variable obstruction/reversibility | persistent post-BD obstruction | clinical viral syndrome | asymmetric exam/imaging/bronchoscopy | hypotension/urticaria/angioedema |
| First danger action | crisis algorithm | oxygen carefully + bronchodilators/steroids if exacerbation | oxygen/support | airway removal/referral | IM epinephrine |
| Trap | wheeze alone | calling all obstruction asthma | overusing bronchodilator as main therapy | missing unilateral clue | treating as asthma only |

Take-home: wheeze is a sound, not a diagnosis.

## 4. Mini-drills

1. Adult with nocturnal cough/wheeze, FEV1/FVC 60%, asked confirmatory test: bronchodilator response.
2. Asthmatic with cyanosis, hypotension, FR 30, SatO2 88%, silent chest: life-threatening crisis.
3. Severe crisis after repeated salbutamol develops arrhythmia: think hypokalemia.
4. Severe/refractory crisis after intensive initial therapy: consider IV magnesium sulfate.
5. Child with recurrent obstructive episodes, rhinitis and dermatitis atopic: asthma becomes likely.
6. Old exam asks intermittent asthma first-line and options include only SABA: answer may be SABA as exam legacy; class/manual must add ICS-containing modern safety frame.

## 5. Traceability

| Claim | Source trace |
|---|---|
| Definition and reversibility concept | ENAM card 057; GINA 2025 diagnosis table |
| Bronchodilator response test as confirmatory | RES-COMBINED-08065; CN-991 |
| Silent chest as life-threatening | RES-COMBINED-00111; GINA 2025 acute care guidance |
| Severe crisis/MgSO4 | RES-COMBINED-06039; CN-274; GINA 2025 exacerbation guidance |
| Hypokalemia from beta-2 agonists | RES-COMBINED-06089; RES-COMBINED-01574 |
| ICS-containing therapy and no SABA-only | GINA 2025; NHLBI 2020 |
| Pediatric persistent mild controller | RES-COMBINED-05818; NHLBI 2020 |
| Atelectasis complication | RES-COMBINED-07074 |

## QA note

This note is student-usable and exam-aligned, but remains `fail_to_publish` as official manual/class ground truth until dose tables, local oxygen targets, local formulary availability and SABA-only legacy wording are source-locked.

units.body:
# Sindrome nefrotico

## Status

- note_type: enfermedad-condicion + cluster-comparativo + mecanismo-basico
- topic_code: MI-NEF-03
- products: ENAM, Residentado, EsSalud, class/manual
- qa_status: qa_pending
- publish_status: fail_to_publish
- source_inputs: ENAM card 125, Residentado direct items, CN-263, CN-358, KDIGO 2021/2025, IPNA 2022/2023

## Take-home point

Sindrome nefrotico is a protein-loss syndrome: nephrotic-range proteinuria causes hypoalbuminemia, edema, lipid response and thrombotic/infectious risk. The exam win is to identify the syndrome first, then route cause by age and context.

## 1. Guion de enfermedad

### 1A. Por que da

The glomerular filtration barrier becomes abnormally permeable to protein. Massive proteinuria exceeds hepatic compensation, albumin falls, oncotic pressure drops, and edema appears. At the same time, the liver increases lipoprotein synthesis, causing hyperlipidemia and lipiduria.

Mechanism chain:

```text
glomerular barrier injury -> proteinuria >3.5 g/day
  -> hypoalbuminemia -> edema
  -> hepatic lipoprotein synthesis -> hyperlipidemia/lipiduria
  -> loss of anticoagulant and immune proteins -> thrombosis/infection
```

Edema has two complementary explanations:

- Underfill: low albumin lowers oncotic pressure and effective circulating volume, activating RAAS/ADH.
- Overfill: primary renal sodium retention, including ENaC and Na+/K+-ATPase activation in collecting duct.

Take-home: the edema is both protein physics and sodium biology.

### 1B. A quien le da

The likely cause changes by age/context:

| Context | Likely cause |
|---|---|
| Child 2-10 years with pure nephrotic syndrome | minimal change disease |
| Adult 40-60 years with nephrotic syndrome | membranous nephropathy is classic exam cause |
| Adult with obesity, HIV, heroin, reduced nephron mass | FSGS/secondary FSGS |
| Adult with long-standing DM + retinopathy | diabetic nephropathy |
| Older adult or chronic inflammatory disease | amyloidosis |
| Young woman/systemic symptoms/complement changes | lupus nephritis or secondary disease |

Take-home: "child = minimal change; adult = membranous" is the exam anchor, but context can override it.

### 1C. Como se presenta

Classic nephrotic syndrome:

- generalized edema, often periorbital in the morning and lower limb/anasarca later
- foamy urine
- proteinuria >3.5 g/day or equivalent nephrotic range
- hypoalbuminemia/hypoproteinemia
- hyperlipidemia
- lipiduria with fatty casts/Maltese crosses
- initially preserved GFR in many pure forms
- PA normal or low in pure nephrotic syndrome

Impure features:

- HTA
- hematuria
- reduced GFR/AKI
- low complement or systemic symptoms

Take-home: HTA, hematuria and low GFR make the case less "pure" and raise biopsy/referral suspicion.

## 2. Manejo

### 2A. Diagnostico

Diagnose the syndrome before naming the glomerulopathy.

| Step | What to confirm |
|---|---|
| 1 | nephrotic-range proteinuria |
| 2 | hypoalbuminemia |
| 3 | edema and/or hyperlipidemia/lipiduria |
| 4 | renal function, BP, hematuria, complement and systemic clues |
| 5 | age/context etiology and biopsy decision |

Useful tests:

- urinalysis and sediment
- urine protein/creatinine ratio or 24-hour protein
- serum albumin and lipid profile
- creatinine/eGFR, electrolytes
- complement, ANA/anti-dsDNA if lupus suspected
- hepatitis B/C, HIV, diabetes evaluation when relevant
- anti-PLA2R in adult suspected membranous nephropathy
- renal biopsy in adults/atypical cases unless a recognized exception applies

Take-home: proteinuria tells you syndrome; age/context plus serology/biopsy tells you cause.

### 2B. Clasificacion

| Axis | Categories |
|---|---|
| Pure vs impure | pure = proteinuria/edema with no HTA/hematuria/GFR fall; impure = HTA, hematuria or renal impairment |
| Primary vs secondary | primary glomerular disease vs diabetes, lupus, infections, drugs, malignancy, amyloid |
| Pediatric vs adult | children often minimal change; adults need broader workup |
| Steroid-sensitive vs resistant | pediatric and podocytopathy treatment-response classification |
| Thrombotic/infectious risk | albumin depth, proteinuria severity, membranous nephropathy, immobility, prior thrombosis |

Take-home: "nephrotic" is a syndrome label, not a final diagnosis.

### 2C. Etiologias clave

| Disease | Typical exam frame | Pathology/lab clue | Management direction |
|---|---|---|---|
| Minimal change disease | child with pure SN, complement normal | LM normal, IF negative, EM foot process effacement | steroids; no initial biopsy in typical child |
| Membranous nephropathy | adult male 40-60 with nephrotic syndrome | anti-PLA2R, subepithelial deposits, spikes, granular IgG/C3 | supportive + risk-based immunosuppression |
| FSGS | adult, obesity/HIV/heroin; worse prognosis | focal segmental sclerosis; primary has diffuse foot process effacement and nephrotic syndrome | primary may need steroids/CNI; secondary supportive |
| Diabetic nephropathy | long-standing DM + retinopathy | Kimmelstiel-Wilson, progressive albuminuria/proteinuria | glycemic/BP/proteinuria control; no biopsy if typical |
| Amyloidosis | older/chronic inflammatory/plasma cell context | Congo red, apple-green birefringence | treat underlying disease |
| Lupus nephritis | systemic lupus clues, low complement | immune-complex GN | lupus-specific regimen, biopsy class |

Take-home: minimal change and membranous are the exam prototypes, but diabetic nephropathy/FSGS/lupus are the trap contexts.

### 2D. Manejo general

Supportive measures:

- salt restriction
- fluid restriction when clinically indicated, especially severe edema/hyponatremia/poor effective volume states
- loop diuretics for edema, carefully if intravascular depletion
- albumin plus diuretic only in selected severe edema/hypovolemia contexts
- ACE inhibitor/ARB or other antiproteinuric therapy when appropriate
- SGLT2 inhibitor may be part of modern proteinuric CKD care in selected adults, but source-lock by etiology/eGFR/diabetes context
- statin if persistent clinically significant dyslipidemia
- vaccination and infection prevention according to immunosuppression risk
- anticoagulation only individualized, not automatic
- etiology-specific therapy

Take-home: edema relief is not the same as disease control.

### 2E. Complicaciones

| Complication | Mechanism | Exam clue |
|---|---|---|
| Thrombosis, including renal vein thrombosis/PE | urinary loss of antithrombin and hypercoagulability; risk high in MN and low albumin | flank pain/hematuria/AKI or dyspnea/pleuritic pain |
| Infection | urinary loss of immune proteins plus edema/immunosuppression | peritonitis/cellulitis/sepsis risk |
| AKI/hypovolemia | low effective volume, aggressive diuresis, renal vein thrombosis | hypotension, oliguria, rising creatinine |
| Dyslipidemia | hepatic lipoprotein overproduction | LDL/VLDL high, lipiduria |
| Malnutrition/growth issues | chronic protein loss and steroid burden | pediatric chronic disease |
| Drug toxicity | steroids, CNI, cyclophosphamide, diuretics | requires source-lock |

Take-home: the danger of nephrotic syndrome is not just swelling; it is clot, infection and kidney injury.

### 2F. Seguimiento

Track:

- weight, edema, BP, urine output
- proteinuria trend
- serum albumin
- creatinine/eGFR and electrolytes
- lipids
- infection/thrombosis symptoms
- medication adverse effects
- vaccine/immunosuppression status
- relapse frequency in children
- anti-PLA2R trend in PLA2R-positive membranous nephropathy

Take-home: proteinuria trend is the pulse of the syndrome.

### 2G. Pronostico

Minimal change disease has excellent prognosis when steroid-responsive, though relapses are common. Membranous nephropathy can remit spontaneously or progress; prognosis depends on proteinuria, albumin, kidney function and immunologic activity. FSGS prognosis depends strongly on whether it is primary vs secondary/genetic and whether remission occurs. Diabetic nephropathy prognosis depends on glycemic/BP/proteinuria control and CKD stage.

Take-home: remission of proteinuria predicts kidney survival better than the label alone.

## 3. Cluster comparativo: nefrotico vs nefritico

| Row | Sindrome nefrotico | Sindrome nefritico |
|---|---|---|
| Main leak | protein | blood/inflammatory cells |
| Proteinuria | >3.5 g/day or nephrotic range | usually subnephrotic |
| Edema mechanism | hypoalbuminemia + sodium retention | salt/water retention from reduced GFR |
| Hematuria | absent or mild | prominent, dysmorphic RBC/casts |
| BP | normal/low in pure SN; may be high if impure | high |
| GFR | often preserved early | reduced/AKI |
| Lipids | hyperlipidemia/lipiduria | not defining |
| Child prototype | minimal change disease | post-strep GN |
| Adult prototype | membranous nephropathy | vasculitis/lupus/rapid GN patterns |

Take-home: nephrotic is "protein-lipid-edema"; nephritic is "blood-pressure-AKI."

## 4. Mini-drills

1. Child with periorbital edema, heavy proteinuria, normal complement, no HTA/hematuria: minimal change disease.
2. Adult male with nephrotic syndrome and PLA2R positive: membranous nephropathy likely.
3. Long-standing DM with retinopathy and proteinuria: diabetic nephropathy, biopsy often avoided if typical.
4. Nephrotic edema mechanism asks renal sodium retention: ENaC and Na+/K+-ATPase activation.
5. Edema + hematuria + HTA + falling GFR: nephrotic impuro or nephritic overlap; do not call pure minimal change.
6. Adult MCD diagnosis: biopsy, not clinical assumption.

## 5. Traceability

| Claim | Source trace |
|---|---|
| Proteinuria >3.5 g/day and classic syndrome cascade | ENAM card 125 |
| Edema ENaC/Na-K-ATPase mechanism | RES-COMBINED-00139; CN-358 |
| Pediatric 50% fluid requirement exam key | RES-COMBINED-01425; CN-263 |
| Child NCM, adult MN prototypes | ENAM card 125 |
| Adult MCD biopsy and high-dose steroids | KDIGO 2021 MCD key takeaways |
| MN PLA2R and risk-based therapy | KDIGO 2021 MN key takeaways |
| FSGS primary vs secondary immunosuppression split | KDIGO 2021 FSGS key takeaways |
| Pediatric update | KDIGO 2025 nephrotic syndrome in children; IPNA SSNS |

## QA note

This note is student-usable and exam-aligned, but remains `fail_to_publish` as official manual/class ground truth until pediatric steroid regimens, fluid restriction, biopsy exceptions, anticoagulation thresholds and immunosuppression pathways are source-locked against KDIGO/local protocol.
