units.title: Prevencion de la Salud
units.body:
# Prevencion de la Salud

## Identidad exam-first

Tema Oro de Salud Publica. Entra como clasificacion de intervenciones, tamizaje, vacunacion y gestion de coberturas. El banco no quiere poesia sanitaria: quiere que ubiques el momento de la historia natural y el objetivo de la intervencion.

Take-home global: prevencion es una decision de tiempo y dano, no una etiqueta moral.

## Guion

### 1. Por que da: concepto preguntable

La enfermedad no aparece de golpe en el examen. El marco clasico asume una historia natural: determinantes, exposicion, enfermedad subclinica, enfermedad clinica, complicaciones y dano. La prevencion interviene en esa linea de tiempo para evitar aparicion, detectar temprano, limitar dano o evitar dano por exceso medico.

Take-home: la pregunta no es "sirve?", sino "en que momento de la historia natural actua?".

### 2. A quien: sujeto epidemiologico

El sujeto no siempre es un paciente. Puede ser una comunidad, poblacion sana, grupo de riesgo, persona asintomatica, paciente con enfermedad establecida o paciente expuesto a intervenciones innecesarias.

Take-home: cambia el sujeto y cambia el nivel de prevencion.

### 3. Como aparece en el banco

El enunciado suele darte una accion concreta y pedir nivel de prevencion o medida de gestion:

- Vacunacion, aislamiento, control vectorial, barreras -> primaria.
- Tamizaje, gota gruesa, prueba en asintomaticos, campana que detecta casos -> secundaria.
- Rehabilitacion, farmacos post-evento para evitar complicaciones, control de secuelas -> terciaria.
- Evitar antibioticos, imagenes, tamizajes o tratamientos innecesarios -> cuaternaria.
- Educacion, politicas publicas, entornos saludables, accion comunitaria -> promocion.

Take-home: si el caso ya detecto enfermedad oculta, la respuesta suele moverse a secundaria.

## Manejo

### 1. Diagnostico: clasificar la intervencion

| Momento | Pregunta | Nivel |
|---|---|---|
| Antes del riesgo individual | Como crear salud o capacidad? | Promocion |
| Antes de enfermar | Como evitar aparicion? | Primaria |
| Enfermedad subclinica/asintomatica | Como detectar temprano? | Secundaria |
| Enfermedad establecida | Como evitar complicacion, discapacidad o muerte? | Terciaria |
| Exceso diagnostico/terapeutico | Como evitar iatrogenia? | Cuaternaria |

Take-home: el "diagnostico" del nivel se hace por timeline.

### 2. Clasificacion

#### Leavell-Clark clasico

- Prevencion primaria: promocion de la salud y proteccion especifica.
- Prevencion secundaria: diagnostico precoz, tratamiento oportuno y limitacion del dano.
- Prevencion terciaria: rehabilitacion.

#### Uso moderno para examen

- Promocion: upstream; fortalece determinantes, capacidades y entornos.
- Primaria: evita incidencia.
- Secundaria: detecta enfermedad precoz y puede reducir duracion/prevalencia.
- Terciaria: evita complicaciones, discapacidad y eventos posteriores.
- Cuaternaria: evita sobrediagnostico, sobretratamiento e iatrogenia.

Take-home: promocion y primaria pueden convivir, pero no son sinonimos perfectos.

### 3. Manejo programatico

#### Si la medida es tamizaje

Verifica cuatro condiciones:

1. La poblacion objetivo esta asintomatica o no diagnosticada.
2. La enfermedad es importante y tiene historia natural conocida.
3. Existe prueba aceptable, valida, segura y factible.
4. Detectar antes cambia desenlaces porque hay tratamiento o intervencion efectiva.

En tamizaje secuencial, el primer test debe priorizar sensibilidad para no perder casos; el segundo confirma con mayor especificidad.

Take-home: screening sin tratamiento efectivo solo fabrica diagnosticos.

#### Si la medida es vacunacion

En examen conceptual, vacuna casi siempre es primaria: evita aparicion de enfermedad. En examen normativo peruano, el calendario debe tener fecha y fuente vigente. Para 2026, MINSA lista VPH como dosis unica 9-18 anos y mantiene esquemas por edad para recien nacido, lactante, nino, adolescente, gestante, adulto mayor y grupos de riesgo.

Take-home: vacuna es primaria, pero calendario es fuente viva.

#### Si la medida es gestion de cobertura

La respuesta no siempre es "vacunar". Si el problema es cobertura menor a meta sin desabastecimiento, piensa como programa: corregir estrategias, mejorar captacion, seguimiento nominal, barrido, monitoreo y cierre de brechas.

Take-home: baja cobertura es problema de sistema, no solo de conocimiento individual.

### 4. Complicaciones y sesgos

Riesgos del mal uso de prevencion:

- Falsos positivos y ansiedad.
- Falsos negativos y falsa seguridad.
- Lead-time bias: parece sobrevivir mas porque se diagnostico antes.
- Length bias: el screening detecta mas enfermedades lentas.
- Sobrediagnostico: detectar enfermedad que nunca habria causado dano.
- Sobretratamiento e iatrogenia.
- Uso ineficiente de recursos.

Take-home: no todo screening mejora mortalidad.

### 5. Seguimiento

Indicadores utiles:

- Cobertura de intervencion.
- Incidencia para primaria.
- Proporcion de positivos, confirmacion y perdida de seguimiento para tamizaje.
- Complicaciones, reingresos, discapacidad y funcion para terciaria.
- Tasa de examenes/tratamientos innecesarios y eventos adversos para cuaternaria.
- Cadena de frio, ESAVI y oportunidad de dosis para vacunacion.

Take-home: un programa preventivo se mide por desenlaces, no solo por actividades.

### 6. Pronostico sanitario

La promocion cambia determinantes y resiliencia comunitaria. La primaria reduce incidencia. La secundaria puede reducir morbimortalidad si la deteccion temprana modifica el curso. La terciaria reduce secuelas y nuevos eventos. La cuaternaria protege al paciente y al sistema de dano evitable.

Take-home: cada nivel tiene un desenlace esperado distinto.

## Cluster comparativo

| Pregunta | Promocion | Primaria | Secundaria | Terciaria | Cuaternaria |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Blanco | determinantes | factor causal/riesgo | enfermedad oculta | dano establecido | dano medico |
| Poblacion | comunidad | sano/en riesgo | asintomatico | enfermo | sobreexpuesto |
| Verbo | empoderar/crear condiciones | evitar aparicion | detectar temprano | limitar secuelas | evitar exceso |
| Ejemplo | escuela saludable | vacuna | sangre oculta en heces | rehabilitacion post-ACV | no RMN lumbar sin alarma |
| Trampa | suena a educacion | campana no cambia nivel | tamizaje no es diagnostico clinico | no todo tratamiento es terciario | no es abandono |

## Mini-drills

1. Gestantes en campana, Hb 9.5, se inicia tratamiento. Respuesta: secundaria.
2. Beta-bloqueador despues de IAM para evitar complicaciones. Respuesta: terciaria.
3. Comunidad sin COVID bloquea ingreso de foraneos. Respuesta: primaria.
4. Gota gruesa para detectar malaria. Respuesta: secundaria.
5. Zona con riesgo de fiebre amarilla y pregunta por control poblacional. Respuesta probable: monitoreo/cierre de coberturas de vacunacion.

## Traceability

- ENAM: card 092, prevencion de la salud.
- Residentado: `RES-COMBINED-03992`, `05853`, `07032`, `08040`, `08074`.
- Oficial vigente: MINSA esquema nacional de vacunacion, actualizado 22 Apr 2026.
- Marco internacional: WHO health promotion glossary, Wilson-Jungner, CDC prevention levels.

## QA de publicacion

La nota conceptual es utilizable para clase. La parte de calendario vacunal no debe publicarse como tabla final hasta cerrar source-lock de normas 2025-2026 y reconciliar ENAM antiguo con MINSA vigente.

units.title: Patologia de cadera
units.body:
# Patologia de cadera

## Identidad exam-first

Tema Oro de Traumatologia. No funciona como una sola enfermedad: es un cluster de fractura, luxacion, DDC, NAV y cadera infantil/adolescente. El examen te da edad, mecanismo, posicion del miembro o edad de imagen; tu tarea es no mezclar columnas.

Take-home global: cadera se resuelve por edad + mecanismo + posicion + imagen.

## Guion

### 1. Por que da: fisiopatologia y concepto preguntable

La cadera falla por tres rutas principales:

- Ruta mecanica/traumatica: fractura, luxacion, acetabulo, implante.
- Ruta biologica/vascular: cabeza femoral con vascularizacion vulnerable, sobre todo cuello femoral desplazado, luxacion y NAV.
- Ruta de desarrollo/crecimiento: DDC, Perthes y epifisiolisis.

Take-home: la cabeza femoral es el organo vulnerable; su perfusion manda el pronostico.

### 2. A quien: epidemiologia y factores de riesgo

| Perfil | Diagnostico que debes activar |
|---|---|
| Mujer anciana + osteoporosis + caida | Fractura de cadera |
| Adulto joven + accidente de transito | Luxacion posterior de cadera |
| RN/lactante femenino, nalgas, familiar | DDC |
| Nino 4-9 anos, varon, claudicacion | Perthes |
| Adolescente obeso, varon | Epifisiolisis femoral proximal |
| Adulto con corticoides/alcohol/lupus/drepanocitosis | NAV |

Take-home: en cadera, la edad casi te entrega la mitad del diagnostico.

### 3. Como: presentacion clinica frecuente

| Hallazgo | Lectura |
|---|---|
| Acortamiento + rotacion externa + impotencia | Fractura de cadera |
| Flexion + aduccion + rotacion interna | Luxacion posterior |
| Abduccion + rotacion externa + alargamiento | Luxacion anterior |
| Ortolani/Barlow positivos | DDC sospechada |
| Limitacion rotacion interna/abduccion en nino | Perthes o SCFE segun edad |
| Fiebre + no camina + dolor intenso | Artritis septica hasta demostrar lo contrario |
| Rx normal + dolor insidioso + corticoides/alcohol | NAV precoz |

Take-home: la posicion del miembro separa fractura de luxacion.

## Manejo

### 1. Diagnostico

Empieza por radiografia en trauma adulto. En fractura de cadera sospechada con Rx negativa, usa MRI; CT si MRI no esta disponible o esta contraindicada. En DDC temprana, el banco usa ecografia durante los primeros meses porque la cabeza femoral no esta bien osificada. En NAV precoz, RMN gana sobre Rx.

Take-home: cada entidad tiene una prueba que falla temprano; saber cual falla evita el distractor.

### 2. Clasificacion

#### Fractura

- Intracapsular: cuello/cabeza femoral; problema biologico por perfusion; riesgo NAV y pseudoartrosis.
- Extracapsular: trocanter/subtrocanter; problema mecanico; riesgo consolidacion viciosa o falla de implante.
- Garden I-II: no desplazada.
- Garden III-IV: desplazada.

#### Luxacion

- Posterior: mas frecuente; flexion, aduccion, rotacion interna; riesgo ciatico y NAV.
- Anterior: abduccion, rotacion externa; riesgo paquete femoral.
- Central: puede dar ligero acortamiento y se vincula a lesion acetabular.

#### Cadera infantil/adolescente

- DDC: RN/lactante, mujer, Ortolani/Barlow, imagen por edad.
- Perthes: nino 4-9, varon, claudicacion, limita rotacion interna.
- SCFE/epifisiolisis: adolescente obeso, dolor cadera/rodilla, marcha antalgica, fijacion in situ.
- Artritis septica: fiebre/toxicidad, urgencia.
- Sinovitis transitoria: post-viral, afebril, autolimitada.

Take-home: la clasificacion no es decorativa; cambia la conducta.

### 3. Manejo terapeutico

| Diagnostico | Conducta exam-first |
|---|---|
| Garden I-II | Osteosintesis con tornillos canulados |
| Garden III-IV joven | Osteosintesis, preservar cabeza |
| Garden III-IV anciano | Artroplastia: hemi o total segun funcion/comorbilidad |
| Extracapsular | Osteosintesis; dispositivo segun patron |
| Luxacion traumatica | Reduccion cerrada urgente bajo anestesia, ideal <6 h |
| DDC <6 meses | Imagen + arnes de Pavlik si confirmada |
| DDC 6-12 meses | Reduccion cerrada + yeso; abierta si falla |
| DDC >12 meses | Reduccion abierta + osteotomias |
| NAV I-II | Descompresion/forage +/- injerto |
| NAV III-IV | Artroplastia si dolor/colapso |
| SCFE | Epifisiodesis/fijacion in situ |
| Artritis septica | Drenaje urgente + ATB IV |

Take-home: joven desplazado no equivale a protesis; anciano desplazado no equivale a tornillos.

### 4. Complicaciones

- Intracapsular desplazada: NAV y pseudoartrosis.
- Extracapsular: consolidacion viciosa, falla de implante.
- Luxacion posterior: ciatico, NAV, coxartrosis.
- DDC/Pavlik mal manejado: NAV de epifisis femoral.
- NAV: colapso, artrosis secundaria.
- Fractura de cadera en anciano: delirium, TVP/TEP, neumonia, ulceras, perdida funcional.
- Artritis septica: dano cartilaginoso, crecimiento alterado, disfuncion permanente.

Take-home: muchas preguntas de cadera son preguntas de complicacion vascular.

### 5. Seguimiento necesario

Fractura/luxacion requieren control neurovascular, imagen post-reduccion o postoperatoria, profilaxis tromboembolica, movilizacion temprana y rehabilitacion. DDC requiere seguimiento clinico e imagenologico para confirmar reduccion y evitar AVN. Perthes/SCFE/NAV requieren vigilancia de rango articular, dolor, progresion radiologica y necesidad de cirugia preservadora o artroplastia.

Take-home: resolver la cadera no termina en la reduccion; termina cuando preservaste perfusion, congruencia y funcion.

### 6. Pronostico

Mejora cuando el diagnostico es temprano, la reduccion no se retrasa, la cabeza femoral no colapsa y la rehabilitacion evita perdida funcional. Empeora con demora >6 h en luxacion, fractura intracapsular desplazada en anciano, NAV avanzada, DDC tardia y artritis septica no drenada.

Take-home: tiempo + perfusion + congruencia articular predicen desenlace.

## Cluster comparativo

| Fila | Fractura cadera | Luxacion cadera | DDC | Perthes | SCFE | NAV |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Edad | anciano | joven trauma | RN/lactante | 4-9 anos | adolescente | adulto 30-60 |
| Pista | caida | tablero/alta energia | nalgas/femenino | claudica | obeso/dolor rodilla | corticoides/alcohol |
| Posicion | rotacion externa | posterior: rotacion interna | abduccion limitada | limita RI/ABD | rotacion externa obligada | dolor con Rx normal |
| Imagen | Rx; MRI si oculta | Rx + CT postreduccion si duda | eco <4m, Rx >4m | Rx/RMN | Rx AP/lateral | RMN precoz |
| Tratamiento | Garden/edad | reduccion urgente | Pavlik o reduccion | contencion/ROM | fijacion in situ | estadio Ficat |
| Trampa | anciano + todo = artroplastia | confundir con fractura | Ortolani no confirma imagen | confundir con sinovitis | dolor de rodilla | Rx normal no descarta |

## Mini-drills

1. Anciana Garden IV: artroplastia.
2. Joven Garden III: osteosintesis con tornillos.
3. Extracapsular pertrocanterica: osteosintesis, no artroplastia por defecto.
4. Accidente de transito, flexion + aduccion + rotacion interna: luxacion posterior.
5. DDC 1-4 meses: ecografia segun banco.
6. DDC <6 meses tratada con arnes, complicacion grave: NAV epifisis femoral.
7. `RES-COMBINED-05886`: clave local Ortolani positivo, pero stem usa "descartar"; tratar como conflicto de banco.

## Traceability

- ENAM: card 050, card 011, card 132.
- Residentado: `RES-COMBINED-00153`, `01408`, `05886`, `00110`, `07739`.
- Guias externas: NICE CG124, AAOS hip fracture, AAOS DDH, AAOS hip dislocation, AAOS Perthes, AAOS SCFE, AAOS osteonecrosis.

## QA de publicacion

Nota usable para clase y manual exam-first. Queda `qa_pending` para protocolo clinico final por conflictos ENAM-vs-guia en implantes extracapsulares y por item Residentado con wording inconsistente.

El examen te da edad, mecanismo, posicion del miembro o edad de imagen; tu tarea es no mezclar columnas. Take-home global: cadera se resuelve por edad + mecanismo + posicion + imagen. La cadera falla por tres rutas principales: - Ruta mecanica/traumatica: fractura, luxacion, acetabulo, implante. - Ruta biologica/vascular: cabeza femoral con vascularizacion vulnerable, sobre todo cuello femoral desplazado, luxacion y NAV. - Ruta de desarrollo/crecimiento:

units.title: Tuberculosis
units.body:
# Tuberculosis

## Exam identity

Tuberculosis is an airborne mycobacterial disease that exams usually test as an algorithm: suspicion -> diagnostic test -> classification -> regimen -> monitoring/contact control. The highest-yield move is separating active TB, latent TB infection and simple exposure.

Takehome: TB is not one diagnosis; it is a routing problem.

## Guion

### 1. Why it happens

- Mycobacterium tuberculosis is transmitted by airborne nuclei from contagious pulmonary/laryngeal disease.
- Initial infection can be contained in granulomas, producing latent infection.
- Reactivation occurs when immune control falls; cavitation increases bacillary burden and transmission.
- Primary complex: pneumonitis/focus, lymphangitis and hilar adenitis.
- Resistance appears by inadequate treatment, poor adherence or transmission of resistant strains.

Takehome: cavitation and resistance are consequences of uncontrolled bacillary ecology.

### 2. Who gets it

- Higher-yield risk groups: close contacts, HIV, diabetes, malnutrition, immunosuppression, children under 5, people with prior TB or treatment interruption.
- Children often have low bacillary load and cannot produce sputum, so contact history becomes diagnostic weight.
- HIV can have atypical imaging and lower PPD thresholds.
- Prior liver disease changes baseline safety evaluation before treatment.

Takehome: in TB, host risk changes the diagnostic threshold.

### 3. How it presents

- Pulmonary TB: productive cough, hemoptysis, fever, night sweats, weight loss, asthenia and apical lung findings.
- Case presumptive in the local ENAM card: at least two compatible symptoms; symptomatic respiratory is classically cough for more than 2 weeks.
- Reactivation radiology: apical/posterior upper-lobe disease, cavitation, fibrotic nodules, tree-in-bud.
- Primary TB: any lobe, hilar/mediastinal adenopathy, pleural effusion, Ghon focus plus node.
- Miliary TB: diffuse bilateral 1-2 mm nodules.
- Extrapulmonary TB: pleural, ganglionic, CNS, genitourinary, abdominal/peritoneal, osteoarticular.
- Pediatric TB: chronic cough, fever over 2 weeks, weight loss/failure to thrive, contact history.

Takehome: chronic respiratory plus constitutional symptoms is TB until routed correctly.

## Manejo

### 1. Diagnostico

- If PDRm/GeneXpert is available, use it early because it detects MTB and rifampicin resistance rapidly.
- If PDRm is unavailable, do bacilloscopy, usually two serial sputum samples.
- Bacilloscopy grading:
  - 0 BAAR in 100 fields: negative.
  - 1-9 BAAR in 100 fields: positive exact count, paucibacillary.
  - 10-99 BAAR in 100 fields: positive +.
  - 1-10 BAAR per field in 50 fields: positive ++.
  - More than 10 BAAR per field in 20 fields: positive +++.
- If two BK are negative but clinical probability remains high, order PDRm and culture.
- Culture is slower but important for confirmation and susceptibility.
- PPD/TST and IGRA diagnose infection; they do not prove active pulmonary TB.
- PPD local thresholds from ENAM card: positive at >=10 mm general; >=5 mm in immunodeficiency contexts such as HIV, severe malnutrition or relevant immunosuppression.
- Urine LAM is a HIV-specific tool in severe immunosuppression contexts; do not use it as a general non-HIV screening test.

Takehome: negative BK does not kill TB when the phenotype still screams TB.

### 2. Clasificacion

- Disease state: exposure, latent TB infection, active TB disease.
- Site: pulmonary vs extrapulmonary.
- Treatment history: new, relapse, recovered after loss to follow-up, failure.
- Drug pattern: drug-susceptible, H-resistant, RR/MDR, pre-XDR, XDR.
- Host modifier: child, pregnancy, HIV, liver disease, renal disease, severe extrapulmonary site.

Takehome: the regimen is chosen after classification, never before.

### 3. Manejo terapeutico

- Drug-susceptible TB in current local ENAM/NTS 221 framing: 2HREZ/4HR, 150 doses, with supervised treatment.
- Start treatment promptly after diagnosis; the local card states within 24 hours for TB-DS.
- Add pyridoxine with isoniazid. ENAM local card uses B6 50 mg/day with each H dose.
- DOT/TOS means each dose is observed and recorded.
- Extend continuation for CNS, miliary and osteoarticular TB per local card: 2HREZ/10HR, total 300 doses.
- Selected non-severe pediatric TB can use a shortened regimen in current norm framing.
- TB-Hr and TB-DR require programmatic/expert route; do not reduce them to "add one drug."
- TPT depends on contact status, age, drug resistance exposure and active TB exclusion.

Takehome: TB treatment is a public-health contract, not a private prescription list.

### 4. Complicaciones

- Disease complications: hemoptysis, cavitation, respiratory destruction, miliary disease, meningitis, pericarditis, pleural disease, intestinal/peritoneal disease, osteoarticular disease.
- Treatment complications:
  - Isoniazid: neuropathy/B6 depletion, hepatitis.
  - Rifampicin: orange body fluids, interactions, hepatotoxicity.
  - Pyrazinamide: hepatotoxicity, hyperuricemia.
  - Ethambutol: optic neuritis.
- Program complications: failure, relapse, loss to follow-up, resistance amplification.

Takehome: adverse-effect stems usually test the drug nickname, not pharmacology trivia.

### 5. Seguimiento

- Monitor bacteriologic response with BK/culture logic according to program pathway.
- Do not use PDRm to monitor response.
- Failure: bacteriology positive at month 5 or later in local ENAM card.
- Loss to follow-up: interruption for at least 2 consecutive months.
- Conversion: two negative cultures, or in DS two negative BK with 30-day interval.
- Trace contacts, rule out active disease and decide TPT.

Takehome: follow-up is where TB becomes epidemiology.

### 6. Pronostico

- Prognosis is good when disease is drug-susceptible, diagnosed early and treatment is completed.
- Prognosis worsens with HIV, malnutrition, CNS/miliary disease, delayed diagnosis, poor adherence and resistance.

Takehome: the exam asks prognosis through adherence, site and resistance.

## Cluster table

| Feature | Active pulmonary TB | Latent TB infection | Pediatric TB | Extrapulmonary TB | TB-DR |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Key clue | Chronic cough + constitutional symptoms | Positive PPD/IGRA, no disease | Contact + nonspecific symptoms | Organ-specific TB syndrome | Resistance test or failure |
| First route | PDRm if available; BK if not | Exclude active disease first | Contact/CXR/scoring + samples | Site-specific fluid/tissue | Rapid resistance + susceptibility |
| Typical trap | Culture as first answer | Calling ILTB "active TB" | Negative PPD rules out TB | Sputum-only thinking | Treating as simple DS TB |
| Treatment | 2HREZ/4HR if DS | TPT | TPT or pediatric regimen | DS regimen or extended by site | Expert/program regimen |

## Mini-drills

1. Cough 3 weeks, fever, night sweats, asthenia, apical findings -> pulmonary TB phenotype.
2. Two BK negative but high clinical probability -> PDRm and culture.
3. BK +++ and sensitive regimen -> 2HREZ/4HR.
4. Child contact, PPD 12 mm, asymptomatic, normal CXR -> latent TB infection.
5. Chronic ascites, lymphocytes, high protein, low SAAG -> peritoneal TB; biopsy confirms.
6. Weakness, paresthesias, stomatitis on anti-TB therapy -> isoniazid effect; think pyridoxine.

## Product modifiers

- Old Residentado `2RHZE/4R3H3` is a historical exam answer, not current default teaching.
- Old pediatric ILTB equals "isoniazid" is a simplification; current TPT has multiple regimens.
- Pregnancy regimen details must be page-locked to the current Peru norm before being used in public MCQ.
- ENCAPS CIS-2.11 remains source-gated; do not use it as unrestricted normative truth.

units.title: Amenorreas
units.body:
# Amenorreas

## Exam identity

Amenorrhea is the absence or abnormal cessation of menses. The exam asks whether you can route the patient through pregnancy, anatomy, endocrine profile and outflow/endometrial integrity.

Takehome: every amenorrhea question is a localization question disguised as a gynecology vignette.

## Guion

### 1. Why it happens

- Normal menstruation requires hypothalamic GnRH pulses, pituitary FSH/LH, ovarian estrogen/progesterone response, responsive endometrium and a patent outflow tract.
- Amenorrhea occurs when one of those layers fails.
- Central failure: low GnRH/FSH/LH, usually from energy deficit, stress, exercise, pituitary injury or tumor.
- Ovarian failure: ovary does not respond, so estrogen is low and FSH rises.
- Endometrial/outflow failure: hormones can be normal, but bleeding cannot occur or the endometrium cannot respond.
- Chronic anovulation: estrogen exists but progesterone cycling fails, classically in PCOS.

Takehome: the broken layer explains the lab pattern.

### 2. Who gets it

- Primary amenorrhea: adolescent without menarche by expected age, with or without secondary sex traits.
- Secondary amenorrhea: reproductive-age patient with prior menses who stops menstruating.
- High-yield phenotypes:
  - Turner/Swyer/POI: high FSH, low E2.
  - Rokitansky/Morris: absent uterus with different androgen pattern.
  - PCOS: oligo/amenorrhea plus hyperandrogenism.
  - FHA: weight loss, anorexia, exercise, stress.
  - Hyperprolactinemia: galactorrhea, antipsychotics/metoclopramide, pituitary.
  - Asherman: post-curettage/endometritis.
  - Sheehan: postpartum hemorrhage plus agalactia.

Takehome: the age plus story usually tells you which branch to enter.

### 3. How it presents

- Primary amenorrhea can present with absent puberty, normal puberty without uterus, cyclic pelvic pain, short stature or genital/outflow anomaly.
- Secondary amenorrhea can present as missed menses, oligomenorrhea, infertility, galactorrhea, hirsutism/acne, vasomotor symptoms, weight change or post-procedure amenorrhea.
- Exam clues:
  - Hirsutism/acne/alopecia -> androgen excess, usually PCOS after excluding mimics.
  - Cyclic pain and no bleeding -> obstruction.
  - No lactation after severe postpartum hemorrhage -> Sheehan.
  - Low BMI/marathon/anorexia -> functional hypothalamic amenorrhea.

Takehome: the best clue is often outside the pelvis.

## Manejo

### 1. Diagnostico

- Primary amenorrhea thresholds:
  - No menses by 15 years with secondary sexual development.
  - No menses by 13 years without secondary sexual development.
- Secondary amenorrhea threshold:
  - No menses for >=6 months, or >=3 cycles in a previously regular patient.
- First rule in secondary amenorrhea: exclude pregnancy with hCG.
- Initial workup after pregnancy exclusion:
  - History: weight, exercise, stress, eating disorder, drugs, galactorrhea, headache/visual symptoms, obstetric hemorrhage, uterine instrumentation.
  - Exam: BMI, Tanner stage, thyroid signs, galactorrhea, hirsutism/virilization, pelvic anatomy.
  - Labs: PRL, TSH, FSH, LH, estradiol.
  - Pelvic ultrasound when anatomy, uterus, ovaries or endometrium matter.
- Progestin challenge:
  - Bleeding after withdrawal: estrogen exposure and patent outflow; think anovulation/PCOS.
  - No bleeding: hipoestrogenism or endometrial/outflow problem; E+P challenge or imaging helps separate.
- E+P challenge:
  - Bleeding: endometrium can respond; central/ovarian hypoestrogenism likely.
  - No bleeding: Asherman or outflow obstruction.

Takehome: hCG first, then PRL/TSH and FSH/E2; challenges are exam tools but not substitutes for localization.

### 2. Clasificacion

| Category | Lab/anatomy pattern | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| Central | FSH/LH low or normal, E2 low | FHA, anorexia, exercise, Sheehan, pituitary disease |
| Ovarian | FSH high, E2 low | POI, Turner, Swyer |
| Anovulatory | FSH often normal, E2 present | PCOS |
| Hyperprolactinemic | PRL high | Prolactinoma, drugs, hypothyroidism |
| Uterine/outflow | Hormones may be normal; bleeding pathway fails | Asherman, imperforate hymen, cervical stenosis |
| Congenital absence/insensitivity | Uterus absent or androgen action abnormal | Rokitansky, Morris |

Takehome: "primary vs secondary" starts the case; compartment classification solves it.

### 3. Manejo

- Pregnancy: manage as pregnancy or ectopic pathway, not as amenorrhea.
- PCOS without fertility goal: combined oral contraceptives for cycle regulation and hyperandrogenism; lifestyle/metabolic screening; antiandrogens only with contraception and selected use.
- PCOS with fertility goal and obesity: weight loss/lifestyle is a high-yield first step; ovulation induction comes later by protocol.
- Hyperprolactinemia/prolactinoma: confirm persistent PRL elevation, check thyroid/drugs, MRI if persistent; dopamine agonist such as cabergoline/bromocriptine when indicated.
- FHA/anorexia/exercise: nutritional rehabilitation, weight restoration, reduce excessive exercise, treat stress/eating disorder; assess bone risk.
- POI: hormone therapy until usual age of menopause unless contraindicated, plus fertility and bone/cardiovascular counseling.
- Turner: pubertal induction with estrogen/progestin as appropriate, screen cardiac/renal issues, fertility counseling.
- Swyer: gonadectomy early because gonadoblastoma risk is high.
- Morris/complete androgen insensitivity: gonadectomy after puberty is classic exam teaching; individualized specialist care.
- Asherman: hysteroscopic lysis of adhesions.
- Imperforate hymen: incision and drainage of hematocolpos.

Takehome: treatment follows the compartment, not the word "amenorrhea."

### 4. Complications

- PCOS: infertility, endometrial hyperplasia, metabolic syndrome, diabetes risk, cardiovascular risk markers.
- FHA/low estrogen: low bone density, infertility, eating disorder morbidity.
- POI: osteoporosis, genitourinary symptoms, cardiovascular risk, fertility reduction.
- Hyperprolactinemia: infertility, hypoestrogenism, mass effect if macroadenoma.
- Outflow obstruction: hematocolpos, pain, endometriosis risk if retrograde flow.
- 46XY gonadal dysgenesis/androgen insensitivity with retained gonads: tumor risk.

Takehome: the complication profile reveals the missing hormone or blocked path.

### 5. Seguimiento

- Reassess cycles and symptoms after treating the cause.
- Monitor metabolic risk in PCOS.
- Monitor bone and nutritional recovery in FHA.
- Monitor PRL and tumor response in prolactinoma.
- Monitor HT adherence and bone/cardiovascular risk in POI.
- Confirm restoration of uterine cavity/outflow after Asherman or obstruction correction.

Takehome: follow-up is targeted to the cause, not generic menstruation counting.

### 6. Pronostico

- PCOS and FHA often improve with targeted management, though recurrence is possible.
- POI has intermittent ovarian activity in some patients but reduced fertility overall.
- Asherman prognosis depends on adhesion severity and successful cavity restoration.
- Sheehan may require long-term pituitary hormone replacement.
- Turner/Swyer/Morris require specialist longitudinal care and fertility counseling.

Takehome: prognosis depends on whether the compartment is reversible.

## Cluster table

| Feature | PCOS | FHA | Hyperprolactinemia | POI/Turner/Swyer | Asherman/outflow |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Dominant clue | Hirsutism/acne/oligo | Low BMI/exercise/stress | Galactorrhea/drug/pituitary | High FSH, low E2 | Procedure history or cyclic pain |
| First exclusion | Pregnancy and mimics | Pregnancy and endocrine causes | Pregnancy, drugs, thyroid | Pregnancy/menopause | Pregnancy/endocrine causes |
| Key test | Androgens, exclusion labs, ultrasound/AMH context | FSH/LH/E2, exclusion workup | PRL, TSH, MRI if persistent | Repeat FSH/E2, karyotype if indicated | Ultrasound, SIS/hysteroscopy |
| Management | ACO/lifestyle/fertility pathway | Nutrition/stress/exercise correction | Dopamine agonist if indicated | HT until menopause age | Hysteroscopic/surgical correction |

## Mini-drills

1. Secondary amenorrhea in reproductive-age patient -> hCG first.
2. Marathon runner, BMI 17, low FSH/LH -> functional hypothalamic amenorrhea.
3. Postpartum hemorrhage, no lactation, amenorrhea -> Sheehan with low FSH/LH/PRL.
4. Hirsutism, acne, oligomenorrhea, hCG negative, enlarged ovaries -> PCOS.
5. Primary amenorrhea, poor secondary sex traits, uterus present -> request FSH.
6. Normal FSH/LH/PRL/TSH and no bleeding despite hormones after prior uterine insult -> Asherman.

## Product modifiers

- Use progestin and E+P challenge as exam-facing tools, but note ASRM 2024 cautions that false positives/negatives occur and hormone profile/ultrasound can streamline diagnosis.
- Do not require ultrasound for PCOS when modern diagnostic criteria can be met by hyperandrogenism plus ovulatory dysfunction after exclusion of mimics.
- Do not generate normative ENCAPS claims from climaterio/menopausia; that adjacent file is draft-only.

units.title: Insuficiencia renal cronica
units.body:
# Insuficiencia renal cronica

## Identidad examinable

La enfermedad renal cronica (ERC) es una anormalidad estructural o funcional del rinon con implicancias para la salud y duracion >=3 meses. En examenes no basta decir "creatinina alta": hay que probar cronicidad, clasificar causa-GFR-albuminuria y anticipar complicaciones.

Takehome: ERC = tiempo + CGA + riesgo, no creatinina aislada.

## Guion

### 1. Por que da

La ERC aparece cuando se pierde masa nefronal funcional y las nefronas remanentes hiperfiltran. Esa hiperfiltracion mantiene el filtrado al inicio, pero aumenta presion intraglomerular, proteinuria, inflamacion y fibrosis. En paralelo, la perdida renal reduce eritropoyetina, altera vitamina D/fosforo/calcio, disminuye excrecion de acidos y potasio, y genera retencion hidrosalina.

Mecanismos preguntables:

- Proteinuria: predictor principal de progresion; no es solo marcador, tambien perpetua dano tubular.
- RAAS: aumenta presion intraglomerular; IECA/ARA-II reducen proteinuria y progresion en fenotipo proteinurico.
- SGLT2: reduce hiperfiltracion y aporta nefroproteccion/cardio-proteccion en pacientes seleccionados.
- CKD-MBD: bajo GFR -> retencion de fosforo -> FGF23 alto -> calcitriol bajo -> calcio bajo -> PTH alta.
- Anemia: EPO baja + inflamacion/hepcidina + deficit de hierro funcional o absoluto.

Takehome: si entiendes proteinuria, fosforo/PTH y EPO, puedes reconstruir casi toda la ERC.

### 2. A quien

Los fenotipos mas examinables son:

- Adulto con diabetes e hipertension de anos, albuminuria y eGFR descendente.
- Adulto mayor con ERC avanzada, anemia, acidosis, hiperK, edema o sintomas uremicos.
- Paciente en dialisis peritoneal con dolor abdominal y liquido turbio.
- Paciente con familiar en dialisis, infecciones/piedras y antecedente neurologico joven: pensar poliquistosis renal autosomica dominante.
- Paciente con DM/HTA y creatinina aun normal pero ACR elevado: ya hay dano renal si persiste.

Etiologias frecuentes:

- Nefropatia diabetica.
- Enfermedad vascular/hipertensiva.
- Glomerulonefritis.
- Tubulointersticial.
- Poliquistosis renal autosomica dominante.
- Desconocida.

Takehome: el examen ama DM/HTA + albuminuria, y tambien ama el contraste entre ERC estable y emergencia de ERC G5.

### 3. Como se presenta

Al inicio puede ser silenciosa. Conforme avanza aparecen HTA, edema, nicturia, anemia, fatiga, prurito, alteraciones oseas, acidosis, hiperpotasemia y sintomas uremicos.

| Estadio/escena | Hallazgos que activan el patron |
|---|---|
| ERC temprana | Albuminuria, HTA, sedimento o imagen anormal; eGFR puede ser normal |
| G3 | Fatiga leve, anemia inicial, PTH alta, vitamina D baja |
| G4 | Hiperfosfatemia, hipocalcemia, acidosis, anemia mas clara, prurito |
| G5 | Uremia, nausea/vomitos, fetor uremico, sobrecarga, hiperK, confusion |
| DP infectada | Dolor abdominal, fiebre/nauseas, efluente turbio |

Laboratorio clasico:

- Creatinina/urea altas, eGFR bajo.
- ACR o proteinuria elevados.
- Hb baja normocitica-normocromica.
- Fosforo alto, PTH alta, calcio bajo, vitamina D baja.
- Potasio alto, bicarbonato bajo, acidosis metabolica.

Takehome: GFR te dice reserva; albuminuria y complicaciones te dicen riesgo y urgencia.

## Manejo

### 1. Diagnostico

Criterios por >=3 meses:

- eGFR <60 mL/min/1.73 m2.
- Albuminuria ACR >=30 mg/g o proteinuria persistente.
- Alteraciones del sedimento.
- Trastornos tubulares/electroliticos por dano renal.
- Imagen anormal: rinones poliquisticos, hidronefrosis, litiasis coraliforme, rinones pequenos cronicos.
- Histologia patologica.
- Trasplante renal previo.

Clasificacion GFR:

| Categoria | eGFR |
|---|---|
| G1 | >=90 |
| G2 | 60-89 |
| G3a | 45-59 |
| G3b | 30-44 |
| G4 | 15-29 |
| G5 | <15 |

Clasificacion albuminuria:

| Categoria | ACR |
|---|---|
| A1 | <30 mg/g |
| A2 | 30-300 mg/g |
| A3 | >300 mg/g |

Reglas de examen:

- G1/G2 no son ERC por GFR solo; requieren otro marcador de dano renal.
- Un resultado aislado no prueba cronicidad.
- La ecografia ayuda a diferenciar AKI vs ERC y detecta poliquistosis/obstruccion.
- En DM/HTA, ACR puede detectar ERC antes de creatinina alta.

Takehome: diagnostico correcto = cronicidad + dano renal + categoria CGA.

### 2. Clasificacion

Se clasifica por:

1. Causa: diabetica, hipertensiva/vascular, glomerular, tubulointersticial, poliquistica, desconocida.
2. GFR: G1 a G5.
3. Albuminuria: A1 a A3.
4. Complicaciones dominantes: anemia, MBD, acidosis, hiperK, volumen, uremia.
5. Estado de reemplazo renal: sin TRS, hemodialisis, dialisis peritoneal, trasplante.

Contraste AKI vs ERC:

| Dato | Sugiere AKI | Sugiere ERC |
|---|---|---|
| Tiempo | Dias-semanas | >=3 meses |
| Ecografia | Rinones normales/grandes | Rinones pequenos y mal diferenciados |
| Excepciones | - | DM, amiloidosis, poliquistosis, infiltrativas pueden tener rinones grandes |
| PTH | Normal o poco alta | Muy alta si avanzada |
| Anemia/acidosis | Mala tolerancia | Mas tolerancia cronica |
| Muerte tipica | Infecciosa | Cardiovascular |

Takehome: la ERC se estratifica, no se etiqueta en bloque.

### 3. Manejo

#### A. Frenar progresion

- Control de presion arterial y diabetes.
- Restriccion de sal, evitar nefrotoxicos y suspender farmacos de riesgo durante hipoperfusion.
- IECA o ARA-II si hay albuminuria/proteinuria, especialmente DM/HTA; monitorizar creatinina y potasio.
- SGLT2 si cumple indicacion y no hay contraindicaciones.
- Abordar tabaquismo, obesidad e hiperuricemia cuando contribuyen a progresion.

Secuencia mental:

```text
DM/HTA + albuminuria persistente
  -> nefroproteccion RAAS/SGLT2
  -> monitor K/Cr
  -> seguir ACR/eGFR
```

Takehome: la proteinuria persistente cambia el tratamiento aunque la creatinina parezca "aceptable".

#### B. Corregir complicaciones

Anemia:

- Normocitica-normocromica por EPO baja.
- Corregir hierro si hay deficit absoluto o funcional.
- Reponer B12/folato si falta.
- Considerar estimulante de eritropoyesis si Hb sigue baja despues de corregir deficit.
- Evitar buscar Hb normal alta: aumenta eventos adversos.

CKD-MBD:

- Restriccion de fosforo y quelantes con comidas.
- Vitamina D/calcitriol cuando el fosforo esta controlado y segun perfil.
- Calcimimeticos en hiperparatiroidismo secundario seleccionado.
- Paratiroidectomia si refractario.

Hiperpotasemia:

- Si hay cambios ECG o emergencia: estabilizar membrana con calcio.
- Luego desplazar K al interior celular y eliminar K.
- En cronico: dieta, revisar farmacos, resinas/binders, y TRS si refractaria.

Acidosis metabolica:

- Bicarbonato bajo en G4-G5.
- Bicarbonato oral si cronica y severa segun contexto.
- TRS si acidosis refractaria.

Volumen/CV:

- La enfermedad cardiovascular es la causa principal de muerte.
- Manejar HTA, sobrecarga, sal, dislipidemia segun riesgo y comorbilidad.

Takehome: en ERC avanzada, corregir complicaciones es tan importante como mirar el eGFR.

#### C. Terapia de reemplazo renal

Indicaciones fuertes:

- Uremia sintomatica.
- HiperK refractaria.
- Acidosis refractaria.
- Sobrecarga de volumen refractaria.
- eGFR muy bajo, usualmente 5-9 mL/min/1.73 m2, individualizado por sintomas y contexto.

Modalidades:

- Hemodialisis: fistula AV ideal; cateter venoso tunelizado si no hay acceso maduro. Remueve urea, creatinina, K y volumen; aporta bicarbonato/calcio segun bano.
- Dialisis peritoneal: usa peritoneo y cateter Tenckhoff; mas autonomia, pero riesgo de peritonitis y depende de entorno/tecnica.
- Trasplante renal: mejor supervivencia y calidad de vida si no hay contraindicaciones; requiere inmunosupresion y seguimiento.

Takehome: TRS se decide por sintomas/refractariedad y plan de vida, no solo por "G5" escrito en la hoja.

#### D. Peritonitis en dialisis peritoneal

Sospechar si hay dolor abdominal, fiebre/nauseas o efluente turbio. Diagnostico con al menos 2:

- Dolor abdominal o efluente turbio.
- WBC en efluente >100/uL con >50% PMN tras permanencia adecuada.
- Cultivo positivo.

Manejo:

- Tomar muestra de efluente para recuento, diferencial, Gram y cultivo.
- Iniciar antibiotico empirico sin esperar cultivo.
- Cubrir gram positivos y gram negativos.
- Para RM local, la respuesta clasica puede ser vancomicina + gentamicina.
- Ruta intraperitoneal preferida si no hay sepsis sistemica.

Takehome: liquido turbio en DP es peritonitis hasta demostrar lo contrario.

### 4. Complicaciones

- Cardiovascular: HTA, hipertrofia ventricular, insuficiencia cardiaca, calcificacion vascular, principal causa de muerte.
- Anemia: fatiga, disnea, intolerancia al ejercicio.
- CKD-MBD: prurito, dolor oseo, fracturas, calcificaciones; osteitis fibrosa si PTH alta.
- Calcifilaxis: ulceras dolorosas por arteriolopatia calcificante uremica, alta mortalidad.
- HiperK: bradiarritmia, QRS ancho, paro.
- Acidosis: Kussmaul, deterioro catabolico.
- Uremia: nauseas, vomitos, fetor uremico, encefalopatia, pericarditis.
- Infecciones: disfuncion inmune, riesgo en dialisis.

Takehome: la complicacion que mata mas es cardiovascular; la que asusta mas en urgencia es hiperK/uremia/acidosis.

### 5. Seguimiento

Vigilar:

- eGFR y ACR/proteinuria.
- Presion arterial, peso, edema y sintomas uremicos.
- Creatinina y potasio despues de cambios en RAAS/SGLT2 o eventos intercurrentes.
- Hb, ferritina, saturacion de transferrina, B12/folato si anemia.
- Calcio, fosforo, PTH, vitamina D y fosfatasa alcalina si CKD-MBD.
- Bicarbonato y potasio en G4-G5.
- Plan de acceso vascular o peritoneal antes de urgencia.
- Vacunacion y prevencion de infecciones segun programa local.

Takehome: seguir ERC es mirar trayectoria, no fotografia.

### 6. Pronostico

Peor pronostico si:

- eGFR mas bajo.
- Albuminuria mas alta.
- Proteinuria persistente.
- HTA o DM no controladas.
- HiperK, acidosis o sobrecarga recurrentes.
- Complicaciones cardiovasculares.
- Inicio no planificado de dialisis.

Mejor pronostico si:

- Se detecta albuminuria temprano.
- Se frena proteinuria.
- Se planifica TRS o trasplante a tiempo.
- Se corrigen anemia/MBD/acidosis sin sobretratar.

Takehome: albuminuria alta + eGFR bajo = riesgo renal y cardiovascular alto.

## Mini-drills

| Stem | Respuesta |
|---|---|
| eGFR 48 + ACR 120 mg/g por 4 meses | ERC G3a A2 |
| eGFR 72 sin albuminuria ni sedimento ni imagen anormal | No basta para ERC |
| DM/HTA + proteinuria 500 mg/d persistente | IECA/ARA-II; considerar SGLT2 si indicado |
| G5 + bradicardia + QRS ancho + hiperK | Gluconato de calcio inicial |
| DP + dolor abdominal + liquido turbio | Peritonitis; muestra y ATB empirico |
| P alto + Ca bajo + PTH alta + prurito | CKD-MBD por hiperparatiroidismo secundario |
| Familiar en dialisis + litiasis + ACV joven | Sospechar poliquistosis; ecografia renal |

En examenes no basta decir "creatinina alta": hay que probar cronicidad, clasificar causa-GFR-albuminuria y anticipar complicaciones. Takehome: ERC = tiempo + CGA + riesgo, no creatinina aislada. La ERC aparece cuando se pierde masa nefronal funcional y las nefronas remanentes hiperfiltran. Esa hiperfiltracion mantiene el filtrado al inicio, pero aumenta presion intraglomerular, proteinuria, inflamacion y fibrosis. En paralelo, la perdida renal reduce erit

units.title: Insectos, artropodos y ofidios venenosos
units.body:
# Insectos, artropodos y ofidios venenosos

## Identidad examinable

Este tema evalua si reconoces un envenenamiento o exposicion de riesgo y tomas la primera decision segura. No es taxonomia animal: es urgencia, toxidromo, severidad, suero/antidoto y errores que no debes cometer.

Takehome: en ponzonosos, el examen premia dos cosas: reconocer el patron y no hacer dano.

## Guion

### 1. Por que da

Los cuadros dependen del tipo de veneno o del agente transmitido:

- Loxosceles laeta: veneno dermonecrotico y hemolitico; puede dar placa livedoide, necrosis, hemolisis, hemoglobinuria e IRA.
- Latrodectus mactans: toxina neuroautonomica; produce dolor intenso, espasmos, sudoracion/sialorrea, alteraciones autonomicas y, si es grave, compromiso sistemico.
- Bothrops/Lachesis: veneno proteolitico-hemotoxico; causa edema, necrosis, coagulopatia, sangrado, shock e IRA.
- Micrurus: veneno neurotoxico; causa debilidad/paralisis y falla respiratoria.
- Abejas/avispas/hormigas: toxicidad local y reacciones alergicas; el riesgo mayor inmediato es anafilaxia.
- Rabia: no es veneno; es exposicion a virus rabico por saliva de animal infectado, prevenible antes de que aparezcan sintomas.

Takehome: cada animal activa un mecanismo; el mecanismo predice el manejo.

### 2. A quien

Escenas tipicas:

- Loxoscelismo: zona urbana/periurbana, costa/sierra, interiores, noche, ropa/cama/objetos.
- Latrodectismo: zona rural, costa/sierra, arana con marca de reloj de arena.
- Ofidismo: selva/ceja de selva, actividad agricola, mordedura en extremidad inferior; Bothrops es el patron peruano mas importante.
- Rabia urbana/silvestre: mordedura de perro/gato o animal silvestre, especialmente murcielago.
- Anafilaxia por himenopteros: picadura de abeja/avispa/hormiga con urticaria, broncoespasmo o hipotension.

Takehome: la escena geografica y el animal probable orientan, pero no deben retrasar ABC ni referencia.

### 3. Como se presenta

| Sindrome | Presentacion clave | Labs utiles |
|---|---|---|
| Loxoscelismo cutaneo | Mordedura poco dolorosa inicial, placa violacea/livedoide, escara, lesion en diana | Usualmente clinico |
| Loxoscelismo sistemico | Fiebre, vomitos, anemia, ictericia, orina oscura, IRA | Hb, LDH, bilirrubina, creatinina, uroanalisis |
| Latrodectismo | Dolor intenso, espasmos musculares, sialorrea/sudoracion, inestabilidad autonomica | Clinico; monitor vital |
| Bothrops/Lachesis | Dolor inmediato, edema progresivo, equimosis, flictenas, sangrado | Hemograma, plaquetas, TP/TTP, fibrinogeno, creatinina, orina |
| Micrurus | Parestesias, ptosis, disfagia, paralisis respiratoria | Clinico; monitor respiratorio |
| Rabia exposicion | Herida + animal + zona + disponibilidad del animal | No esperar laboratorio para PEP si indicada |
| Anafilaxia | Urticaria, broncoespasmo, edema, hipotension | Clinico |

Takehome: edema + coagulopatia en selva = Bothrops hasta que el contexto diga otra cosa.

## Manejo

### 1. Diagnostico

El diagnostico es clinico con apoyo laboratorial segun severidad.

Preguntas obligatorias:

1. Que animal o escena hubo?
2. Cuanto tiempo paso?
3. Hay progresion local?
4. Hay compromiso sistemico?
5. Hay coagulopatia, hemolisis, IRA, neurotoxicidad o anafilaxia?
6. Hay exposicion rabica leve o grave?

Examenes por sindrome:

- Loxoscelismo sistemico: hemograma, LDH, bilirrubinas, creatinina, examen de orina.
- Ofidismo: hemograma/plaquetas, TP/TTP, fibrinogeno, creatinina, electrolitos, orina, ECG si severo.
- Anafilaxia: diagnostico clinico, no esperar pruebas.
- Rabia: clasificar exposicion; la decision de PEP no depende de "esperar sintomas".

Takehome: si preguntas por labs, busca el dano que mata: sangre, rinon, respiracion y choque.

### 2. Clasificacion

#### Loxoscelismo

- Cutaneo: placa livedoide/tricolor, dolor variable, necrosis local, sin hemolisis ni dano renal.
- Sistemico o viscerocutaneo: hemolisis intravascular, hemoglobinuria, anemia, coagulopatia, IRA, fiebre/vomitos.

#### Ofidismo

- Sin envenenamiento: marcas sin edema progresivo ni datos sistemicos.
- Leve: dolor y edema local.
- Moderado: edema progresivo mas alla del sitio, sintomas sistemicos leves o alteracion laboratorial.
- Grave: edema extenso, coagulopatia, sangrado, shock, neurotoxicidad, IRA o falla respiratoria.

#### Rabia

- Sin riesgo: lamedura en piel intacta o contacto sin saliva en herida.
- Exposicion leve: mordedura/aranazo superficial unico por perro/gato sin sospecha, fuera de zonas de alto riesgo.
- Exposicion grave: cara, cabeza, cuello, genitales, pulpejos; mordeduras profundas, desgarradas o multiples; animal sospechoso, confirmado, silvestre, huido, desconocido o que muere en observacion.

Takehome: la severidad no es "el animal"; es dano local progresivo y dano sistemico.

### 3. Manejo

#### A. Primeros auxilios seguros

Para ofidismo:

- Mantener calma, ABC y traslado rapido.
- Inmovilizar la extremidad y retirar anillos/relojes/ropa ajustada.
- Lavar la herida y cubrir con aposito limpio.
- Marcar borde de edema/dolor y hora.
- Tomar foto del animal solo si es seguro; no capturarlo.

No hacer:

- Torniquete.
- Incisiones.
- Succion.
- Hielo o inmersion.
- Alcohol o remedios tradicionales.
- Esperar a que aparezcan sintomas.

Takehome: el primer tratamiento es transportar vivo y no agravar la lesion.

#### B. Loxoscelismo

Cutaneo leve o localizado:

- Limpieza local, analgesia, antihistaminicos si prurito.
- Observacion de la herida si no hay datos sistemicos.
- Corticoide sistemico segun protocolo local/examen.
- No desbridar en fase aguda; cirugia se reserva para necrosis establecida.

Sistemico o grave:

- Internamiento.
- Hidratacion IV y control de diuresis.
- Hemograma, hemolisis, funcion renal y orina.
- Corticoides/soporte segun protocolo local.
- Dialisis si IRA grave.
- Suero antiloxoscelico si disponible, idealmente temprano.

Clave RM:

- Tiempo ideal exam para suero antiloxoscelico: 6 horas.
- Loxosceles cutaneo sin datos sistemicos a 24 h puede tener como respuesta "observacion de la herida".

Takehome: loxoscelismo cutaneo se observa y se cuida; loxoscelismo sistemico se interna.

#### C. Latrodectismo

Patron:

- Arana con marca de reloj de arena.
- Dolor intenso.
- Hipersalivacion/sudoracion.
- Espasmos musculares.
- Inestabilidad autonomica.

Manejo:

- ABC, monitorizacion y analgesia.
- Manejo de espasmos y soporte respiratorio si progresa.
- Antidoto/antiveneno especifico EV si cuadro severo y disponible.

Clave RM:

- Reloj de arena + dolor intenso + hipotension + hipersalivacion + espasmos = antidoto especifico EV.

Takehome: reloj de arena no es Loxosceles; es Latrodectus y cambia el manejo.

#### D. Ofidismo

Primeros auxilios y traslado son inmediatos. En el establecimiento:

- ABC y via IV.
- Monitor vital, dolor, edema y neurologia.
- Hemograma, plaquetas, coagulacion, fibrinogeno, creatinina, orina.
- Suero antiofidico especifico IV si hay envenenamiento clinico o laboratorial.
- Preparar manejo de reacciones alergicas al suero.
- Hidratacion para prevenir IRA.
- Profilaxis antitetanica segun estado vacunal.
- Antibioticos solo si hay infeccion o herida manipulada/contaminada.
- Fasciotomia solo si sindrome compartimental confirmado; no profilactica.

Serpientes clave:

- Bothrops: edema, dolor, necrosis, hemorragia, coagulopatia.
- Lachesis: parecido a Bothrops, puede ser grave en selva amazonica.
- Micrurus: neurotoxicidad y falla respiratoria.
- Crotalus: neurotoxicidad/miotoxidad, posible IRA.

Takehome: antiveneno se da por envenenamiento, no por toda marca de colmillo.

#### E. Rabia PEP

Primer paso siempre:

- Lavar con agua y jabon por 10 minutos.
- Antiseptico viricida si disponible.
- Evaluar tetanos y antibiotico segun herida.
- Clasificar exposicion.

Local ENAM/NTS 131 historica:

- Esquema post-exposicion IM tipo Essen: dias 0, 3, 7, 14 y 28.
- Exposicion grave: vacuna + ERIG 40 UI/kg; infiltrar en y alrededor de herida lo posible, resto IM.
- Persona con profilaxis pre-exposicion completa y nueva exposicion: 2 refuerzos dias 0 y 3, sin suero.
- Perros/gatos identificados: observacion 10 dias.
- No aplicar vacuna en gluteo.
- Embarazo no contraindica PEP.
- Estado vacunal del animal no debe tranquilizar falsamente si la exposicion es de riesgo.

Modifier actual:

- RM 1176-2023 modifica la NTS 131; para publicacion vigente, page-lock del esquema actualizado antes de fijar calendario.

Takehome: en rabia, la ventana util es antes de sintomas; lavar y clasificar no se negocia.

#### F. Abejas, avispas y anafilaxia

- Retirar aguijon por raspado si hay lanceta.
- Analgesia y cuidado local si reaccion local.
- Anafilaxia: adrenalina IM, ABC, oxigeno, fluidos y traslado/observacion.
- Antihistaminicos y corticoides son adyuvantes; no reemplazan adrenalina en anafilaxia.

Takehome: si hay hipotension o broncoespasmo tras picadura, no es "alergia leve": es anafilaxia.

### 4. Complicaciones

- Necrosis cutanea y cicatriz.
- Hemolisis intravascular.
- IRA por hemolisis, rabdomiolisis, shock o venom nephrotoxicity.
- Coagulopatia, CID, sangrado intracraneal o gastrointestinal.
- Shock.
- Falla respiratoria por neurotoxicidad.
- Sindrome compartimental.
- Anafilaxia.
- Rabia humana clinica: casi siempre fatal.

Takehome: los finales malos son sangre, rinon, respiracion y shock.

### 5. Seguimiento

Vigilar:

- Progresion de edema y dolor con marca horaria.
- Coloracion, perfusion, sensibilidad y motricidad distal.
- Hemograma, plaquetas, coagulacion, creatinina, orina segun sindrome.
- Signos de hemolisis en loxoscelismo.
- Signos respiratorios en neurotoxicidad.
- Reaccion inmediata o tardia al suero heterologo.
- Calendario PEP rabia segun norma vigente.
- Notificacion epidemiologica si corresponde.

Takehome: seguimiento = detectar progresion antes de que el dano sea irreversible.

### 6. Pronostico

Mejor pronostico:

- Consulta temprana.
- Primeros auxilios correctos.
- Acceso rapido a suero especifico apropiado.
- Reconocimiento temprano de coagulopatia, hemolisis, IRA o neurotoxicidad.

Peor pronostico:

- Ninos por menor masa corporal.
- Retraso por remedios tradicionales.
- Torniquete/incisiones/succion.
- Mordedura con veneno neurotoxico o hemotoxico grave.
- Loxoscelismo sistemico.
- Exposicion rabica grave sin PEP.

Takehome: tiempo + suero correcto + soporte correcto cambian mortalidad y discapacidad.

## Mini-drills

| Stem | Respuesta |
|---|---|
| Lesion tricolor con escara central tras despertar | Loxoscelismo cutaneo |
| Loxoscelismo + orina oscura + anemia + creatinina alta | Loxoscelismo sistemico |
| Arana con reloj de arena + dolor intenso + espasmos | Latrodectismo; antidoto especifico si severo/disponible |
| Selva + mordedura en pierna + edema rapido + encia sangra | Bothrops; antiofidico si envenenamiento |
| Mordedura de serpiente sin edema ni labs alterados | Observar; no antiveneno automatico |
| Mordedura de perro en cara | Exposicion grave rabica; lavado + PEP segun norma |
| Abeja + broncoespasmo + hipotension | Anafilaxia; adrenalina IM |
| Pregunta SERUMS: loxoscelismo probable periodicidad | 7 dias como clave historica source-gated |

units.title: Patologias respiratorias: Orofaringe
units.body:
# Patologias respiratorias: Orofaringe

## Exam Identity

This is a pediatric upper-airway cluster. The recurring exam error is to reduce every case to "pharyngitis" and miss the unsafe airway or the non-GAS mimic.

Take-home: in pediatric oropharynx, airway triage comes before throat diagnosis.

## Guion

### 1. Why It Happens

The same anatomic neighborhood can create three different exam worlds:

- Mucosal infection: viral URI, viral pharyngitis, GAS pharyngitis, EBV mononucleosis.
- Airway edema: croup affects the subglottic region and produces barking cough plus inspiratory stridor.
- Deep infection or obstruction: epiglottitis, bacterial tracheitis, peritonsillar abscess, retropharyngeal abscess, and foreign body can compromise the airway.

Mechanisms that matter:

- GAS pharyngitis matters because treatment prevents acute rheumatic fever when given in time.
- Viral pharyngitis matters because unnecessary antibiotics create harm and exam traps.
- Croup matters because subglottic edema worsens with agitation and improves with corticosteroid; nebulized epinephrine buys rapid but temporary improvement.
- Epiglottitis matters because manipulating the throat can precipitate obstruction.
- Deep neck abscess matters because pus plus distorted anatomy can become an airway problem.

Take-home: mechanism predicts the first safe action; not every red throat is safe to inspect.

### 2. Who Gets It

| Condition | Typical patient |
|---|---|
| Common cold / viral URI | Any age, especially infants and young children |
| GAS pharyngitis | School-age child, classically 5-15 years |
| EBV mononucleosis | Child/adolescent with systemic symptoms and generalized adenopathy |
| Croup | 3 months-5 years, often worse at night |
| Epiglottitis | Classically 2-6 years; consider if incomplete Hib protection or toxic presentation |
| Bacterial tracheitis | Any age, often after URI with sudden worsening |
| Peritonsillar abscess | Older child/adolescent |
| Retropharyngeal abscess | Usually <5 years |
| Foreign body aspiration | Usually <5 years during eating/play |
| Acute bacterial rhinosinusitis | Persistent or worsening URI pattern |

Take-home: age narrows the differential, but toxicity and airway signs override age.

### 3. How It Presents

| Pattern | Diagnosis to retrieve | Differentiator |
|---|---|---|
| Watery rhinorrhea, sneezing, cough, hoarseness, low fever | Common cold / viral URI | Viral symptoms dominate; no antibiotics |
| Sudden sore throat, fever, exudate, tender anterior nodes, absent cough | GAS pharyngitis | Centor/McIsaac-compatible |
| Exudative tonsillitis, fatigue, generalized nodes, splenomegaly, rash after amoxicillin | EBV mononucleosis | Systemic lymphoid pattern |
| Viral prodrome then barking cough, hoarse voice, inspiratory stridor, worse at night | Croup | Child is usually not toxic |
| High fever, toxic, drooling, tripod, muffled voice, absent cough | Epiglottitis | Do not force throat exam |
| URI then high fever, toxicity, barking/productive cough, mixed or biphasic stridor | Bacterial tracheitis | Thick secretions, severe course |
| Unilateral throat pain, trismus, hot potato voice, uvula deviation | Peritonsillar abscess | Trismus plus asymmetry |
| Fever, neck stiffness/torticollis, dysphagia/drooling, posterior pharyngeal bulge | Retropharyngeal abscess | Toddler with neck posture |
| Sudden choking, persistent cough, unilateral wheeze, air trapping | Foreign body | Normal X-ray does not exclude |
| Persistent URI >10 days or worsening fever/purulent drainage/halitosis/facial pressure | Acute bacterial rhinosinusitis | Residentado exact stem: postnasal purulence and frontal pressure |

Take-home: cough type and drooling are more discriminating than pharyngeal redness.

## Manejo

### 1. Diagnosis

Start with danger signs:

- Stridor at rest.
- Marked retractions or hypoxemia.
- Drooling or inability to swallow.
- Tripod or hyperextended neck.
- Altered mental status, lethargy, inability to drink.
- Toxic appearance.

If danger signs are present:

- Keep the child calm and with caregivers.
- Avoid unnecessary mouth/throat manipulation.
- Defer imaging/labs until airway is secure if obstruction is significant.
- Call airway/ENT/anesthesia early.

Sore throat testing:

- Viral features such as cough, rhinorrhea, hoarseness, conjunctivitis, diarrhea, oral ulcers, or vesicles support viral diagnosis and no GAS testing.
- Without viral features, use age and GAS clinical features to decide RADT/culture.
- Current-public modifier: positive RADT or culture confirms GAS; negative RADT in children should be culture-confirmed when testing is needed.
- Local exam modifier: ENAM card allows empiric treatment at Centor/McIsaac 4-5.

Take-home: a test is useful only after deciding the child is safe and the syndrome is not clearly viral.

### 2. Classification

#### Sore Throat Cluster

- Viral URI/pharyngitis: cough/rhinorrhea/hoarseness prominent.
- GAS pharyngitis: fever, exudate, tender anterior cervical nodes, absent cough, school-age.
- EBV mononucleosis: systemic symptoms, generalized adenopathy, splenomegaly, amoxicillin rash.
- Abscess: trismus, muffled voice, uvula deviation, neck stiffness, drooling.

#### Stridor Cluster

- Inspiratory stridor: laryngeal/supraglottic process.
- Biphasic or mixed stridor: tracheal process.
- Sudden stridor/choking: foreign body.
- Chronic stridor worse supine/feeding: laryngomalacia.

#### Croup Severity

- Mild: barking cough, no stridor at rest, minimal distress.
- Moderate: stridor at rest or retractions, still interactive.
- Severe: marked retractions, hypoxemia, fatigue, poor air entry, altered behavior.

Take-home: classification is action-based; it tells you who can be observed, tested, treated, drained, or intubated.

### 3. Management

#### Common Cold / Viral Pharyngitis

- Supportive care.
- No antibiotics.
- Educate on alarm signs: breathing difficulty, inability to drink, persistent fever, lethargy, stridor.

#### GAS Pharyngitis

Local ENAM treatment options:

- Benzathine penicillin G IM single dose, especially if adherence is an issue.
- Amoxicillin 50 mg/kg/day for 10 days.
- Macrolide option for true severe beta-lactam allergy, with local resistance awareness.

Current-public modifier:

- Treat confirmed GAS by RADT/culture when possible.
- Do not treat viral pharyngitis with antibiotics.

Exam pearl:

- Antibiotic treatment prevents rheumatic fever, not post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis.

#### EBV Mononucleosis

- Supportive care.
- Avoid labeling the amoxicillin rash as a primary penicillin allergy without context.
- Avoid contact sports if splenomegaly is present.

#### Croup

- Minimize agitation.
- Dexamethasone is the local exam anchor; ENAM uses 0.6 mg/kg single dose.
- Nebulized epinephrine for moderate/severe disease or worsening distress.
- Observe after epinephrine because the effect is temporary and rebound/worsening can occur.
- Oxygen if hypoxemic.
- Intubation is rare but needed for life-threatening obstruction or nonresponse.

#### Epiglottitis

- Airway first in controlled setting.
- Do not force oropharyngeal examination in ED.
- ICU/OR pathway.
- IV broad therapy in local card: third-generation cephalosporin plus vancomycin.

#### Bacterial Tracheitis

- Suspect when URI becomes toxic with high fever, barking/productive cough, and mixed/biphasic stridor.
- Airway support.
- IV antibiotics: local card uses third-generation cephalosporin plus vancomycin.
- Intubation if severe obstruction or respiratory failure.

#### Peritonsillar Abscess

- Drainage when appropriate: needle aspiration or incision/drainage.
- Antibiotics covering GAS and anaerobes.
- Analgesia and hydration.
- ENT involvement if airway risk, failed drainage, recurrence, or uncertain diagnosis.

#### Retropharyngeal Abscess

- Airway assessment first.
- CT neck with contrast only if stable.
- IV antibiotics.
- Surgical drainage if airway compromise, large collection, complications, or poor response.

#### Foreign Body

- If clear choking history plus persistent symptoms, normal radiograph does not rule it out.
- Bronchoscopy is diagnostic and therapeutic.

#### Acute Bacterial Rhinosinusitis

- Exam pattern: persistent URI, worsening fever, purulent postnasal drainage, halitosis, facial/frontal pressure.
- Local Residentado exact key: amoxicillin.
- Public modifier: antibiotic choice depends on local resistance, severity, and guideline.

Take-home: management is a chain: airway -> syndrome -> test only if useful -> narrow therapy -> follow-up.

### 4. Complications

- GAS: acute rheumatic fever, suppurative complications; antibiotic does not prevent post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis.
- Croup: respiratory fatigue, hypoxemia, rare intubation.
- Epiglottitis: sudden complete airway obstruction, shock, death if untreated.
- Bacterial tracheitis: airway obstruction from secretions, pneumonia, respiratory failure.
- Peritonsillar abscess: airway compromise, deep neck extension, recurrence.
- Retropharyngeal abscess: mediastinitis, sepsis, airway obstruction.
- Foreign body: atelectasis, recurrent pneumonia, bronchiectasis if delayed.
- EBV: splenic rupture risk when splenomegaly is present.

Take-home: complications cluster into airway, suppuration, immune sequelae, and delayed obstruction.

### 5. Follow-Up

- GAS: clinical improvement expected within 24-48 hours after antibiotics; reassess if persistent fever, neck swelling, or respiratory symptoms.
- Croup: return if rest stridor, increasing work of breathing, cyanosis, lethargy, dehydration, or recurrence after epinephrine.
- Abscess: close reassessment after drainage/antibiotics; PTA often needs follow-up within 24-48 hours.
- Sinusitis: reassess if worsening, orbital symptoms, neurologic symptoms, or no improvement.
- Foreign body: persistent cough/wheeze after choking requires escalation even with normal X-ray.

Take-home: follow-up is designed to catch airway recurrence, abscess progression, and missed foreign body.

### 6. Prognosis

- Viral URI and viral pharyngitis are self-limited.
- GAS has excellent prognosis with correct antibiotic therapy.
- Croup is usually self-limited; severe cases are uncommon but time-sensitive.
- Epiglottitis, bacterial tracheitis, and deep neck abscess are dangerous because deterioration can be abrupt.
- EBV usually resolves, but fatigue and splenic precautions matter.
- Foreign body prognosis depends on early recognition.

Take-home: most cases are benign, but the rare airway diagnoses are too dangerous to miss.

## Mini-Drills

1. Barking cough, hoarse voice, inspiratory stridor, worse at night after URI -> croup.
2. Drooling, tripod, high fever, no cough -> epiglottitis; do not inspect throat aggressively.
3. Exudate, no cough, fever, anterior nodes in school-age child -> GAS pathway.
4. Exudate plus generalized nodes, splenomegaly, rash after amoxicillin -> EBV.
5. Trismus plus uvula deviation -> peritonsillar abscess.
6. Toddler with fever, neck stiffness, drooling -> retropharyngeal abscess.
7. Sudden choking with unilateral wheeze -> foreign body.
units.example: This is a pediatric upper-airway cluster. The recurring exam error is to reduce every case to "pharyngitis" and miss the unsafe airway or the non-GAS mimic. units.title: Anemias macrociticas
units.body:
# Anemias macrociticas

## Exam Identity

Anemia macrocitica means anemia with MCV >100 fL. It is not a final diagnosis.

The central question is whether the macrocytosis is megaloblastic from impaired DNA synthesis or non-megaloblastic from alcohol, liver disease, hypothyroidism, reticulocytosis, marrow disease, or drugs.

Take-home: always cross MCV with smear, reticulocytes, neurologic findings, and context.

## Guion

### 1. Why It Happens

Megaloblastic anemia happens because DNA synthesis is slow. The cytoplasm matures but the nucleus lags, creating nuclear-cytoplasmic asynchrony.

Core mechanisms:

- B12 deficiency blocks DNA synthesis and also disrupts neurologic metabolism.
- Folate deficiency blocks DNA synthesis but does not produce the classic B12 myelopathy in exam logic.
- Bone marrow produces abnormal large precursors, many die inside marrow, and output falls.
- This ineffective erythropoiesis raises LDH and indirect bilirubin, while reticulocytes are low at diagnosis.
- All fast-dividing cell lines can be affected, so leukopenia and thrombocytopenia can appear.

Non-megaloblastic macrocytosis does not follow the same DNA-synthesis pattern:

- Alcohol and liver disease alter red-cell membrane/toxicity/nutrition.
- Hypothyroidism lowers hematopoietic turnover.
- Reticulocytosis raises MCV because reticulocytes are large.
- Myelodysplastic syndrome produces clonal dysplasia, especially in older adults.

Take-home: high LDH with low retics in megaloblastosis is ineffective erythropoiesis, not ordinary hemolysis.

### 2. Who Gets It

| Cause | Typical context |
|---|---|
| B12 deficiency | Older adult, vegan/strict vegetarian diet, gastrectomy, bariatric surgery, ileal Crohn/resection, pernicious anemia, metformin, PPI/H2 blocker |
| Pernicious anemia | Older adult, autoimmune background, intrinsic factor/parietal cell antibody pattern |
| Folate deficiency | Alcohol use, malnutrition, pregnancy, hemolysis, dialysis, enteropathy, anticonvulsants, methotrexate, trimethoprim, pyrimethamine |
| Alcohol/liver disease | Macrocytosis with alcohol history or hepatopathy; can coexist with folate deficiency |
| Hypothyroidism | Fatigue/weight gain/cold intolerance with high TSH/low T4 |
| Reticulocytosis | Recovery after bleeding or hemolysis |
| Myelodysplastic syndrome | Older adult with persistent cytopenias and dysplastic smear |
| Aplasia/marrow failure | Pancytopenia with low production, no megaloblastic smear pattern |

Take-home: B12 is ileum/intrinsic factor/animal foods; folate is jejunum/greens/short stores/increased demand.

### 3. How It Presents

| Pattern | Diagnosis to retrieve | Differentiator |
|---|---|---|
| MCV >100, macroovalocytes, hypersegmented neutrophils | Megaloblastic anemia | DNA synthesis failure |
| Macrocytosis + paresthesias + ataxic gait + loss vibration/proprioception + cognitive/psychiatric symptoms | B12 deficiency | Neurology points to B12 |
| Autoimmune disease + anti-intrinsic factor/parietal cell context + B12 deficiency | Pernicious anemia | Intrinsic factor failure |
| Pregnancy/alcohol/malnutrition + macrocytosis + no neuro signs | Folate deficiency | MMA normal, homocysteine high |
| Methotrexate + macrocytosis | Functional folate problem | Folinic acid can bypass activation |
| High MCV + high reticulocytes | Hemolysis/bleeding recovery | Reticulocytes are large |
| High MCV + high TSH/low T4 | Hypothyroidism | No classic megaloblastic smear needed |
| Older adult + cytopenias + dysplasia | Myelodysplastic syndrome | Do not call every case B12 |

Take-home: neurologic signs are the fork that turns "megaloblastic" into "B12 until proven otherwise".

## Manejo

### 1. Diagnosis

Start with:

- CBC with MCV and other cell lines.
- Peripheral smear.
- Reticulocyte count/index.
- B12 level.
- Folate testing when supported by diet, malabsorption, pregnancy, alcohol, hemolysis, or medication history.
- LDH, indirect bilirubin, and haptoglobin if ineffective erythropoiesis vs hemolysis matters.
- TSH, liver tests, medication review, alcohol history.

Interpret the smear:

- Macroovalocytes + hypersegmented neutrophils -> megaloblastic.
- Round macrocytes or non-specific macrocytosis -> consider alcohol/liver/hypothyroid/drugs.
- Dysplasia or persistent cytopenias -> consider myelodysplastic syndrome or marrow failure.

Interpret metabolites:

- MMA high + homocysteine high -> B12 deficiency.
- MMA normal + homocysteine high -> folate deficiency more likely.
- MMA normal + homocysteine normal -> B12 deficiency unlikely in local ENAM logic.

Current-public modifier:

- NICE 2024: use total B12 or active B12 initially in most adults; use active B12 in pregnancy; consider MMA when B12 results are indeterminate and symptoms fit.
- CAP 2024: borderline or discordant B12/folate results can be clarified by MMA and homocysteine, interpreted with clinical context.

Take-home: the diagnostic unit is not one lab; it is CBC + smear + retic + context + B12/folate/metabolites.

### 2. Classification

#### Megaloblastic Macrocytosis

- B12 deficiency.
- Folate deficiency.
- Functional folate inhibition: methotrexate, trimethoprim, pyrimethamine.
- Some marrow-toxic drugs that impair DNA synthesis.

#### Non-Megaloblastic Macrocytosis

- Alcohol.
- Liver disease.
- Hypothyroidism.
- Reticulocytosis.
- Myelodysplastic syndrome.
- Aplasia/marrow failure.
- Medication effect without classic B12/folate pattern.

#### B12 Etiology Subtypes

- Dietary: strict vegan/vegetarian without supplementation.
- Gastric: pernicious anemia, total/partial gastrectomy, bariatric surgery.
- Ileal: Crohn disease, ileal resection.
- Medication-associated: metformin, PPI, H2 blockers.
- Nitrous oxide: functional inactivation of B12; current sources emphasize MMA/homocysteine if suspected.

#### Folate Etiology Subtypes

- Low intake: malnutrition, alcohol use.
- Increased demand: pregnancy, infancy, hemolysis.
- Malabsorption: enteropathy.
- Drug-related: anticonvulsants, methotrexate, trimethoprim, pyrimethamine.

Take-home: classify first by smear, then by B12-vs-folate clues, then by cause.

### 3. Management

#### General

- Treat the cause, not just the MCV.
- If neurologic symptoms and suspected B12 deficiency are present, do not delay B12 treatment while waiting for all results.
- Do not give folate alone when B12 deficiency is possible.
- If pancytopenia, dysplasia, unclear cause, or poor response: refer to hematology.

#### B12 Deficiency

Local ENAM treatment lock:

- Vitamin B12 IM 1000 mcg daily x7 days, then weekly x4 weeks, then monthly lifelong in pernicious anemia.
- High-dose oral B12 1000-2000 mcg/day can be used in selected cases if malabsorption is not total.

Current-public modifier:

- NICE 2024: lifelong IM B12 for autoimmune gastritis, total gastrectomy, or complete terminal ileal resection.
- If malabsorption is not autoimmune gastritis/total gastrectomy/complete ileal resection, consider IM instead of oral depending severity and context.
- Oral B12 at least 1 mg/day can be considered in some dietary or selected malabsorption contexts.

Monitoring:

- Reticulocyte response is expected after treatment.
- Symptoms may begin improving within weeks, but neurologic recovery can take longer and may be incomplete if delayed.
- For IM replacement, NICE advises not repeating the initial diagnostic B12 test as routine monitoring.

#### Pernicious Anemia

- Treat as B12 malabsorption from autoimmune gastric/intrinsic factor failure.
- Intrinsic factor antibody is more specific; parietal cell antibody is common but less specific.
- Local card flags gastric cancer risk and need for endoscopic follow-up/source-lock.

#### Folate Deficiency

Local ENAM treatment lock:

- Folic acid 1-5 mg/day orally.
- In pregnancy, local card uses 5 mg/day as treatment and continuation through pregnancy if deficient.
- For methotrexate-type folate reductase inhibition, use folinic acid rather than folic acid when the exam asks for the bypass.

Current-public modifier:

- NHS Highland/Right Decisions adult folate-deficient megaloblastic anemia: folic acid 5 mg daily for 4 months; until term in pregnancy; higher doses can be required in malabsorption.
- Confirm or treat B12 if B12 deficiency is possible before giving folate alone.

#### Non-Megaloblastic Causes

- Alcohol: abstinence, nutrition review, folate/B12 assessment if indicated.
- Liver disease: evaluate and treat hepatopathy.
- Hypothyroidism: confirm with TSH/T4 and treat hypothyroidism.
- Reticulocytosis: evaluate hemolysis or bleeding.
- MDS/aplasia: hematology evaluation, marrow studies when indicated.
- Medication-related: identify the drug and adjust with risk-benefit logic.

Take-home: treatment follows the branch: B12 gets B12, folate gets folate only after B12 safety, non-megaloblastic disease gets cause-specific therapy.

### 4. Complications

- B12 deficiency: irreversible neurologic injury if delayed, subacute combined degeneration, ataxia, cognitive/psychiatric symptoms.
- Pernicious anemia: recurrent/lifelong deficiency if not maintained; local card flags gastric cancer risk.
- Folate deficiency in pregnancy: fetal neural tube defect prevention is a separate prevention frame; treatment deficiency still requires B12 safety.
- Severe megaloblastosis: pancytopenia, infections, bleeding, ineffective erythropoiesis mimicking hemolysis.
- Myelodysplastic syndrome: marrow failure and progression risk depending subtype.

Take-home: the high-stakes harm is not anemia itself; it is untreated B12 neurologic damage and missed marrow disease.

### 5. Follow-Up

- Reassess symptoms and CBC response after replacement.
- Reticulocytosis should rise after effective therapy.
- Hemoglobin and MCV should improve over weeks if the diagnosis and adherence are correct.
- If neurologic symptoms persist, worsen, or new symptoms appear: reassess treatment intensity, alternative diagnoses, and need for specialist input.
- If cytopenias persist despite correction of B12/folate/endocrine/liver/drug causes: evaluate marrow disease.

Take-home: response is part of the diagnosis; no response means the branch was wrong, incomplete, or complicated.

### 6. Prognosis

- Nutritional B12/folate deficiency usually responds well if treated early.
- Neurologic B12 deficits can be slow or incomplete if treatment is delayed.
- Pernicious anemia requires long-term/lifelong replacement in most exam and guideline frames.
- Alcohol/liver/hypothyroid macrocytosis improves only when the cause is corrected.
- MDS prognosis depends on marrow genetics/risk and is outside this topic package.

Take-home: macrocytosis is reversible when the cause is reversible, but B12 neurologic injury and marrow clonal disease change the game.

## Mini-Drills

1. VCM 118 + hypersegmented neutrophils + LDH high + indirect bilirubin high + low retics -> ineffective erythropoiesis from megaloblastosis.
2. Gastrectomy + paresthesias + ataxia + glositis + VCM 110 -> B12 deficiency; treat with cobalamin.
3. Pregnancy + no folate + VCM 108 + MMA normal -> folate deficiency.
4. Methotrexate + macrocytosis + hypersegmentation -> folate activation blockade; think folinic acid if asked mechanism/rescue.
5. High MCV + retic high after bleeding -> reticulocytosis, not megaloblastosis.
6. Elderly + persistent leukopenia/thrombocytopenia + dysplasia -> consider MDS.
7. Pernicious anemia biometrics can show leukopenia because all cell lines are affected.
