units.title: Hipertension arterial
units.body:
# Hipertension arterial

## Guion de la enfermedad

La hipertension arterial es presion arterial persistentemente elevada que aumenta riesgo de ACV, cardiopatia, insuficiencia renal, retinopatia y muerte vascular. En examen, HTA no es solo memorizar cifras; es reconocer si debes confirmar, estratificar, tratar cronico, buscar causa secundaria o actuar como emergencia.

La regla mental es: confirma la medicion, busca dano agudo, luego elige el farmaco por comorbilidad.

**Take-home point:** Una cifra alta no basta; la pregunta real es confirmacion, dano de organo o seleccion terapeutica.

## 1. Por que da

### Mecanismos preguntables

- Presion arterial = gasto cardiaco x resistencia vascular periferica.
- Sal/volumen elevan precarga y gasto; por eso ayudan diureticos.
- RAAS aumenta angiotensina II, aldosterona, vasoconstriccion y retencion de sodio; por eso ayudan ACEI/ARB.
- Sistema simpatico aumenta frecuencia, contractilidad y renina; beta-bloqueadores sirven cuando hay indicacion especifica.
- Calcio en musculo liso vascular aumenta vasoconstriccion; calcioantagonistas dihidropiridinicos vasodilatan.
- Cronica: remodelado vascular, hipertrofia ventricular izquierda, nefroesclerosis, retinopatia y dano cerebrovascular.
- Aguda con dano de organo: falla la autorregulacion, aparece dano endotelial, edema, isquemia o diseccion.

### Conceptos de examen

- HTA primaria/esencial es la causa mas frecuente, >90%.
- HTA secundaria se sospecha por edad rara, inicio brusco, severidad, hipokalemia, dano renal, paroxismos, OSA o resistencia.
- HTA resistente exige descartar mala tecnica, mala adherencia y bata blanca.
- Crisis hipertensiva no es solo PA alta; emergencia = PA alta + dano agudo de organo.

**Take-home point:** La fisiopatologia se convierte en farmaco: volumen, RAAS, calcio vascular y simpatico.

## 2. A quien

| Perfil | Pensar |
|---|---|
| Adulto 30-60 con obesidad, sal alta, sedentarismo, alcohol, antecedente familiar | HTA primaria |
| Inicio <30 anos, abrupto, severo o resistente | HTA secundaria |
| HTA + hematuria/proteinuria/creatinina alta | Renal parenquimatosa |
| Creatinina sube con ACEI/ARB, soplo abdominal, rinones asimetricos | Estenosis de arteria renal |
| HTA + hipokalemia/alcalosis | Hiperaldosteronismo primario |
| Crisis paroxisticas + cefalea + sudoracion + palpitaciones | Feocromocitoma |
| Obesidad + ronquidos + somnolencia + non-dipper | SAOS |
| HTA en brazos + pulsos femorales debiles o PA baja en piernas | Coartacion aortica |
| Gestante o posibilidad de embarazo | Evitar ACEI/ARB; usar ruta obstetrica |

### Local frequency

- ENAM card: rank #87/191; 5 questions in 3 years.
- Residentado: 7 direct RM-GT-76 cases plus 1 RM-GT-244 pharmacology case.
- Essalud: topics_current=2; frequency ledger n=11; priority ledger Plata.
- ENCAPS: CIS-2.18 has strong ENT package signal with recurrent HTA questions.

**Take-home point:** HTA comun es primaria; HTA rara, brusca, hipokalemica, renal o resistente es secundaria hasta demostrar lo contrario.

## 3. Como se presenta

### HTA cronica

- Frecuentemente asintomatica.
- Puede aparecer como hallazgo en consulta.
- Cefalea, mareos o vision borrosa no prueban dano agudo por si solos.
- El dano cronico se ve como LVH, albuminuria, deterioro renal, retinopatia, ACV, cardiopatia isquemica o IC.

### Crisis hipertensiva

| Tipo | Definicion practica | Ejemplos |
|---|---|---|
| Urgencia/severa asintomatica | PA muy alta sin dano agudo de organo | Cefalea leve, ansiedad, no focalidad, no EAP/ACS/AKI |
| Emergencia | PA muy alta + dano agudo de organo | Encefalopatia, convulsion, papilledema, EAP, MI, diseccion, stroke, AKI, eclampsia |

### Hallazgos de dano de organo

- Cerebro: encefalopatia, convulsion, confusion, deficit focal, ACV.
- Retina: hemorragias, exudados, papilledema.
- Corazon: dolor toracico, STEMI/NSTEMI, edema pulmonar, IC.
- Aorta: dolor desgarrador, deficit de pulso, diseccion.
- Rinon: AKI, creatinina sube, hematuria/proteinuria.
- Embarazo: preeclampsia/eclampsia.

**Take-home point:** El dano de organo convierte un numero en emergencia.

## Manejo

## 1. Diagnostico

### Paso 1. Medir bien

- Paciente sentado y en reposo.
- Brazalete adecuado.
- Brazo a nivel del corazon.
- Medir ambos brazos al inicio.
- Repetir si esta elevada.
- No diagnosticar HTA cronica por una cifra aislada durante dolor, ansiedad, abstinencia o crisis aguda.

### Paso 2. Confirmar segun contexto

- Local ENAM/ENCAPS: minimo 2 mediciones elevadas en dias distintos.
- MAPA/ABPM o home BP ayudan a confirmar y descartar bata blanca.
- ENCAPS HIST-088: PA 140/90 en consulta puede pedir confirmar con MAPA.
- Si hay dano agudo de organo, no esperas confirmacion ambulatoria; manejas emergencia.

### Paso 3. Usar el umbral correcto

| Sistema/producto | Umbral que debes recordar |
|---|---|
| MINSA/OMS/ENCAPS | HTA >=140/90 en 2 mediciones |
| ENAM/ESC-ESH | Grado 1 desde 140/90; grado 2 desde 160/100; grado 3 desde 180/110 |
| ACC/AHA 2017/2025 si lo nombran | Stage 1 desde 130/80; stage 2 desde 140/90 |
| ESC 2024 current modifier | Elevated BP debajo de 140/90; hypertension alrededor de >=140/90 |

### Paso 4. Evaluacion inicial

Basica:

- Creatinina/eGFR.
- Electrolitos, especialmente potasio.
- Glucosa/HbA1c segun riesgo.
- Perfil lipidico.
- Orina: proteinuria/hematuria; albuminuria si disponible.
- ECG para LVH/ischemia/ritmo.
- Fondo de ojo si severa, sintomas visuales o sospecha maligna.
- Chest X-ray/echo segun disnea, IC, LVH o disponibilidad.

Local RM lock: en un paciente con HTA y sospecha de compromiso cardiopulmonar, `RES-COMBINED-06033` responde EKG + creatinina + chest X-ray.

**Take-home point:** Confirmas HTA cronica con medicion; evalua dano con rinon, orina, ECG y organos blanco.

## 2. Clasificacion

### Por cifras ENAM/ESC-ESH

| Categoria | PAS | PAD |
|---|---|---|
| Optima | <120 | <80 |
| Normal | 120-129 | 80-84 |
| Normal-alta | 130-139 | 85-89 |
| HTA grado 1 | 140-159 | 90-99 |
| HTA grado 2 | 160-179 | 100-109 |
| HTA grado 3 | >=180 | >=110 |
| Sistolica aislada | >=140 | <=90 |

### Por situacion clinica

- HTA primaria/esencial.
- HTA secundaria.
- HTA de bata blanca.
- HTA enmascarada.
- HTA resistente.
- HTA maligna.
- Urgencia hipertensiva.
- Emergencia hipertensiva.

### Por riesgo

Sube riesgo si hay:

- Diabetes.
- CKD/albuminuria/proteinuria.
- LVH.
- Enfermedad cardiovascular establecida.
- ACV/AIT.
- Tabaquismo.
- Dislipidemia.
- Edad avanzada.
- Obesidad.
- Antecedente familiar.

**Take-home point:** Clasificar por cifra ayuda, pero clasificar por organo y riesgo decide manejo.

## 3. Manejo

### A. Estilo de vida

Siempre:

- Bajar peso si sobrepeso/obesidad.
- Dieta tipo DASH o patron saludable.
- Reducir sal; ENCAPS/OMS pregunta <5 g/dia de sal.
- Ejercicio aerobico y fuerza segun tolerancia.
- Reducir alcohol.
- Dejar tabaco.
- Dormir y tratar OSA si existe.
- Evitar AINE excesivos, descongestionantes/simpaticomimeticos, estimulantes y exceso de regaliz si aplica.

**Take-home point:** Estilo de vida no es decoracion: puede decidir grado 1 bajo riesgo y potencia todos los farmacos.

### B. Tratamiento cronico inicial

Opciones de primera linea:

- Thiazide/thiazide-like diuretic.
- ACEI or ARB.
- Long-acting dihydropyridine CCB, e.g., amlodipine/nifedipine.
- Beta-blocker when there is a specific indication or European/local exam framing.

Local/product anchors:

- ENCAPS uncomplicated essential HTA without comorbidity: thiazide diuretic.
- DM or CKD with albuminuria/proteinuria: ACEI or ARB if no contraindication.
- Older adult with isolated systolic HTA: dihydropyridine CCB is classic.
- CAD/tachyarrhythmia/HFrEF: beta-blocker can be useful, but not universal.
- Resistant HTA: confirm with MAPA/adherence, then spironolactone if renal function/potassium allow.

Combination logic:

- Grade 1 low risk or frail elderly: lifestyle first or monotherapy depending source/risk.
- Grade 2-3 or high risk: pharmacotherapy from start, often combination.
- Avoid ACEI + ARB routine combination.
- Avoid triple RAAS blockade ACEI + ARB + spironolactone.

**Take-home point:** The drug answer comes from the comorbidity, not from the word HTA.

### C. Hypertensive urgency/severe asymptomatic BP

If no acute target-organ damage:

- Confirm BP and technique.
- Assess symptoms and organ damage carefully.
- Restart, adjust, or begin oral therapy.
- Gradual reduction over 24-48 hours or days depending setting/protocol.
- Close follow-up.
- Do not rapidly normalize with IV drugs just because the number is high.

**Take-home point:** Severe number without acute damage is not an ICU-IV reflex.

### D. Hypertensive emergency

If severe BP plus acute organ damage:

- Admit/monitor.
- IV therapy.
- Reduce BP in controlled fashion; common exam anchor: about 25% reduction in first hour, then gradual.
- Choose drug by organ context.

Local RM locks:

- Encephalopathy/papilledema/seizure: nitroprusside in `RES-COMBINED-00001`.
- STEMI/ACS with severe BP: nitroglycerin in `RES-COMBINED-03207`.
- Pulmonary edema with severe BP: nitroprusside in `RES-COMBINED-04029`.
- Retinopathy grade III treated with IV labetalol: target DBP 100-105 in `RES-COMBINED-05830`.

Special emergency logic:

- Aortic dissection usually needs rapid HR/BP control with beta-blockade first, plus vasodilator if needed.
- Stroke BP handling is protocol-specific; do not automatically lower aggressively.
- Eclampsia/preeclampsia belongs to obstetric route with magnesium sulfate and pregnancy-safe antihypertensives.

**Take-home point:** Emergency HTA is organ-specific: MI, EAP, encephalopathy and dissection do not use the same reflex.

### E. HTA secundaria

Basic clue-to-test table:

| Suspicion | Clue | Test |
|---|---|---|
| Renal parenchymal | Hematuria, proteinuria, creatinine high, recurrent UTI | Urinalysis, creatinine/eGFR, renal ultrasound |
| Renal artery stenosis | Bruit, asymmetric kidneys, creatinine rise after ACEI/ARB | Doppler/CTA/MRA by protocol |
| Primary aldosteronism | Hypokalemia, resistant HTA | Aldosterone-renin ratio |
| Pheochromocytoma | Paroxysms, headache, sweating, palpitations | Plasma or urine metanephrines/catecholamines |
| Cushing | Central obesity, striae, moon facies | Cortisol testing |
| OSA | Snoring, sleepiness, obesity, non-dipper | Polysomnography |
| Coarctation | Arm-leg BP difference, weak femoral pulses | Aortic imaging |

**Take-home point:** Resistant or atypical HTA deserves a cause, not just a fourth random pill.

## 4. Complicaciones

- ACV ischemic or hemorrhagic.
- AIT.
- Coronary artery disease and MI.
- Heart failure, especially diastolic HF with LVH.
- Atrial fibrillation.
- CKD and albuminuria/proteinuria.
- Retinopathy.
- Peripheral artery disease.
- Aortic dissection.
- Cognitive decline/vascular dementia.

**Take-home point:** HTA kills by brain, heart, kidney, retina and vessels.

## 5. Seguimiento

- Recheck BP after treatment start or change according severity and protocol.
- Monitor home BP/MAPA if available.
- Check creatinine and potassium after ACEI/ARB/MRA/diuretic changes.
- Monitor adverse effects: cough/angioedema, edema, hypokalemia, hyperkalemia, gout, bradycardia, orthostasis.
- Assess adherence, cost, access, salt/alcohol/AINEs.
- Annual or periodic organ-damage review: kidney, urine albumin/protein, ECG, cardiovascular risk.
- In frail older adults, check orthostatic symptoms and falls.

**Take-home point:** Follow-up is not "BP only"; it is BP plus kidney, potassium, adherence and side effects.

## 6. Pronostico

- BP reduction lowers stroke, MI, HF and kidney progression risk.
- Best prognosis: confirmed diagnosis, adherence, comorbidity-tailored treatment, risk-factor control.
- Worse prognosis: diabetes/CKD, prior CVD, LVH, albuminuria, smoking, persistent severe BP, poor access, resistant/secondary HTA untreated.
- Hypertensive emergency prognosis depends on speed, organ involved and avoiding overcorrection.

**Take-home point:** Chronic control saves decades; emergency control saves organs today.

## Trampas de examen

- Using 130/80 in a MINSA/ENCAPS question without AHA/ACC wording.
- Using 140/90 when the question explicitly says ACC/AHA.
- Calling severe asymptomatic BP an emergency.
- Normalizing BP rapidly in urgency.
- Forgetting organ damage: papilledema, pulmonary edema, MI, AKI, dissection.
- Giving beta-blocker to asthma as if universal.
- Giving ACEI/ARB in pregnancy.
- Combining ACEI + ARB routinely.
- Missing ACEI cough/angioedema.
- Treating resistant HTA before confirming MAPA/adherence.
- Ignoring secondary HTA clues.

units.title: Paciente terminal
units.body:
# Paciente terminal

## Guion del concepto

El tema no pregunta "la muerte" en abstracto. Pregunta si el medico reconoce que en un paciente terminal el objetivo cambia: ya no siempre es curar o prolongar vida, sino aliviar sufrimiento, respetar autonomia, evitar tratamientos futiles y acompanar una muerte natural.

**Take-home point:** En paciente terminal, la respuesta correcta casi siempre sale de 3 preguntas: que se intenta, si es proporcionado y quien puede decidir.

## Modelo cognitivo de aplicacion

### Tarea cognitiva

Clasificar una conducta de fin de vida y elegir la accion eticamente correcta.

### Pregunta mental madre

```text
Ante este paciente terminal, la accion busca causar muerte, aliviar sufrimiento, evitar futilidad, respetar rechazo, o prolongar agonia?
```

### Regla de oro

Si la muerte es el objetivo directo, piensa en eutanasia/homicidio piadoso. Si el objetivo es aliviar sufrimiento o evitar futilidad, piensa en palliative care, sedacion paliativa, LET u ortotanasia.

## Definicion operativa

| Concepto | Definicion usable | Que NO es | Como se pregunta |
|---|---|---|---|
| Paciente terminal | Persona con enfermedad avanzada, irreversible, progresiva, sin expectativa razonable de curacion, con necesidad de control de sintomas y decisiones proporcionales | No es sinonimo de abandono | Cancer avanzado, organ failure, agonia, familia presente |
| Cuidados paliativos | Atencion activa para mejorar calidad de vida de paciente y familia, controlando sufrimiento fisico, psicologico, social y espiritual | No es "no hacer nada" | Dolor, disnea, delirium, apoyo familiar |
| Ortotanasia | Permitir muerte natural con acompanamiento y alivio | No es eutanasia | Oxigeno/analgesia/confort sin encarnizamiento |
| Distanasia | Prolongacion artificial, dolorosa e inutil de la agonia | No es maximalismo correcto | Intubar/proceder sin beneficio en terminal irreversible |
| LET | No iniciar o retirar medidas desproporcionadas/futiles | No es matar; no es abandono | No RCP/VM/dialisis/aminas si no benefician |
| Sedacion paliativa | Disminucion deliberada de conciencia para sintoma refractario en paciente terminal, con consentimiento y proporcion | No busca causar muerte | Midazolam, disnea/dolor/delirium refractario |
| Eutanasia | Accion directa orientada a terminar la vida del paciente, a peticion suya, realizada por medico | No es LET ni sedacion | "Le administra farmaco para que muera" |
| Suicidio asistido | Medico facilita el medio; paciente se autoadministra | No es retiro de tratamiento | Prescripcion para autoadministracion letal |
| Futilidad | Medida incapaz de lograr beneficio fisiologico o clinico relevante | No es "familia no quiere" | Procedimiento sin beneficio real |

**Take-home point:** La misma consecuencia externa, muerte posterior, cambia de nombre segun intencion, proporcionalidad y contexto.

## Marco oficial y fuente de verdad

| Fuente | Que establece | Ambito | Preguntabilidad |
|---|---|---|---|
| ENAM CTO Bioetica | Diferencia eutanasia, sedacion paliativa, LET, ortotanasia, distanasia | Examen ENAM | Muy alta |
| CMP 2023 | Derecho a informacion, rechazo de tratamiento, muerte natural sin prolongacion injustificada, cuidados paliativos, no encarnizamiento | Peru deontologico | Alta |
| Codigo Penal Peru Art. 112 | Homicidio piadoso: matar a enfermo incurable que lo solicita por dolores intolerables esta tipificado | Peru legal | Alta para no confundir con palliation |
| MINSA RM 939-2021 | Plan Nacional de Cuidados Paliativos para enfermedades oncologicas y no oncologicas | Peru salud publica | Media; vigencia operativa QA |
| WHO | Palliative care improves quality of life of patient and family; early, integrated, team-based | Salud global | Alta conceptual |
| WMA Venice 2022 | End-of-life palliative care is good medical care, focused on dignity and symptom relief | Etica internacional | Media |

## Tabla concepto x aplicacion x distractor

| Concepto | Cuando aplicarlo | Caso tipico | Distractor | Como descartarlo |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Eutanasia | Acto directo cuyo objetivo es causar muerte | Medico administra farmaco letal a pedido | Sedacion paliativa | En sedacion, el objetivo es aliviar sintoma |
| Sedacion paliativa | Sintoma refractario con sufrimiento intolerable | Disnea terminal, midazolam, consentimiento | Eutanasia indirecta | Termino inseguro; muerte no es objetivo |
| LET | Tratamiento desproporcionado/futil | No iniciar VM o retirar aminas en terminal irreversible | Eutanasia pasiva | LET evita futilidad; no causa muerte directa |
| Ortotanasia | Muerte natural con comfort care | Analgesia, oxigeno, familia, no encarnizamiento | Abandono | Hay cuidado activo de sintomas |
| Distanasia | Medidas invasivas sin beneficio prolongan agonia | Intubacion en agonia irreversible | Beneficencia | Beneficencia no obliga a dano futil |
| Refusal | Paciente competente rechaza tratamiento | Rechaza quimioterapia paliativa toxica | LET | Refusal nace del paciente; LET del juicio clinico |
| Autonomia | Paciente decide informado | Quiere pasar ultimos meses en casa | Beneficencia paternalista | El paciente define su propio bien |
| Privilegio terapeutico | Retener informacion solo si dano grave directo | Situacion excepcional | "No preocupar a la familia" | Familia no es razon valida |

**Take-home point:** La trampa mas rentable del examen es confundir LET/sedacion con eutanasia.

## Algoritmo de aplicacion en caso

```text
Paciente terminal o en agonia
-> Hay decision de fin de vida?
   -> si: identificar intencion
      -> muerte como objetivo directo: eutanasia / homicidio piadoso
      -> alivio de sintoma refractario: sedacion paliativa
      -> evitar medida futil/desproporcionada: LET
      -> acompanamiento y muerte natural: ortotanasia
      -> prolongar agonia sin beneficio: distanasia
   -> luego: verificar competencia/consentimiento/familia/documentacion
```

## Subbloque: Bioetica

| Dilema | Principio implicado | Conducta correcta | Distractor frecuente |
|---|---|---|---|
| Paciente competente rechaza quimio | Autonomia | Respetar, documentar, ofrecer paliativos | Forzar por beneficencia |
| Familia pide ocultar diagnostico | Autonomia, veracidad | Informar al paciente de forma comprensible salvo excepcion real | "No preocuparlo" |
| Dolor/disnea refractaria terminal | Beneficencia, no maleficencia | Sedacion paliativa proporcional con consentimiento | Eutanasia indirecta |
| UCI futil en agonia irreversible | No maleficencia | LET y cuidados paliativos | "Todo lo posible" |
| Solicitud de muerte directa | Vida/dignidad/legalidad | No realizar accion directa de muerte; aliviar sufrimiento | Confundir con sedacion |
| Recurso escaso en UCI | Justicia | Proporcionalidad y beneficio esperado | Usar por presion familiar |

## Manejo clinico-educativo

### Diagnostico de situacion terminal

- Confirmar enfermedad avanzada, irreversible, progresiva y sin expectativa razonable de curacion.
- Reconocer fase de ultimos dias si hay deterioro rapido, somnolencia, disfagia, debilidad extrema, oliguria, delirium o disnea refractaria.
- Definir objetivo de cuidado: curativo, modificador de enfermedad, paliativo, confort, o ultimos dias.
- Revaluar farmacos y medidas: retirar lo que no da confort ni beneficio real.

**Take-home point:** La terminalidad no elimina el cuidado; cambia el objetivo del cuidado.

### Manejo de comunicacion

- Informar diagnostico, pronostico y opciones en lenguaje comprensible.
- Verificar comprension con "teach-back".
- Preguntar metas del paciente: vivir mas, estar en casa, no sufrir, despedirse, evitar UCI, recibir tratamiento si aporta.
- Integrar a la familia si el paciente lo autoriza o si el paciente no puede decidir.
- Documentar preferencias, capacidad, informacion dada, decisiones y plan.

**Take-home point:** Buena bioetica no es elegir por el paciente; es hacer posible que el paciente elija.

### Manejo paliativo

- Control de dolor: usar escalera analgesica y opioides si corresponde.
- Control de disnea: oxigeno si hipoxemia, opioides para sensacion de falta de aire, medidas de confort.
- Delirium: buscar causas reversibles si aporta; en ultimos dias, tratar agitacion y sufrimiento.
- Nauseas, secreciones, ansiedad y insomnio: tratar por sintoma dominante.
- Sedacion paliativa: considerar solo si sintoma refractario, sufrimiento intolerable, terminalidad, consentimiento y documentacion.

**Take-home point:** Paliativo no significa menos medicina; significa medicina alineada con dignidad y sufrimiento.

## Errores frecuentes

| Error | Por que seduce | Regla correctiva |
|---|---|---|
| Llamar sedacion "eutanasia indirecta" | La muerte puede ocurrir despues | La intencion decide: alivio no es matar |
| Llamar LET "eutanasia pasiva" | Se retira/no inicia soporte | LET evita futilidad; la enfermedad causa la muerte |
| Creer que palliative care es abandono | No busca curar | Es atencion activa de sintomas y familia |
| Dejar que familia anule al paciente competente | Familia presiona y esta angustiada | Autonomia del paciente competente prevalece |
| Ocultar diagnostico para "beneficio" | Parece compasivo | Es paternalismo si no hay dano grave directo |
| Dar medidas invasivas solo por "hacer todo" | Confunde tecnologia con cuidado | Si no beneficia y dana, es distanasia |
| Crear preguntas DNR/directiva peruana sin fuente | CTO lo ensena | ENCAPS guardrail: bloquear hasta legal source-lock |

## Product modifiers

### ENAM

- Resolver por definicion precisa.
- Fenotipo P15: dilema etico.
- Mayor rendimiento: distinguir eutanasia, sedacion paliativa, LET, ortotanasia y distanasia.
- No dejar que los distractores "pasiva" o "indirecta" borren la intencion.

### EsSalud

- Esperar definiciones, deberes institucionales, no encarnizamiento, palliative care y documentacion.
- Local policy exacta queda en QA.

### ENCAPS

- Usar CMP/autonomia/consentimiento/rechazo/cuidado paliativo.
- No generar MCQ Peru con DNR/directiva anticipada/no intubacion como clave legal hasta cerrar QA.
- Si el caso es paciente competente que rechaza tratamiento: respetar, documentar y ofrecer alternativas/paliativos.

### Residentado

- No hay RM directo encontrado.
- Si aparece, probablemente sera fineza de bioetica clinica: autonomia, proporcionalidad, futility, comite de etica, ICU, o cuidados paliativos.

## Mini-drills

1. Cancer terminal, dolor refractario, midazolam para dormir y aliviar sufrimiento: sedacion paliativa.
2. Medico administra dosis letal para que el paciente muera: euthanasia/homicidio piadoso frame.
3. No se inicia VM en paciente agonico irreversible y se dan opioides: LET/orthotanasia segun el stem.
4. Familia pide no decirle al paciente que tiene cancer: autonomia/informacion; no ocultar por comodidad familiar.
5. Paciente competente rechaza quimioterapia que prolonga 3 meses pero deteriora calidad de vida: respetar autonomia y activar paliativos.

## Trazabilidad

- Guias / normas: MINSA RM 939-2021; CMP 2023; Codigo Penal Peru Art. 112.
- Ground truths / manuales: CTO Bioetica in ENAM cards; ENCAPS EI-1.2/EI-1.3 guardrails.
- Bancos / fenotipos: ENAM `072_paciente_terminal.md`, `023_principios_bioeticos.md`.
- Transcripts: no direct transcript promoted.
- Literatura externa: WHO palliative care; WMA Venice 2022; WMA euthanasia/assisted suicide 2019.

## QA

- Estado: `qa_pending`.
- Riesgos de drift: palliative-care national policy updates; advance directives; DNR/no-RCP; local institutional protocols.
- Pendientes: source-lock Peru legal/institutional implementation before publication as protocol.

units.title: Sindrome de ulcera genital
units.body:
# Sindrome de ulcera genital

## Guion del cluster

El sindrome de ulcera genital es una pregunta de patron. La vineta te entrega dolor, numero, base, borde, vesiculas y adenopatias; con eso debes elegir agente, diagnostico, prueba o tratamiento.

**Take-home point:** No empieces por memorizar antibioticos; empieza por dolor + base + adenopatia.

## Modelo cognitivo de aplicacion

### Tarea cognitiva

Reconocer el patron clinico y separar el imitador mas cercano: sifilis versus chancroide versus herpes, con LGV/donovanosis como diferenciales de menor frecuencia.

### Pregunta mental madre

```text
La ulcera es dolorosa o indolora, limpia o sucia, vesicular o indurada, y que tipo de ganglio la acompana?
```

### Regla de oro

Hard-clean-painless = sifilis. Vesicles-painful = herpes. Soft-dirty-painful-node = chancroid.

## Definicion operativa

| Concepto | Definicion usable | Que NO es | Como se pregunta |
|---|---|---|---|
| Sindrome de ulcera genital | Ulcera genital, anal o perianal de probable transmision sexual | No siempre se puede diagnosticar solo por examen fisico | Diagnostico, agente, tratamiento o prueba |
| Sifilis primaria | Chancro duro, limpio, indoloro, con nodes no dolorosos si aparecen | No requiere siempre adenopatia | Ulcera unica indurada sin dolor |
| Herpes genital | Vesiculas dolorosas agrupadas que ulceran | No es solo "ulcera dolorosa" sin vesiculas | Ardor, fiebre, vesiculas en racimo |
| Chancroide | Chancro blando, doloroso, sucio/purulento, nodes dolorosos | No es sifilis si es blando y doloroso | Ulceras profundas/excavadas dolorosas |
| LGV | Ulcera fugaz + linfadenitis o proctitis por C. trachomatis L1-L3 | No es uretritis simple | MSM/proctitis o bubo inguinal |
| Donovanosis | Ulcera granulomatosa indolora, sin adenopatia verdadera | No es frecuente local | Cuerpos de Donovan |

**Take-home point:** El examen premia reconocer el patron, no recitar todas las ITS.

## Diagnostico y presentacion

### Sifilis primaria

- Agente: `Treponema pallidum`.
- Incubacion clasica: alrededor de 21 dias.
- Ulcera: unica, dura, cartilaginosa, limpia, indolora.
- Adenopatias: bilaterales, duras, indoloras, no supurativas.
- Histologia en card: celulas plasmaticas.
- Puede resolver sola en semanas; eso no significa curacion.
- En VIH puede ser multiple o atipica.

**Take-home point:** Painless and indurated is syphilis until proven otherwise.

### Herpes genital

- Agente: HSV/VHS-2 mas frecuente, HSV/VHS-1 tambien posible.
- Lesion: vesiculas dolorosas agrupadas que se ulceran.
- Sintomas: ardor, dolor, fiebre/malestar en primoinfeccion.
- Adenopatias: dolorosas, usualmente bilaterales.
- Diagnostico: PCR/NAAT de lesion si disponible; Tzanck muestra celulas gigantes multinucleadas como clue clasico.
- Tratamiento: aciclovir/valaciclovir/famciclovir; recidivas son frecuentes, sobre todo con HSV-2.

**Take-home point:** Si la vineta dice "vesiculas en racimo", la respuesta ya casi esta escrita.

### Chancroide

- Agente: `Haemophilus ducreyi`.
- Incubacion: 1-3 dias, el mas precoz en la tabla ENAM.
- Ulcera: blanda, dolorosa, sucia/purulenta, profunda o excavada, a menudo multiple.
- Adenopatias: dolorosas, pueden supurar o fistulizar.
- Tratamiento clasico: azithromycin 1 g PO once.
- Diagnostico de protocolo: excluir syphilis and HSV when possible.

**Take-home point:** Painful dirty ulcer plus painful node is chancroid in RM/ENAM stems.

### LGV

- Agente: `Chlamydia trachomatis` L1-L3.
- Clasico: ulcera inicial pequena/fugaz, luego adenopatias inguinales dolorosas y fistulizantes.
- Moderno/high-yield: MSM with proctitis or rectal ulcer.
- Tratamiento clasico: doxycycline 100 mg PO every 12 h for 21 days.

**Take-home point:** LGV is lymphatic chlamydia; the node/proctitis can dominate more than the ulcer.

### Donovanosis

- Agente: `Klebsiella granulomatis`.
- Lesion: ulceras granulomatosas, beefy, indoloras, sangran facil.
- Adenopatia verdadera: absent.
- Diagnostico: biopsy or smear with Donovan bodies.
- Tratamiento: azithromycin-based prolonged treatment until healing in guideline framing.
- ENAM card: rare locally; keep as distractor.

**Take-home point:** Painless granulomatous ulcer plus no nodes = donovanosis, but local exams prioritize syphilis/herpes/chancroid.

## Pruebas

| Scenario | Test clave | Interpretation |
|---|---|---|
| Suspected syphilis | RPR/VDRL plus treponemal test | Need both type and context |
| Follow-up syphilis | Quantitative RPR/VDRL | Titers should fall after treatment |
| Treponemal test positive | FTA-ABS/TPHA/TPPA | Can stay positive for life |
| Early primary syphilis | Serology can be negative | Treat/retest if high suspicion |
| Active herpes lesion | PCR/NAAT | More sensitive than Tzanck |
| Tzanck clue | Multinucleated giant cells | Classic but not specific |
| Donovanosis | Biopsy/smear | Donovan bodies |
| Neurosyphilis | VDRL in CSF | Specific; negative does not fully exclude |

**Take-home point:** RPR/VDRL tracks activity; treponemal tests track exposure/confirmation, not cure.

## Manejo

### Etiologic ENAM/RM treatment

| Diagnosis | Treatment anchor |
|---|---|
| Primary/secondary/early latent syphilis | Benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million IU IM once |
| Late latent/unknown duration syphilis | Benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million IU IM weekly x3 |
| Neurosyphilis/ocular syphilis | Aqueous penicillin G IV 10-14 days |
| Chancroid | Azithromycin 1 g PO once |
| LGV | Doxycycline 100 mg PO q12h x21 days |
| Genital herpes | Acyclovir/valacyclovir/famciclovir depending episode/protocol |
| Donovanosis | Azithromycin-based prolonged regimen until lesions heal |

### Peru/ENCAPS syndromic management

- If first-level setting lacks etiologic diagnosis, use syndromic management.
- Local ENCAPS NTS 240-2026 lock for genital ulcer syndrome:
- Benzathine benzylpenicillin 2,400,000 IU IM single dose.
- Plus acyclovir 400 mg PO every 12 h for 5 days.
- Treat sexual contacts from previous 90 days.
- Offer rapid tests for HIV, syphilis, and hepatitis B in all STI syndromes.
- Counsel with 4C: counseling, compliance, contacts, condoms.

**Take-home point:** Etiologic exam asks one disease; first-level Peru asks safe syndromic coverage and screening.

## Complications and follow-up

- Syphilis untreated can progress to secondary, latent, tertiary, cardiovascular and neurologic disease.
- Syphilis in pregnancy risks congenital syphilis; penicillin is required.
- HSV recurs and increases HIV transmission risk through mucosal lesions.
- Chancroid can cause suppurative buboes/fistulas.
- LGV can cause strictures, fistulas, chronic proctocolitis, and elephantiasis.
- Donovanosis can scar and destroy tissue.
- All ulcerative STIs increase HIV acquisition/transmission risk.

**Take-home point:** The ulcer is also an HIV-risk amplifier; screening is part of treatment.

## Product modifiers

### ENAM

- Use exact differential table.
- Syphilis: hard, painless, clean.
- Herpes: painful grouped vesicles.
- Chancroid: painful soft dirty ulcer plus painful node.
- LGV: Chlamydia L1-L3 and doxycycline 21 days.
- Donovanosis: Donovan bodies, no nodes, rare.

### EsSalud

- Single local count; likely asks exact definition, treatment, or test.
- Institutional STI pathway still QA pending.

### ENCAPS

- Use Peru NTS 240-2026 syndromic regimen for first-level care.
- Always offer rapid HIV/syphilis/HepB testing in STI syndromes.
- RPR quantitative for syphilis monitoring; treponemal tests stay positive.
- Pregnancy syphilis: penicillin, not doxycycline.

### Residentado

- RM-GT-27 is pattern recognition plus treatment key.
- Do not overcomplicate a clean painless indurated ulcer: answer syphilis/penicillin.
- Do not call painful deep irregular ulcers herpes unless vesicles are described.
- Historical RM chlamydia key is azithromycin 1 g once; current guideline tension remains QA.

## Mini-drills

1. Painless clean indurated penile ulcer: syphilis; benzathine penicillin.
2. Painful grouped vesicles plus burning: herpes genital; acyclovir/valacyclovir frame.
3. Painful deep irregular excavated ulcers plus painful node: chancroid; azithromycin 1 g once.
4. Transient ulcer plus painful inguinal nodes/proctitis: LGV; doxycycline 21 days.
5. First-level Peru ulcer syndrome without lab: benzathine penicillin plus acyclovir plus rapid tests.

## Trazabilidad

- Guias / normas: Peru NTS 240-2026 page; CDC STI guidelines; WHO symptomatic STI guideline.
- Ground truths / manuales: ENAM CTO infectious diseases/dermatology card.
- Bancos / fenotipos: ENAM `105_sindrome_de_ulcera_genital.md`; RM-GT-27 cases.
- Transcripts: no direct transcript promoted.
- Literatura externa: CDC/WHO official guidance.

## QA

- Estado: `qa_pending`.
- Riesgos de drift: STI treatment regimens, antimicrobial resistance, local NTS tables, chlamydia regimen updates.
- Pendientes: extract NTS 240-2026 PDF and EsSalud local protocol.

units.title: Glandula suprarrenal: Patologias
units.body:
# Glandula suprarrenal: Patologias

## 0. Idea nuclear

- La suprarrenal se pregunta como una matriz de hormonas, no como una lista de enfermedades.
- Cortex:
  - Glomerulosa -> aldosterone -> volumen, sodio, potasio, presion.
  - Fasciculata -> cortisol -> metabolismo, estres, presion, glucosa.
  - Reticularis -> androgens -> virilizacion/HSC.
- Medulla:
  - Catecholamines -> paroxismos adrenergicos.
- El examen casi siempre da una pista dominante:
  - Fenotipo cushingoide -> cortisol alto.
  - Hipotension, hiperpigmentacion, Na bajo, K alto -> cortisol/aldosterone bajo.
  - HTA mas K bajo -> aldosterone alto.
  - Cefalea, palpitaciones, sudoracion -> catecholamines altas.

Take-home point: primero nombra la hormona; despues nombra la enfermedad.

## 1. Guion de enfermedad y mecanismo

### Cushing syndrome

- Concepto: exposicion cronica a glucocorticoides.
- Causa mas comun global: glucocorticoides exogenos.
- Causa endogena mas comun: hipofisaria ACTH-dependiente, llamada enfermedad de Cushing.
- ACTH-independiente: adenoma/carcinoma suprarrenal o hiperplasia adrenal.
- ACTH-dependiente ectopico: cancer microcitico y otros tumores neuroendocrinos.
- Mecanismo examinable:
  - Cortisol alto causa hiperglicemia, catabolismo muscular, fragilidad cutanea, HTA, osteoporosis e inmunosupresion.
  - ACTH alta causa hiperpigmentacion por actividad melanotropica relacionada.

Take-home point: Cushing se confirma por hipercortisolismo y se localiza por ACTH.

### Addison / adrenal insufficiency

- Concepto: deficit de cortisol; si es primaria tambien hay deficit de mineralocorticoides.
- Primaria: falla suprarrenal; ACTH alta.
- Central: falla hipofisaria/hipotalamica o supresion por corticoides; ACTH baja o inadecuada.
- Causas de primaria:
  - Autoimmune adrenalitis en paises de altos recursos.
  - Tuberculosis como gatillo mundial y local de examen.
  - Hemorragia bilateral, infeccion severa, metastasis, infiltracion.
- Causa comun de crisis: retiro brusco de corticoides cronicos o estres/infeccion sin aumentar dosis.
- Mecanismo examinable:
  - Falta cortisol -> hipotension, hipoglucemia, debilidad, mala respuesta al estres.
  - Falta aldosterone -> perdida de sodio, hipovolemia, hiperpotasemia, acidosis.
  - ACTH alta -> hiperpigmentacion.

Take-home point: hiperpigmentacion mas hiperpotasemia significa primaria hasta demostrar lo contrario.

### Primary aldosteronism

- Concepto: secrecion autonoma de aldosterone con renina suprimida.
- Causas principales:
  - Hiperplasia bilateral.
  - Adenoma productor de aldosterone, classicamente sindrome de Conn.
- Mecanismo examinable:
  - Aldosterone retiene sodio/agua y elimina potasio/hidrogeniones.
  - Resultado clasico: HTA, hipokalemia, alcalosis metabolica.
- Caveat moderno:
  - La hipokalemia no siempre esta presente; no excluye el diagnostico.

Take-home point: HTA resistente o HTA con K bajo debe activar aldosteronismo primario.

### Pheochromocytoma/paraganglioma

- Concepto: tumor productor de catecholamines; adrenal si nace en medulla, extra-adrenal si paraganglioma.
- Asociaciones: MEN2/RET, VHL, NF1, SDH.
- Mecanismo examinable:
  - Descargas de catecholamines causan vasoconstriccion, taquicardia, hiperglicemia, sudoracion, crisis hipertensiva.
- La regla vieja del "10%" sirve como memoria historica, pero no debe reemplazar genetica moderna.

Take-home point: paroxismos adrenergicos mas HTA = metanephrines y alpha bloqueo antes de beta.

### HSC / adrenal incidentaloma

- HSC: defecto congenito de sintesis esteroidea, classically 21-hydroxylase deficiency.
- Marcador de tamizaje: 17-OH progesterone.
- Riesgo: perdida de sal, shock neonatal, alteraciones genitales externas.
- Incidentaloma: masa adrenal encontrada por imagen no pedida por sospecha adrenal.
- El incidentaloma exige dos preguntas:
  - Parece maligno?
  - Produce hormonas?

Take-home point: HSC entra aqui como puente ENCAPS neonatal; incidentaloma entra como puente clinico moderno.

## 2. A quien: epidemiologia y factores de riesgo

| Condition | Patient/exam setting | Risk clues |
|---|---|---|
| Cushing | Adult woman, diabetes/HTA/obesity atypical, steroid exposure | Chronic glucocorticoids, pituitary adenoma, adrenal mass, ectopic ACTH |
| Addison | Adult with chronic asthenia, GI symptoms, hypotension | Autoimmune disease, TB, chronic steroid withdrawal, sepsis/hemorrhage |
| Primary aldosteronism | Hypertensive adult | Resistant HTN, hypokalemia, adrenal nodule, sleep apnea, early stroke/HTN family history |
| Pheochromocytoma | Paroxysmal symptoms or adrenal mass | MEN2, VHL, NF1, SDH, young patient, bilateral/multifocal tumor |
| HSC | Newborn/child or neonatal screen | Salt-wasting, ambiguous genitalia, high 17-OHP |

Take-home point: local RM loves TB/Addison; ENAM expects the entire adrenal map.

## 3. Como: clinical presentation

### Cushing clinical anchors

- More specific:
  - Wide red-purple striae >1 cm.
  - Proximal myopathy.
  - Easy bruising.
  - Facial plethora.
- Common but nonspecific:
  - Central obesity.
  - Moon face.
  - Dorsocervical fat pad.
  - Diabetes, HTA, mood symptoms, osteoporosis, infections.
- Ectopic ACTH clue:
  - Severe hypercortisolism with hypokalemia, alkalosis, hyperpigmentation, muscle weakness, sometimes without classic habitus.

Take-home point: proximal weakness and wide purple striae beat generic obesity.

### Addison/adrenal insufficiency clinical anchors

- Chronic:
  - Asthenia, weight loss, anorexia.
  - Nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain.
  - Orthostatic hypotension.
  - Salt craving.
  - Hyperpigmentation in primary disease.
- Labs:
  - Hyponatremia.
  - Hyperkalemia in primary disease.
  - Hypoglycemia.
  - Metabolic acidosis in primary disease.
- Crisis:
  - Shock/hypotension, vomiting/diarrhea, abdominal pain, fever/trigger, altered mental status, hypoglycemia.

Take-home point: RM stem of TB plus hypotension plus pigmentation plus low Na is Addison.

### Primary aldosteronism clinical anchors

- HTA, often resistant.
- Hypokalemia may cause weakness, cramps, paresthesias, polyuria.
- Metabolic alkalosis can appear.
- No edema is classic because of aldosterone escape.

Take-home point: HTA plus K low is not just "give potassium"; it is a renin-aldosterone question.

### Pheochromocytoma clinical anchors

- Classic triad:
  - Headache.
  - Palpitations.
  - Profuse sweating.
- BP:
  - Paroxysmal or sustained HTA.
- Other clues:
  - Pallor, tremor, anxiety-like spells, hyperglycemia, cardiomyopathy.
- Triggers:
  - Surgery, anesthesia, abdominal pressure, some drugs.

Take-home point: anxiety symptoms plus paroxysmal HTA and sweating should not be dismissed as panic.

## 4. Manejo - Diagnostico

### Cushing diagnosis

- Step 0: ask about exogenous steroids, including injections, creams, inhaled/high-dose forms, supplements.
- First-line screening options:
  - 24 h urinary free cortisol.
  - Late-night salivary cortisol.
  - Overnight 1 mg dexamethasone suppression test.
- Exam threshold from ENAM card:
  - After 1 mg dexamethasone, cortisol >1.8 ug/dL is positive in many algorithms.
- If high suspicion:
  - Use at least 2 abnormal tests before moving to localization.
- Then measure ACTH:
  - Low ACTH -> adrenal source, do adrenal CT.
  - High/inappropriately normal ACTH -> pituitary versus ectopic.
- Localization tools:
  - Pituitary MRI.
  - High-dose dexamethasone/CRH response as classic exam tools.
  - IPSS/CSPI if discordant or uncertain.

Take-home point: diagnosis before localization; ACTH before imaging chase.

### Adrenal insufficiency diagnosis

- If crisis suspected:
  - Treat immediately.
  - Draw cortisol and ACTH only if it does not delay hydrocortisone.
- If stable:
  - 8 AM cortisol:
    - Very low supports diagnosis.
    - Clearly normal/high makes adrenal insufficiency unlikely.
    - Intermediate requires ACTH stimulation test.
  - Standard ACTH stimulation test:
    - Inadequate cortisol rise supports adrenal insufficiency.
- Classify:
  - Primary: ACTH high, renin high, aldosterone low, K high, hyperpigmentation.
  - Central: ACTH low/inappropriately normal, usually no hyperkalemia and no hyperpigmentation.

Take-home point: ACTH and potassium classify the insufficiency.

### Primary aldosteronism diagnosis

- Screen:
  - Aldosterone-renin ratio.
  - Interpret with medications, potassium status, posture, salt intake, and local lab units.
- Strong classic picture:
  - Elevated aldosterone with suppressed renin and spontaneous hypokalemia can be highly suggestive.
- Confirmatory tests:
  - Saline infusion.
  - Oral sodium loading.
  - Captopril challenge.
  - Fludrocortisone suppression.
- Subtype:
  - Adrenal CT first for anatomy.
  - Adrenal vein sampling when surgery is considered and results will change management.

Take-home point: ARR screens; AVS decides surgery in many candidates.

### Pheochromocytoma diagnosis

- Initial biochemical test:
  - Plasma free metanephrines or urinary fractionated metanephrines.
- Then localize:
  - CT or MRI.
  - Functional imaging for metastatic, recurrent, multifocal, or inconclusive cases.
- Genetic evaluation:
  - Important especially in young, bilateral, multifocal, extra-adrenal, malignant, or family-history cases.

Take-home point: metanephrines first, then imaging.

## 5. Manejo - Clasificacion

| Condition | Classification that matters | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| Cushing | Exogenous vs endogenous; ACTH-dependent vs independent; pituitary vs ectopic | Determines surgery/medical therapy |
| Adrenal insufficiency | Primary vs central; chronic vs crisis | Determines mineralocorticoid need and emergency treatment |
| Primary aldosteronism | Unilateral vs bilateral | Determines adrenalectomy vs MRA |
| Pheochromocytoma | Adrenal vs extra-adrenal; hereditary vs sporadic; localized vs metastatic | Determines surgery, genetics, surveillance |
| HSC | Classic salt-wasting vs simple virilizing vs nonclassic | Determines salt/mineralocorticoid and stress dosing |
| Incidentaloma | Benign-appearing vs indeterminate/malignant; hormone-active vs silent | Determines surgery, follow-up, endocrine care |

Take-home point: in adrenal disease, classification is not taxonomy; it changes treatment.

## 6. Manejo - Treatment chains

### Cushing

- Remove exogenous steroid if possible, but taper safely if chronic exposure.
- Pituitary Cushing:
  - Transsphenoidal surgery is the core treatment.
- Adrenal cortisol-producing lesion:
  - Adrenalectomy if appropriate.
- Ectopic ACTH:
  - Treat/resect source if possible.
- Medical bridge or non-surgical:
  - Steroidogenesis inhibitors such as ketoconazole or metyrapone in classic teaching; specialist selection required.
- Severe hypercortisolism:
  - Treat urgently because infection, VTE, hypokalemia, and psychiatric/metabolic complications kill.

Take-home point: source control when possible; medical cortisol control when source control is delayed or impossible.

### Chronic primary adrenal insufficiency

- Glucocorticoid replacement:
  - Hydrocortisone 15-25 mg/day in divided doses is classic exam anchor.
- Mineralocorticoid replacement:
  - Fludrocortisone 0.05-0.1 mg/day is classic exam anchor.
- Education:
  - Sick-day rules.
  - Emergency steroid card/bracelet where available.
  - Injectable emergency steroid access when feasible.

Take-home point: primary Addison needs glucocorticoid plus mineralocorticoid; central disease usually does not need fludrocortisone.

### Adrenal crisis

- Do not wait for labs in unstable patient.
- Hydrocortisone:
  - 100 mg IV/IM bolus.
  - Then high-dose hydrocortisone by repeated doses or infusion per protocol.
- Fluids:
  - Isotonic saline, with dextrose if hypoglycemia.
- Treat trigger:
  - Infection, vomiting/diarrhea, surgery, trauma, missed steroids.
- Fludrocortisone:
  - Usually not needed acutely while hydrocortisone dose is high; add/return during chronic replacement transition.

Take-home point: RM answer in crisis is hydrocortisone.

### Primary aldosteronism

- Unilateral aldosterone-producing adenoma:
  - Laparoscopic adrenalectomy if candidate.
- Bilateral hyperplasia or non-surgical:
  - Mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist: spironolactone or eplerenone.
- Monitor:
  - BP, K, renal function, renin/aldosterone depending protocol.

Take-home point: unilateral cuts; bilateral blocks.

### Pheochromocytoma/paraganglioma

- Pre-op:
  - Alpha blockade first for 7-14 days or per protocol.
  - Liberal salt/fluid repletion after blockade if appropriate.
  - Beta blockade only after alpha blockade if tachycardia persists.
- Surgery:
  - Adrenalectomy or tumor resection by location and malignancy risk.
- Avoid:
  - Beta blocker first.
  - Unprepared surgery/anesthesia.

Take-home point: alpha before beta is the safety law.

## 7. Complications

- Cushing:
  - Infection, VTE, diabetes, HTA, osteoporosis/fractures, psychiatric symptoms, myopathy.
  - Nelson syndrome after bilateral adrenalectomy for Cushing disease: pituitary tumor progression with hyperpigmentation/high ACTH.
- Adrenal insufficiency:
  - Crisis, shock, hypoglycemia, death.
  - Overreplacement: weight gain, HTA, osteoporosis, metabolic harm.
  - Underreplacement: fatigue, hypotension, recurrent crisis.
- Primary aldosteronism:
  - Stroke, atrial fibrillation, CKD, LVH; risk may exceed essential HTN at same BP.
- Pheochromocytoma:
  - Hypertensive crisis, arrhythmia, cardiomyopathy, stroke, perioperative collapse.
- HSC:
  - Salt-wasting crisis, growth/puberty complications, fertility/androgen issues depending subtype.
- Incidentaloma:
  - Missed malignancy or missed autonomous cortisol secretion.

Take-home point: adrenal complications are often cardiovascular or crisis-related; do not reduce them to hormone numbers.

## 8. Follow-up

- Cushing:
  - Reassess cortisol status after treatment.
  - Monitor recurrence, adrenal insufficiency after cure, and metabolic/bone/infectious sequelae.
- Addison:
  - Monitor symptoms, weight, BP/orthostasis, Na, K, glucose, renin when adjusting fludrocortisone.
  - Reinforce sick-day rules at every visit.
- Primary aldosteronism:
  - BP, K, kidney function, medication side effects, renin response, post-adrenalectomy biochemical cure.
- Pheochromocytoma:
  - BP and metanephrines after surgery; long-term surveillance in hereditary/high-risk cases.
- HSC:
  - Growth, electrolytes, 17-OHP/androgens per specialist protocol, stress-dose education.
- Incidentaloma:
  - Imaging and hormone follow-up based on malignancy and hormonal activity risk.

Take-home point: adrenal follow-up is how you prevent the second crisis or missed recurrence.

## 9. Exam Traps

- If the stem says TB, hypotension, pigmentation, nausea/vomiting, and low sodium:
  - Answer adrenal insufficiency/Addison.
- If known Addison gets pneumonia and then vomiting/hypotension:
  - Answer hydrocortisone now.
- If chronic Addison treatment is asked:
  - Hydrocortisone plus fludrocortisone.
- If HTA plus hypokalemia:
  - Primary aldosteronism.
- If Cushing has no classic body habitus but has severe hypokalemia and hyperpigmentation:
  - Think ectopic ACTH.
- If pheo has tachycardia:
  - Alpha blockade first; beta only after alpha.
- If newborn screening asks adrenal disease marker:
  - HSC, 17-OHP.

Take-home point: this topic is high ROI because each disease has a small, testable signature.

units.title: Choque en general
units.body:
# Choque en general

## 0. Idea nuclear

- Shock is not simply "low blood pressure".
- Shock is tissue hypoperfusion: oxygen delivery is not meeting tissue demand.
- The useful exam sequence is:
  - Is there hypoperfusion?
  - Which mechanism dominates?
  - What first action fits that mechanism?
  - Did the patient improve after that action?
- HDCO:
  - H: hypovolemic, low volume.
  - D: distributive, low vascular tone or maldistribution.
  - C: cardiogenic, pump failure.
  - O: obstructive, mechanical block.

Take-home point: in shock, the label matters only because it changes the first action.

## 1. Guion: why shock happens

Shock happens when effective oxygen delivery to tissue fails.

| Mechanism | What fails | Typical result |
|---|---|---|
| Low volume | Not enough preload/circulating volume | Low cardiac output, vasoconstriction, cold skin |
| Low tone | Vessels dilate or leak; flow is maldistributed | Warm early shock, low SVR, relative hypovolemia |
| Bad pump | Heart cannot eject enough | Pulmonary congestion, JVP, low output |
| Blocked circuit | Mechanical obstruction to filling/output | High JVP, low output, procedure-needed cause |

The body compensates with sympathetic tone, RAAS, ADH, and stress hormones. RM has a direct recall item where the expected neuroendocrine response is increased ACTH release.

Take-home point: shock is a circulation circuit problem; HDCO tells you which circuit piece failed.

## 2. A quien: common exam scenes

| Scene | First shock to suspect | Pivot clue |
|---|---|---|
| Trauma, bleeding, GI bleed, HPP | Hypovolemic hemorrhagic | cold skin, tachycardia, flat veins, source of loss |
| Diarrhea, vomiting, dehydration | Hypovolemic non-hemorrhagic | history of fluid loss, dry mucosa, low preload |
| Fever, focus, lactate, altered sensorium | Septic distributive | warm early shock, infection, organ dysfunction |
| Penicillin/food/sting plus airway/skin/hypotension | Anaphylactic distributive | exposure plus stridor/edema/urticaria |
| AMI, arrhythmia, heart failure | Cardiogenic | crackles, JVP, S3/S4, poor contractility |
| PE, tamponade, tension pneumothorax | Obstructive | JVP high plus mechanical sign |
| Spinal cord injury | Neurogenic distributive | hypotension plus bradycardia and warm skin |

Take-home point: the context primes the branch, but the pivot clue decides.

## 3. Como: presentation and cues

### Universal hypoperfusion cues

- Altered sensorium: anxiety, confusion, somnolence, coma.
- Skin: cold, sweaty, mottled, pale; distributive shock can be warm early.
- Kidney: oliguria, often taught as less than 0.5 mL/kg/h.
- Vitals: tachycardia is common; exceptions include neurogenic shock and bradyarrhythmia-related cardiogenic shock.
- Blood pressure: SBP <=90 mmHg, low MAP, or large fall from baseline.
- Laboratory: high lactate, metabolic acidosis, base deficit when available.
- Capillary refill: delayed refill supports poor perfusion.

### Hot and cold profiles

| Profile | Read it as | Do not do |
|---|---|---|
| Warm, febrile, confused, cap refill slow | Distributive septic until proven otherwise | Exclude shock because skin is warm |
| Urticaria/erythema, edema, stridor, hypotension | Anaphylaxis | Start with antihistamine/steroid |
| Cold, pale, flat veins, blood or fluid loss | Hypovolemic | Give vasopressor and ignore loss |
| Cold, JVP, crackles, AMI | Cardiogenic | Flood with crystalloids |
| Cold, JVP, mechanical chest/pericardial/PE clue | Obstructive | Wait for support to solve a block |

Take-home point: skin temperature is a clue to mechanism, not a yes/no shock test.

## 4. Diagnosis

Shock is diagnosed at the bedside. Tests help classify and monitor response.

| Tool | Use | Trap |
|---|---|---|
| Serial vitals | trend and response | using one value only |
| Lactate/gas | severity and response | delaying care until lactate returns |
| Urine output | renal perfusion | ignoring oliguria |
| ECG/troponin | AMI/arrhythmia | missing cardiogenic shock |
| Echo/POCUS | volume, pump, tamponade, RV strain | using imaging to delay urgent actions |
| Chest imaging | pneumothorax, congestion, hemothorax | waiting for x-ray in classic tension pneumothorax |
| Cultures | sepsis work-up | delaying antibiotics when cultures are hard |
| Hb/coagulation | bleeding/coagulopathy | trusting early normal hematocrit in acute hemorrhage |

Bedside algorithm:

```text
hypoperfusion
-> ABC, oxygen if needed, monitor, IV/IO access, glucose if altered sensorium
-> immediate killer?
   -> anaphylaxis: IM epinephrine
   -> tension pneumothorax: decompression
   -> massive bleeding: hemorrhage control
-> classify HDCO
-> treat cause plus support
-> reassess
```

Take-home point: the diagnostic label is correct only if it changes the next step.

## 5. Classification HDCO

| Type | Mechanism | Clues | CVP/preload | Cardiac output | SVR | First action |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Hypovolemic | low volume | bleeding, diarrhea, cold skin, flat veins | low | low | high | volume/blood plus stop loss |
| Distributive septic | vasodilation/leak by infection | fever, focus, warm early, lactate | low/normal | high early | low | fluids, antibiotics, source control, norepinephrine if needed |
| Distributive anaphylactic | allergic vasodilation, bronchospasm, edema | allergen, urticaria/edema, stridor, hypotension | low/normal | variable | low | IM epinephrine and airway |
| Cardiogenic | pump failure | AMI, crackles, JVP, poor contractility | high | low | high | support MAP/output and treat cardiac cause |
| Obstructive | mechanical block | PE, tamponade, tension pneumothorax | high | low | high | unblock cause |
| Neurogenic | loss sympathetic tone | spinal trauma, bradycardia, warm skin | variable | variable | low | exclude bleeding, fluids/vasopressor per protocol |

Take-home point: HDCO is a treatment map, not an acronym for memorization.

## 6. Management by shock type

### Hypovolemic shock

- Hemorrhagic:
  - Stop bleeding: compression, tourniquet when appropriate, surgery, endoscopy, embolization, obstetric source control.
  - If severe/major hemorrhage: think blood products or massive transfusion pathway, not endless crystalloid.
  - ATLS class III-IV is a board signal for blood and source control.
- Non-hemorrhagic:
  - Replace with isotonic crystalloid.
  - Correct ongoing losses and electrolytes.
  - If no improvement after reasonable volume, reopen HDCO.

Hemorrhagic class, exam memory:

| Class | Blood loss | HR | BP | RR | Mental status |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| I | <750 mL, <15% | <100 | normal | 14-20 | normal |
| II | 750-1500 mL, 15-30% | 100-120 | normal or low | 20-30 | anxious |
| III | 1500-2000 mL, 30-40% | 120-140 | low | 30-40 | confused |
| IV | >2000 mL, >40% | >140 | very low | >35 | lethargic/coma |

Take-home point: class III-IV hemorrhage is not a "more saline" problem.

### Septic distributive shock

- Current adult guideline modifier: SSC 2026.
- Treat as emergency:
  - Start resuscitation immediately.
  - Give crystalloids for sepsis-induced hypoperfusion/septic shock; adult SSC 2026 suggests at least 30 mL/kg in the first 3 hours, individualized and reassessed.
  - Use antibiotics early and pursue source control when indicated.
  - Use norepinephrine as first-line vasopressor for adult septic shock.
  - Initial MAP target is commonly around 65 mmHg in adults receiving vasopressors.
  - Reassess with perfusion endpoints: sensorium, capillary refill, urine output, lactate trend, dynamic fluid response when available.

Product warning:

- Do not apply adult sepsis treatment dosing to pediatric cases unless pediatric guidance is source-locked.

Take-home point: septic shock needs fluids, antibiotics, source control, and norepinephrine in the right order and response context.

### Anaphylactic distributive shock

- Trigger: allergen exposure with skin/mucosa plus airway, breathing, or circulation compromise.
- First-line:
  - Epinephrine/adrenaline IM in the anterolateral thigh.
  - Adult common dose: 0.3-0.5 mg IM; weight-based 0.01 mg/kg up to 0.5 mg is guideline language.
  - Repeat if ABC problems persist, commonly 5-15 minutes depending protocol.
- Adjuncts:
  - Oxygen, position, IV fluids if hypotensive.
  - Bronchodilator for bronchospasm.
  - Antihistamines and corticosteroids are adjuncts, not first-line rescue.
- Airway:
  - Prepare early if edema/stridor progresses.
  - RM exact case: severe face/neck edema, SatO2 70%, stridor, difficult air entry -> cricothyrotomy key.
  - Do not generalize cricothyrotomy to routine anaphylaxis.

Take-home point: anaphylaxis is epinephrine first; the "allergy combo" is not rescue.

### Cardiogenic shock

- Clues:
  - AMI or arrhythmia.
  - Hypotension with crackles, pulmonary edema, JVP, oliguria, cold skin.
  - Echo: poor contractility.
- Core management:
  - Avoid aggressive fluids when congested.
  - ECG/echo/monitoring early.
  - If ACS/AMI-related, prompt revascularization/cause control is central.
  - Use vasopressor/inotrope support based on BP and low-output profile.
- Local exam anchor:
  - Dobutamine is the classic inotrope if BP allows.
  - If BP is profoundly low, norepinephrine plus dobutamine may appear as combined support in local card logic.

Take-home point: cardiogenic shock is pump/coronary/cause control plus tailored support, not liters by reflex.

### Obstructive shock

| Cause | Clues | First causal action |
|---|---|---|
| Tension pneumothorax | trauma, hypotension, JVP, absent breath sounds, tracheal deviation | decompression immediately, then definitive chest tube |
| Tamponade | hypotension, JVP, muffled heart sounds, paradoxical pulse, effusion | urgent pericardiocentesis/drainage if unstable |
| Massive PE | dyspnea/syncope, hypoxemia, RV dilation, shock | reperfusion strategy if high-risk/unstable plus anticoagulation when appropriate |

- Fluids and vasopressors are bridges.
- The definitive action is to remove the obstruction.

Take-home point: in obstructive shock, the procedure is often the real vasopressor.

### Neurogenic shock

- Clues:
  - Spinal injury.
  - Hypotension with bradycardia or relative bradycardia.
  - Warm skin/good pulses can appear.
- Trap:
  - In trauma, exclude hemorrhage before calling hypotension neurogenic.

Take-home point: neurogenic shock is distributive physiology after spinal injury, but trauma bleeding must be ruled out.

## 7. Complications

| Complication | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Acute kidney injury | renal hypoperfusion or multiorgan dysfunction |
| Persistent lactate/acidosis | incomplete resuscitation or uncontrolled source |
| ARDS | sepsis, trauma, transfusion, inflammation |
| Coagulopathy/DIC | sepsis, trauma, obstetric catastrophe |
| Myocardial ischemia/arrhythmia | shock plus catecholamines stress the heart |
| Multiorgan failure | sustained hypoperfusion |
| Biphasic anaphylaxis | recurrence after initial improvement |
| Pulmonary edema | cardiogenic shock or fluid overload |

Take-home point: shock complications usually mean source not controlled, mechanism not corrected, or resuscitation has created a new problem.

## 8. Follow-up and reassessment

During resuscitation:

- Recheck ABC after each intervention.
- Monitor BP/MAP, HR, RR, SpO2, temperature, sensorium.
- Follow capillary refill, skin, urine output, lactate trend if available.
- Use POCUS/echo when it clarifies volume, pump, or obstruction.
- Ask after every step: did perfusion improve?

After stabilization:

- ICU or monitored care if vasopressors, ventilation, persistent lactate, organ dysfunction, uncontrolled source, or recurrent shock risk.
- De-escalate fluids after rescue phase; excess fluid can harm.
- Finish cause control:
  - Antibiotics/source control.
  - Hemostasis.
  - Revascularization.
  - Pericardiocentesis/drainage.
  - PE reperfusion/anticoagulation.
  - Anaphylaxis observation and prevention plan.

Take-home point: shock is managed in short loops, not one heroic order.

## 9. Exam Traps

- No hypotension yet:
  - Shock can be compensated; look for hypoperfusion.
- Warm skin:
  - Distributive shock can be warm early.
- Sepsis:
  - Norepinephrine, not dopamine, is first-line adult septic shock vasopressor.
- Anaphylaxis:
  - Epinephrine/adrenaline IM first, not antihistamine/steroid.
- Cardiogenic:
  - Do not give aggressive fluids into pulmonary edema.
- Obstructive:
  - Do not wait for x-ray in classic unstable tension pneumothorax.
- Tamponade:
  - Pericardiocentesis/drainage is causal; fluids are bridge.
- Neurogenic:
  - Hypotension with bradycardia after spine trauma is a clue, but exclude bleeding.
- ENCAPS:
  - Dengue/obstetric shock are product-specific lanes; do not import their doses into general shock.

Take-home point: most wrong answers are real treatments in the wrong shock type or wrong order.

## 10. Mini-Drills

1. Penicillin IM, eyelid edema, dysphonia, stridor, PA 70/50. First drug?
   - Epinephrine/adrenaline IM.

2. Penicillin exposure, face/neck edema, SatO2 70%, severe stridor, difficult air entry. RM procedure?
   - Cricothyrotomy.

3. Fever, petechiae, warm skin, capillary refill >2 sec, altered sensorium. Shock type?
   - Distributive.

4. AMI, hypotension, crackles, JVP, oliguria. Dangerous wrong move?
   - Aggressive fluids.

5. Trauma, absent breath sounds on one side, tracheal deviation, JVP, hypotension. First action?
   - Decompression without waiting for x-ray.

6. Estimated blood loss 1800 mL, HR 130, low BP, confusion. Hemorrhagic class?
   - Class III.

7. Direct recall: neuroendocrine response in shock in local RM bank?
   - Increased ACTH release.

## 11. Product Modifiers

- ENAM: HDCO, hemodynamic profiles, type recognition, first management, hemorrhagic class, anaphylaxis, tamponade, cardiogenic and neurogenic shock.
- RM: anaphylaxis and airway are disproportionately important; keep exact case keys visible.
- ENCAPS/SERUMS: shock appears as obstetric, dengue, sepsis, or referral modifier; not the core truth source here.
- EsSalud: adjacent sepsis/shock signal only; no exact independent priority lock.
- Class/manual: usable as decision-training ground truth with `qa_pending` caveats.

## 12. Trazabilidad

Local:

- `../../3-output/usamedic-enam/Cards/096_choque_en_general.md`
- `../../3-output/usamedic-enam/Cards/136_trauma_shock_y_rcp.md`
- `../../3-output/usamedic-enam/Cards/187_sepsis_y_shock_septico.md`
- `../../3-output/usamedic-enam/Cards/044_arresto_cardiopulmonar.md`
- RM cases from `../../3-output/usamedic-residentado-fenotipos/index.html`
- ENCAPS modifiers from CIS-1.4, CIS-2.23, CIS-2.25

External current guidance:

- SCCM SSC 2026 for adult sepsis/septic shock.
- WAO 2020 and Resuscitation Council UK 2021 for anaphylaxis.
- ACC/AHA 2025 ACS guidance for cardiogenic shock in ACS context.
- European trauma bleeding guideline 2023 for major traumatic bleeding caveats.

- `qa_status: qa_pending`

units.example: - Shock is not simply "low blood pressure". - Shock is tissue hypoperfusion: oxygen delivery is not meeting tissue demand. - The useful exam sequence is: - Is there hypoperfusion? - Which mechanism dominates? - What first action fits that mechanism? - Did the patient improve after that action? - HDCO: - H: hypovolemic, low volume. - D: distributive, low vascular tone or maldistribution. - C: cardiogenic, pump failure. - O: obstructive, mechanical block. Take-home point: in shock, the label matters only because it changes the first action. Shock happens when effective oxygen delivery to tissue

units.title: Note - PN-NEO-05 Asfixia y reanimacion cardiopulmonar
units.body:
# Note - PN-NEO-05 Asfixia y reanimacion cardiopulmonar

## Idea Nuclear

Neonatal resuscitation is mostly ventilation rescue. The exam wants you to run
the first minutes in order:

```text
3 questions -> stabilize -> HR branch -> 30-second reassessment -> brain follow-up
```

Take-home point: never let Apgar replace the immediate clinical algorithm.

## Guion

### 1. Why It Happens

- Most newborns transition from placental gas exchange to lung gas exchange
  without help.
- A minority need support, and preterm newborns need it more often.
- The usual emergency mechanism is failed ventilation/oxygenation after birth,
  which then produces bradycardia.
- In neonatal resuscitation, bradycardia is usually a ventilation problem until
  proven otherwise.
- Severe/prolonged hypoxia can cause neonatal asphyxia and hypoxic-ischemic
  encephalopathy (EHI), especially in term newborns.

Take-home point: fix ventilation first because the neonatal heart rate often
recovers when the lungs are opened effectively.

### 2. Who Gets It

High-yield risk contexts:

- Prematurity.
- Acute fetal distress.
- Cord prolapse.
- Placental abruption.
- Meconium-stained amniotic fluid.
- Emergency cesarean.
- Abnormal presentation.
- Maternal diabetes, hypertension, anemia/isoinmunization, oligohydramnios or
  polyhydramnios.
- Narcotics close to delivery.
- Congenital anomaly.

Take-home point: risk factors prepare the team, but the first action is still
decided by the newborn's breathing, tone, and heart rate.

### 3. How It Presents

Delivery-room failure-to-transition pattern:

- No cry.
- Apnea or gasping.
- Hypotonia.
- HR <100.
- Cyanosis or poor perfusion may appear, but do not wait for color alone.

EHI/asphyxia pattern after the initial event:

- Term newborn.
- Sentinel event: acute fetal distress, cord prolapse, DPPNI, severe intrapartum
  compromise.
- Low Apgar at 5 minutes and/or cord pH <7.0.
- Abnormal neurologic exam: lethargy, weak suck, altered tone, seizures.

Take-home point: delivery-room RCP is an action algorithm; EHI is a post-event
diagnostic pattern.

## Manejo

### 1. Immediate Diagnosis: The 3 Questions

At birth, ask:

1. Is the newborn term or late-preterm enough for routine transition?
2. Is the newborn breathing or crying?
3. Does the newborn have good tone?

If all are yes:

- Routine care.
- Skin-to-skin.
- Timely/delayed cord clamping per local newborn-care card.
- APGAR at 1 and 5 minutes as assessment.

If any is no:

- Start stabilization immediately.
- Do not wait for the 1-minute Apgar.

Take-home point: Apgar is an outcome/assessment score, not the entry ticket to
resuscitation.

### 2. Initial Stabilization

Do:

- Warm the newborn.
- Dry term/near-term newborn; local card says do not dry the hands.
- Stimulate.
- Position in sniffing position.
- Clear airway only if secretions/obstruction interfere.
- Place pulse oximeter on the right hand when oxygen/ventilation is needed.

For very preterm or very low birth weight:

- If <32 weeks or <1500 g, use sterile polyethylene bag plus cap immediately.
- Do not dry before placing in the bag.

Take-home point: stabilization buys ventilation, temperature, and time for the
heart rate decision.

### 3. Classification by HR and Breathing

| Finding after stabilization | Classify as | Action |
|---|---|---|
| HR >100 and normal breathing | Transition OK | Routine care/skin-to-skin |
| HR >100 and labored breathing | Breathing with support need | CPAP/PEEP |
| HR <100 or apnea/gasping | Ventilation failure | VPP by mask |
| HR <60 after effective VPP | Severe compromise | Compressions 3:1 plus optimize airway |
| HR <60 after compressions | Refractory compromise | Epinephrine IV/UVC |

Take-home point: CPAP requires spontaneous breathing; apnea needs VPP.

### 4. Management Chain

#### Step A - VPP

Use VPP when:

- Apnea.
- Gasping.
- HR <100.

Exam details:

- VPP should start within the first minute of life when indicated.
- Initial FiO2 for term newborn VPP is 21%.
- Look for chest expansion and HR response.
- If there is no improvement, correct mask seal, position, airway obstruction,
  and ventilation technique before escalating.

#### Step B - Compressions

Use compressions when:

- HR remains <60 after about 30 seconds of effective VPP.

Technique:

- Two-thumb technique is preferred in local exam teaching.
- Ratio: 3 compressions : 1 ventilation.
- Coordinate ventilation and compressions.
- Local RM key: FiO2 becomes 100% during assisted ventilation with chest
  compressions.
- Consider intubation/advanced airway when VPP is ineffective or compressions
  are needed.

#### Step C - Epinephrine

Use when:

- HR remains <60 after effective VPP plus compressions.

Exam details:

- Concentration: 0.1 mg/mL = 1 mg/10 mL.
- Preferred route: IV via umbilical venous catheter.
- Intratracheal route may appear historically, but it is not the preferred
  route.
- IM adrenaline is a distractor from anaphylaxis, not neonatal RCP.

Take-home point: VPP first, compressions second, epinephrine third.

### 5. Oxygen and Saturation

| Context | Answer |
|---|---|
| Starting VPP in term newborn | 21% |
| Already on FiO2 40% with acceptable oxygenation | Maintain/titrate; do not reflexively jump |
| Coordinated ventilation with compressions | 100% in local RM key |
| Saturation probe site | Right hand/preductal |
| First minutes | Saturation rises gradually; may not reach 90% until around 10 min |

Take-home point: oxygen is phase-specific; "100% for every newborn" is the trap.

### 6. Meconium

Current local ENAM card:

- Use the same algorithm.
- Do not make meconium alone the reason for routine tracheal suction.
- If VPP fails and obstruction is suspected, intubation/airway clearance becomes
  reasonable.

RM historical key:

- One 2018 RM case with depressed post-term meconium-stained newborn keys
  endotracheal intubation and aspiration.

How to teach it:

- For modern class/manual ground truth: ventilation-first, suction only if
  obstruction or ineffective ventilation.
- For historical RM recall: recognize the old key and flag the conflict.

Take-home point: meconium is a risk cue, not an automatic suction command in
current framing.

## Asfixia and EHI

### Diagnosis

Think neonatal asphyxia/EHI when:

- Term newborn.
- Sentinel hypoxic event.
- Need for resuscitation.
- Apgar <5 at 5 minutes and/or cord pH <7.0.
- Abnormal neurologic exam: lethargy, weak suck, altered consciousness, tone
  abnormality, or seizures.

Exam pattern:

- Acute fetal distress.
- Apgar 1 at 1 minute, 3 at 5 minutes.
- Cord pH 6.9.
- Seizure.
- Most likely diagnosis: neonatal asphyxia/EHI pattern.

### Mechanism

- Hypoxia-ischemia injures brain tissue through energy failure, excitotoxicity,
  inflammation, and reperfusion injury.
- In term newborns, injury pattern tends toward cortical/diffuse involvement.
- In premature newborns, hypoxic/ischemic vulnerability often involves germinal
  matrix/intraventricular hemorrhage and periventricular leukomalacia.

### Treatment

- Therapeutic hypothermia is the disease-modifying treatment in eligible
  term/near-term newborns with EHI.
- Local ENAM card lock: around 33.5 C for 72 hours.
- Anticonvulsants may treat seizures, but they are not the disease-modifying
  EHI therapy.

Take-home point: EHI is not "just seizures"; the board answer for disease
modification is therapeutic hypothermia when eligible.

## Complications

Immediate:

- Persistent bradycardia.
- Need for advanced airway/vascular access.
- Hypothermia, especially in preterm newborns.
- Hypoglycemia or metabolic instability after severe stress.

Neurologic:

- Neonatal seizures.
- EHI.
- Cerebral palsy risk.
- In preterm: intraventricular hemorrhage, periventricular leukomalacia, spastic
  diplegia pattern.

Take-home point: the resuscitation note must end in neurologic risk
recognition, not only in "baby started breathing".

## Follow-Up

After significant resuscitation or suspected EHI:

- Monitor temperature, glucose, perfusion, respiratory status, and neurologic
  exam.
- Check gas/acid-base context when available.
- Identify eligibility for therapeutic hypothermia early.
- Plan neonatal unit observation and neurologic follow-up.
- Continue routine newborn prophylaxis only when the newborn is clinically
  stable enough and local workflow permits.

Take-home point: after RCP, ask whether the brain is injured and whether the
window for hypothermia is open.

## Adjacent Immediate Newborn Care

Do not let this become the whole topic, but know the exam-adjacent facts:

- Vitamin K:
  - >1500 g: 1 mg IM.
  - <=1500 g: 0.3-0.5 mg/kg IM.
  - Within first 6 hours in local card.
- Ocular prophylaxis:
  - Tetracycline ointment 1%, 1 cm in each eye.
- Skin-to-skin:
  - Minimum 60 minutes when stable and not contraindicated.
- Cord care:
  - Avoid iodinated antiseptics in local newborn care card.

Take-home point: prophylaxis is second-hour/routine-care logic; it should not
delay indicated ventilation.

## Classic Traps

| Trap | Correct move |
|---|---|
| "Apgar is low, so start RCP" | Start RCP based on breathing/tone/HR, not Apgar |
| "Apgar unknown, wait" | Do not wait; run 3Q-HR-30 |
| HR 80 and apnea -> CPAP | VPP |
| HR >100 and labored breathing -> VPP | CPAP/PEEP |
| VPP starts with 100% oxygen | Term starts 21% |
| Compressions before effective VPP | Correct ventilation first |
| Adrenaline IM | IV/UVC preferred in neonatal RCP |
| Every meconium case gets suction | Ventilation-first unless obstruction/ineffective VPP |
| Preterm <32 w is dried first | Bag plus cap, no drying before bag |
| EHI treatment is only phenobarbital | Hypothermia is disease-modifying when eligible |

## Mini-Drills

1. Term RN, crying, good tone:
   - 3Q all yes.
   - Answer: skin-to-skin/routine care.
   - Reject: RCP because Apgar not yet available.

2. RN apneic, HR 80:
   - 3Q has a no; HR <100.
   - Answer: VPP.
   - Reject: CPAP.

3. After 30 seconds effective VPP, HR 50:
   - Answer: chest compressions 3:1 and optimize airway.
   - Reject: continue unchanged VPP forever.

4. After compressions, HR 40:
   - Answer: epinephrine IV/UVC.
   - Reject: IM adrenaline.

5. Fetal distress, pH 6.9, seizure:
   - Answer: neonatal asphyxia/EHI.
   - Reject: primary epilepsy as the main diagnosis.

## Product Modifiers

- `qa_pending`: official Peru NTS page-level source lock required before
  publishable normative MCQ.
- `fail_to_publish_until_source_lock`: bedside protocol claims need full local
  and guideline passage verification.
- Keep local historical RM meconium key visible, but do not teach it as the
  default modern rule.
