units.title: Emesis gravidica: del vomito esperado a la hiperemesis peligrosa
units.body:
# Emesis gravidica

## Guion

La pregunta no es "gestante vomita, entonces hiperemesis". La pregunta es si el vomito es parte frecuente del primer trimestre, si ya produce dano sistemico o si hay una causa no obstetrica/obstetrica peligrosa.

Take-home point: emesis leve se maneja por escalones; hiperemesis se reconoce por repercusion; red flags rompen el cierre diagnostico.

## 1. Por que da / fisiopatologia / mecanismos

- Nauseas y vomitos del embarazo se asocian a cambios hormonales tempranos; hCG, estrogenos, progesterona, enlentecimiento gastrointestinal y sensibilidad central al vomito participan, pero la causa exacta no es unica.
- hCG alta explica una parte del patron temprano y abre dos diferenciales de alto rendimiento: embarazo multiple y enfermedad trofoblastica gestacional.
- hCG tambien puede estimular el receptor de TSH: TSH baja + T4 libre alta en HG sin bocio/oftalmopatia suele ser tirotoxicosis gestacional transitoria, no Graves de reflejo.
- Vomito persistente -> ayuno -> cetonuria; perdida de volumen -> mucosas secas, taquicardia, hipotension, oliguria y posible injuria renal.
- Vomito prolongado + malnutricion -> deficit de tiamina. Si se administra glucosa sin tiamina, puede precipitar o empeorar encefalopatia de Wernicke.

Concepto preguntable: la via mecanistica del examen es `hCG alta -> vomitos/tiroides/mola` y `vomitos prolongados -> deficit de B1 -> Wernicke`.

## 2. A quien / epidemiologia / factores de riesgo

- Nauseas y vomitos son muy frecuentes en el embarazo temprano; hiperemesis gravidica es la forma severa y menos frecuente.
- Inicio tipico: primer trimestre. Si comienza tarde, empeora despues de la ventana habitual o trae sintomas sistemicos, buscar otra causa.
- Banco ENAM local: vinetas directas entre 8 y 14 semanas.
- Factores de riesgo de alto rendimiento: antecedente personal o familiar de HG, embarazo multiple, mola hidatiforme, primigestacion, migrana/cinetosis y contextos de hCG alta.
- Si hay utero mayor que edad gestacional, sangrado, beta-hCG muy alta o eco anormal, el diagnostico diferencial deja de ser opcional: pensar mola.

Take-home point: primer trimestre + vomito puede ser fisiologico; primer trimestre + vomito desproporcionado obliga a buscar severidad y hCG alta.

## 3. Como se presenta / clinica / examen / labs

| Escenario | Clinica | Labs/auxiliares | Lectura exam-first |
|---|---|---|---|
| NVE leve | nauseas/vomitos, tolera algo VO, peso estable, SV normales | orina normal, sin cetonuria | dieta/hidratacion + B6 +/- doxilamina |
| HG | vomitos incoercibles o persistentes, baja de peso, mucosas secas, hipotension/taquicardia, oliguria | cetonuria, hipoNa/hipoK, urea/Cr altas | soporte, labs, fluidos, antiemetico, ingreso si grave |
| Wernicke | HG/vomitos prolongados + confusion + nistagmo/oftalmoplejia + ataxia | deficit nutricional probable | tiamina urgente |
| Tirotoxicosis gestacional | HG + TSH baja/T4 alta, sin bocio ni oftalmopatia | hCG alta posible | soporte, no antitiroideos si transitoria |
| Mola/ETG | vomitos intensos + sangrado + utero mayor/hCG alta | eco molar, hCG muy alta | no cerrar como NVE |

Labs utiles si significativo: cetonas en orina, electrolitos, magnesio, urea/creatinina, hemograma, pruebas hepaticas, glucosa, EGO/urocultivo si urinario, TSH/T4 si clinica o severidad, ecografia si severo/persistente o sospecha mola/multiple.

Take-home point: el numero de vomitos no basta; la pregunta se decide por peso, hidratacion, cetonas, electrolitos, neurologia y red flags.

## Manejo

## 1. Diagnostico

- NVE/HG son diagnosticos de exclusion: primero verificar que el patron sea temprano, tipico y sin red flags.
- NVE leve: nausea/vomito con estabilidad clinica, tolerancia parcial de via oral, sin perdida ponderal importante, sin deshidratacion y sin cetonuria.
- HG exam-first: vomitos incoercibles/persistentes + incapacidad para mantener ingesta o repercusion: perdida de peso, cetonuria, deshidratacion, electrolitos alterados, AKI o deterioro funcional.
- Red flags que bloquean cierre simple: fiebre, dolor abdominal focal, diarrea, dolor lumbar/disuria, ictericia, cefalea, confusion, focalidad neurologica, hematemesis, vomito bilioso, peritonismo, inicio tardio o sintomas persistentes/empeorando.

Take-home point: hiperemesis no es "nausea intensa"; es vomito del embarazo con dano medible o riesgo clinico.

## 2. Clasificacion

| Clase practica | Clave | Conducta |
|---|---|---|
| Leve | tolera VO, peso estable, sin cetonas/deshidratacion | ambulatorio + medidas dietarias + primera linea si persiste |
| Moderada/refractaria | vomitos repetidos, ingesta pobre, falla primer escalon | antiemetico adicional + control clinico/labs |
| Grave/HG | perdida de peso, deshidratacion, cetonuria, electrolitos alterados, intolerancia VO | fluidos IV, electrolitos, antiemetico, tiamina si riesgo, ingreso |
| Complicada | Wernicke, AKI, DKA, sepsis, abdomen agudo, mola complicada | manejo urgente y multidisciplinario |

Take-home point: la misma palabra "vomitos" no define conducta; la severidad define el escalon.

## 3. Manejo en cadena

1. Confirmar estabilidad materna y edad gestacional.
2. Buscar red flags y diferenciales: mola/multiple, ITU/pielonefritis, gastroenteritis, apendicitis, colecistitis/litiasis, pancreatitis, hepatitis, higado graso agudo, colestasis, DKA, hipertiroidismo/Graves.
3. Si leve: comidas pequenas y frecuentes, evitar gatillos/olores, hidratacion oral, liquidos fraccionados y retirar temporalmente hierro si empeora la nausea.
4. Primer escalon farmacologico de examen: piridoxina/vitamina B6, sola o asociada a doxilamina; ENAM reciente favorece doxilamina + piridoxina o doxilamina segun opciones.
5. Si persiste o es moderada: metoclopramida, prometazina u ondansetron como escalones posteriores segun contexto, riesgo y protocolo local.
6. Si hay deshidratacion/intolerancia VO: cristaloides IV, corregir Na/K/Mg, monitorizar diuresis y reevaluar labs.
7. Si hay vomitos prolongados, malnutricion o se dara dextrosa: tiamina antes de glucosa.
8. Si no responde: considerar soporte nutricional, preferir enteral si viable; parenteral solo con indicacion y control por riesgos.
9. Si comorbilidad severa y la paciente rechaza aborto: respetar autonomia, manejar hiperemesis y enfermedad de fondo.

Take-home point: el error caro es saltar la escalera en casos leves y olvidar tiamina en casos graves.

## 4. Complicaciones

- Deshidratacion, cetosis, hiponatremia, hipokalemia, hipocloremia, alcalosis/acidosis segun contexto e injuria renal.
- Malnutricion secundaria: no es falta primaria de comida, es incapacidad de retener/aprovechar la ingesta.
- Wernicke: confusion + nistagmo/oftalmoplejia + ataxia.
- Mallory-Weiss/hematemesis por vomitos repetidos.
- Tromboembolismo por deshidratacion e inmovilidad, especialmente si hospitalizada.
- Bajo peso o restriccion de crecimiento si perdida ponderal/malnutricion materna es severa y sostenida.

Take-home point: fetalmente suele ir bien si se trata, pero la malnutricion sostenida cambia el pronostico.

## 5. Seguimiento

- Controlar peso, tolerancia oral, diuresis, signos vitales, hidratacion y adherencia al plan antiemetico.
- En moderada/severa: repetir electrolitos, creatinina, cetonas y labs segun evolucion.
- Reconsulta urgente: no tolera liquidos, orina escasa/oscura, sincope, dolor abdominal, fiebre, ictericia, sangre o bilis en vomito, confusion, ataxia, nistagmo o perdida de peso progresiva.
- Alta hospitalaria solo si tolera via oral, electrolitos corregidos o en correccion segura, plan farmacologico claro y control cercano.
- Si sintomas prolongados o mala ganancia ponderal: valorar crecimiento fetal y salud mental.

Take-home point: seguimiento no es "ya dejo de vomitar"; es peso, hidratacion, electrolitos, nutricion y red flags.

## 6. Pronostico

- NVE leve suele mejorar hacia el segundo trimestre.
- HG puede recurrir en futuras gestaciones y puede requerir hospitalizaciones.
- Wernicke es el punto neurologico critico: retrasar tiamina puede dejar dano permanente.
- El pronostico depende de tratamiento temprano, reposicion hidroelectrolitica, nutricion, comorbilidades y soporte psicosocial.

Take-home point: la hiperemesis tratada temprano suele ser manejable; la hiperemesis minimizada produce dano.

## Product modifiers

### ENAM

- 8-9 semanas + nauseas/vomitos + estable + sin cetonuria + falla dieta: doxilamina + piridoxina o doxilamina.
- 11 semanas + vomitos incoercibles + baja ponderal + mucosas secas + cetonas + Na 130: hiperemesis gravidica.
- 12-14 semanas + vomitos + confusion + nistagmo/ataxia: tiamina.
- Vomitos incoercibles + deficit ponderal: malnutricion secundaria.
- Enfermedad renal cronica + HG grave + rechazo de aborto: manejar HG y enfermedad de fondo.

### Residentado

- Cuadro leve sin peso/deshidratacion/cetonas: piridoxina, sola o con doxilamina.
- HG + T4 libre alta/TSH baja sin bocio/oftalmopatia: soporte, no antitiroideos de reflejo.
- Neurologia en HG: tiamina, no potasio ni doxilamina.
- Ondansetron/metoclopramida/prometazina son distractores si el stem pide primera linea leve.

### Manual/clase

- Separar NVE, HG y mimicos en todo slide/item.
- No convertir dosis o disponibilidad en verdad publica sin norma local.
- Usar la triada clinica "patron, severidad, peligro" como hilo conductor.

## Mini-drills

1. Gestante 8 semanas, vomitos ocasionales, orina normal, no baja de peso. Conducta inicial farmacologica?
2. Gestante 11 semanas, vomitos incoercibles, cetonuria, Na 130, mucosas secas. Diagnostico?
3. Gestante con HG prolongada, confusion, nistagmo y ataxia. Tratamiento?
4. Vomitos + sangrado + utero mayor que edad gestacional. Que diferencial no puedes perder?
5. HG severa con comorbilidad y rechazo de aborto. Cual es la conducta etica?

## Trazabilidad y QA

- Ground truth fuerte: BD ENAM 2020-2026, RM-GT-114, CM-181, Card 098.
- Transcript: uso secundario para enfasis de mola/hCG alta y sintomas tempranos de embarazo.
- Fuentes externas: RCOG, NHS, Merck Manual Professional.
- Pendiente antes de `qa_pass`: norma local/MINSA o protocolo institucional para farmacos, dosis, rutas, ingreso y derivacion.

Take-home point: emesis leve se maneja por escalones; hiperemesis se reconoce por repercusion; red flags rompen el cierre diagnostico. - Nauseas y vomitos del embarazo se asocian a cambios hormonales tempranos; hCG, estrogenos, progesterona, enlentecimiento gastrointestinal y sensibilidad central al vomito participan, pero la causa exacta no es unica. - hCG alta explica una parte del p

units.title: Tuberculosis en el infante
units.body:
# Tuberculosis en el infante

## Exam identity

TB infantil is not adult TB resized. Exams ask whether the learner can route a child from exposure to infection to active disease, while respecting the fact that children often cannot expectorate and often have negative bacilloscopy.

Takehome: in infants, TB is diagnosed by pattern convergence; a negative test never outranks close contact plus compatible clinical-radiologic disease.

## Guion

### 1. Por que da / fisiopatologia

- Mycobacterium tuberculosis spreads by airborne nuclei from an infectious pulmonary or laryngeal TB case, usually an adult in the household.
- Infants and young children usually develop primary TB: pulmonary focus plus lymphatic spread plus hilar/mediastinal adenopathy.
- Immature cell-mediated immunity increases risk of progression from infection to disease.
- Young age increases risk of disseminated disease: miliary TB and TB meningitis.
- Pediatric disease is often paucibacillary, so BK and even molecular tests can be negative despite real disease.
- BCG does not prevent infection reliably; its high-yield role is protection against severe infant TB forms.

Takehome: child TB is a transmission event plus an immature immune response, not a cavitary-adult template.

### 2. A quien / epidemiologia / factores de riesgo

- Highest-yield child: under 5 years old, especially infant/toddler, with household TB contact.
- Major risk modifiers: HIV, immunosuppression, malnutrition, no/uncertain BCG, crowding, poverty, previous untreated exposure and source case with MDR/RR TB.
- A child with TB should trigger source-case thinking: who is transmitting in the house?
- ENAM/RM stems often test contacts before they test symptoms.
- BCG history does not rule out TB and does not remove the need to evaluate the child.

Takehome: the source case is not background flavor; it is often the diagnostic spine of the question.

### 3. Como presenta

- Frequent symptoms: persistent cough, fever for more than 2 weeks, weight loss or poor weight gain, failure to thrive, night sweats, fatigue and less play.
- Infants can be nonspecific: irritability, anorexia, poor feeding, lethargy, poor growth or persistent fever.
- Primary pulmonary TB can cause hilar/mediastinal adenopathy; this can produce wheeze, stridor, atelectasis or nonresolving pneumonia.
- ENAM radiology anchor: hilar or mediastinal adenopathies in primary pediatric TB.
- Severe red flags: convulsions, altered mental status, persistent vomiting, meningeal signs, miliary pattern, hepatosplenomegaly or respiratory distress.
- Pleural TB appears more often as a schoolchild/adolescent extrapulmonary route than as the classic infant stem.

Takehome: in children, adenopathy beats cavitation as the default image clue.

## Manejo

### 1. Diagnostico

- Start with the triad: contact history, child symptoms and chest X-ray.
- Then add tests:
  - PPD/TST or IGRA: infection evidence; they do not prove active disease.
  - CXR: normal supports ILTB if asymptomatic; hilar/mediastinal adenopathy supports active primary TB.
  - PDRm/Xpert MTB/RIF: detects MTB and rifampicin resistance when an adequate sample is obtained.
  - Culture and susceptibility: slower, but important for confirmation and drug-resistance decisions.
- Pediatric sample logic:
  - If the child can expectorate, respiratory sample.
  - If the child cannot expectorate, use pediatric alternatives such as induced sputum, early-morning gastric aspirate or bronchoalveolar sample according to context and norm.
  - Do not use serology as the answer for active TB.
- Negative BK does not rule out TB in children.
- Negative PPD does not rule out TB in infants, severe disease, recent infection, malnutrition or immunosuppression.
- PPD thresholds are risk-based:
  - HIV/immunosuppression/recent high-risk contact can use lower thresholds.
  - Several local exam examples use 10 mm, but one direct ENAM item used 8 mm in a close under-5 contact and still chose TPT.
  - Therefore: do not teach a universal 10 mm rule.

Takehome: PPD/IGRA say "infected"; symptoms and CXR decide whether infection has become disease.

### 2. Clasificacion

- Exposure/contact:
  - Contact with infectious TB source.
  - No infection documented yet.
  - No clinical/radiologic evidence of disease.
- TB infection / ILTB:
  - PPD/IGRA positive by risk threshold.
  - Asymptomatic.
  - Normal CXR.
  - No evidence of active disease.
- Probable active TB:
  - Compatible symptoms and/or CXR.
  - Contact history strongly supportive.
  - Microbiology may be negative or unavailable.
- Confirmed active TB:
  - MTB detected by PDRm/Xpert/culture or other accepted method from appropriate sample.
- Site:
  - Pulmonary, pleural, ganglionar, miliary, meningeal, osteoarticular or other extrapulmonary site.
- Severity:
  - Non-severe vs severe is source-gated; meningitis and miliary disease are always high-risk.
- Resistance:
  - Drug-susceptible, H-resistant, RR/MDR, pre-XDR/XDR according to source case or DST.

Takehome: exposure, ILTB and active TB are different diagnoses with different treatments.

### 3. Manejo terapeutico

- First rule: rule out active disease before TPT.
- Contact/ILTB:
  - TPT is indicated according to age, exposure intensity, test result, HIV/immunosuppression status and source-case resistance.
  - Historical exam items may answer "isoniazid", but the current product should not reduce all pediatric TPT to one regimen until NTS 221 is page-locked.
- Active drug-susceptible TB:
  - Treat with a pediatric TB regimen according to current national norm, site, severity and weight.
  - Do not publish doses, DFC bands or exact regimen variations without page-lock.
- Suspected RR/MDR exposure:
  - Do not start drug-susceptible logic automatically.
  - Link the child to source-case drug susceptibility and program/expert management.
- Meningitis, miliary and other severe/extrapulmonary disease:
  - Do not use the short/non-severe pulmonary route.
  - Duration, corticosteroids and regimen details remain source-gated.
- Operational care:
  - Supervised therapy/DOT/TOS.
  - Weight-based dose adjustment.
  - Adherence review.
  - Adverse-effect surveillance.
  - Contact tracing and source-case control.

Takehome: prevention treats risk of disease; active TB treatment treats disease and transmission ecology.

### 4. Complicaciones

- TB meningitis: irritability, somnolence, vomiting, seizures, focal deficits, high morbidity.
- Miliary TB: persistent fever, systemic illness, diffuse micronodular pattern, hepatosplenomegaly.
- Airway compression from adenopathy: wheeze, stridor, atelectasis or persistent pneumonia.
- Pleural TB: pleuritic pain, effusion, reduced breath sounds; diagnostic route is not the same as pulmonary sample logic.
- Growth failure and malnutrition.
- Drug toxicity:
  - H: neuropathy, hepatitis.
  - R: interactions, orange secretions, hepatotoxicity.
  - Z: hepatotoxicity, hyperuricemia.
  - E: optic neuritis.

Takehome: severe pediatric TB is usually dissemination or compression, not just cough intensity.

### 5. Seguimiento

- Follow clinically: fever, cough, energy, appetite, weight gain and respiratory status.
- Recalculate dose with weight gain when treatment is used.
- Check adherence and adverse effects at every control.
- Verify source-case evaluation and contact management.
- Do not use PDRm/Xpert as response monitoring.
- If the child does not improve, reassess:
  - adherence,
  - alternate diagnosis,
  - drug resistance,
  - wrong classification as ILTB vs active disease,
  - complication or extrapulmonary site.

Takehome: follow-up in pediatric TB is clinical plus programmatic; it is not repeated PPD as a cure marker.

### 6. Pronostico

- Better prognosis: early recognition, drug-susceptible disease, complete treatment, good nutrition and reliable follow-up.
- Worse prognosis: infant age, HIV, severe malnutrition, delayed diagnosis, MDR/RR exposure, meningitis, miliary disease or poor adherence.
- BCG improves risk profile for severe forms but does not erase TB risk.

Takehome: the exam hides prognosis inside age, site, immunity and resistance.

## Product modifiers ENAM/RM

- ENAM loves: contact + PPD/CXR + "TPT or disease?"
- ENAM loves: hilar/mediastinal adenopathy as primary pediatric TB.
- ENAM loves: HIV threshold logic; 4 mm can be negative, 5 mm becomes meaningful.
- ENAM loves: child who cannot expectorate -> Xpert MTB/RIF in an appropriate respiratory sample.
- RM loves: separating infection from active disease.
- RM loves: negative BK/PPD traps, aspirate/sample traps, resistance of source case and severe TB exceptions.
- Historical answers such as isoniazid-only TPT should be tagged as exam lock/source-gated, not as universal current norm.
units.example: TB infantil is not adult TB resized. Exams ask whether the learner can route a child from exposure to infection to active disease, while respecting the fact that children often cannot expectorate and often have negative bacilloscopy. Takehome: in infants, TB is diagnosed by pattern convergence; a negative test never outranks close contact plus compatible clinical-radiologic disease. - Mycobacterium tuberculosis spreads by airborne nuclei from an infectious pulmonary or laryngeal TB case, usually an adult in the household. - Infants and young children usually develop primary TB: pulmonary focus

units.title: Enfermedad ulcero-peptica
units.body:
# Enfermedad ulcero-peptica

## Exam identity

Enfermedad ulcero-peptica is an acid-mucosa imbalance syndrome that exams ask through five surfaces: classic pain, H. pylori, NSAID/aspirin injury, endoscopic bleeding risk and atypical/refractory ulcer syndromes.

Takehome: EUP is a routing problem: danger first, driver second, drug/regimen last.

## Guion

### 1. Por que da / fisiopatologia

- Ulceration happens when aggressive factors exceed mucosal defense.
- H. pylori and NSAIDs are the two dominant drivers.
- H. pylori can damage mucus barrier, alter acid physiology and drive chronic gastritis, atrophy, metaplasia, dysplasia, cancer risk and MALT lymphoma risk.
- NSAIDs/aspirin reduce prostaglandin-mediated mucosal defense: less mucus, bicarbonate and blood-flow protection.
- H. pylori + NSAID is a risk-amplifying pair.
- Duodenal ulcer often reflects acid-driven injury; gastric ulcer requires a stronger malignancy-exclusion reflex.
- Zollinger-Ellison is the hypergastrinemia/acid hypersecretion exception: recurrent, multiple, postbulbar or refractory ulcers plus diarrhea and MEN1 clues.

Takehome: the exam usually gives the driver; do not treat all epigastric pain as the same disease.

### 2. A quien / epidemiologia / factores de riesgo

- Classic ENAM patient: adult with burning epigastric pain, nocturnal symptoms, or pain several hours after meals.
- NSAID patient: chronic diclofenac/ibuprofen/aspirin exposure, especially with prior ulcer or bleeding history.
- H. pylori patient: dyspepsia/ulcer history or documented infection.
- Alarm/risk patient: older age, weight loss, anemia, bleeding, persistent vomiting, dysphagia, family/risk background or gastric lesion.
- Z-E/MEN1 patient: recurrent or atypical postbulbar ulcers, diarrhea, elevated gastrin, acidic pH, hypercalcemia/PTH.

Takehome: age/risk and drug exposure decide how aggressive the workup becomes.

### 3. Como presenta

- Duodenal-type pattern:
  - Burning epigastric pain.
  - Appears hours after meals.
  - May wake the patient at night.
  - Often improves with food or antacids.
- Gastric-type pattern:
  - Epigastric pain may be immediate/postprandial or less stereotyped.
  - More associated with NSAIDs in local card.
  - Needs biopsy/follow-up logic when seen endoscopically.
- Bleeding:
  - Hematemesis, coffee-ground emesis, melena, syncope, weakness or shock.
- Perforation:
  - Sudden intense pain, peritonism, rigid abdomen, free air.
- Obstruction:
  - Persistent vomiting, early satiety, bloating, retained gastric contents.

Takehome: melena or peritonism changes the question from "what is it?" to "what do you do now?"

## Manejo

### 1. Diagnostico

- Stable dyspepsia/ulcer pattern:
  - Ask for alarm symptoms and risk.
  - If no danger, test for H. pylori when appropriate and consider acid suppression by protocol.
- Alarm or gastric lesion:
  - Endoscopy with biopsy logic.
  - Gastric ulcer is not left as "just ulcer" without malignancy thinking.
- H. pylori:
  - Active infection tests: urea breath test, stool antigen, or biopsy-based tests if endoscopy is done.
  - Serology is weak for cure confirmation because it can remain positive after treatment.
  - PPI, antibiotics and bismuth can create false-negative active tests; timing is source-gated and should be checked before public release.
- Bleeding:
  - Stabilize first.
  - Then endoscopy and risk classification.
  - Forrest high-risk vs low-risk stigmata guides endoscopic therapy, but exact IIc/III naming is source-gated.
- Z-E:
  - Gastrin alone is not enough if the patient is on PPI.
  - ENAM lock: stop PPI with H2 bridge and confirm with secretin stimulation when safe/appropriate.

Takehome: the right test is determined by the clinical question, not by the word "stomach".

### 2. Clasificacion

- By clinical surface:
  - Dyspepsia not yet investigated.
  - Duodenal-type ulcer.
  - Gastric ulcer / alarm ulcer.
  - Complicated ulcer: bleeding, perforation, obstruction.
  - Refractory/atypical ulcer: suspect Z-E/MEN1, malignancy, persistent H. pylori, NSAID exposure.
- By driver:
  - H. pylori.
  - NSAID/aspirin.
  - Hypersecretory state.
  - Premalignant gastric pathology.
- By pharmacology axis:
  - H2 antagonist: H2 receptor.
  - PPI: H+/K+-ATPase.
  - Sucralfate: adherent polymer/barrier, pepsin inhibition.
  - Misoprostol: PGE1 analog mucosal protection.
  - Metronidazole: alcohol interaction.

Takehome: classify by danger and driver before choosing treatment.

### 3. Manejo terapeutico

- First move:
  - Unstable bleeding -> resuscitation before endoscopy.
  - Peritonitis/free air -> surgical route.
  - Stable ulcer/dispepsia -> driver-based route.
- Acid suppression:
  - PPI is the modern high-yield acid suppression class.
  - H2 blockers are still exam-relevant by mechanism.
  - Do not call cimetidine a modern drug of choice; use it only when the stem asks H2 receptor mechanism.
- H. pylori:
  - Treat confirmed infection.
  - Confirm eradication after therapy using active infection tests.
  - ACG 2024 control: avoid empiric clarithromycin or levofloxacin regimens unless susceptibility is known.
  - Direct ENAM 2026 lock: when clarithromycin resistance is >15%, choose PPI + bismuth + tetracycline + metronidazole.
  - Doses, duration and local Peru availability/resistance remain source-gated.
- NSAID/aspirin:
  - Stop NSAID if possible.
  - If NSAID/aspirin must continue, assess high-risk features and protect according to protocol.
  - Prior complicated ulcer is a major risk signal.
- Bleeding ulcer:
  - Stabilize, PPI, endoscopy.
  - High-risk stigmata require endoscopic hemostasis.
  - Low-risk stigmata/base clean do not require hemostasis; local RM key uses flat pigmented spot but Forrest naming is source-gated.
- Perforation:
  - Surgical route; local card mentions Graham patch plus later cause management.
- Obstruction:
  - Decompression/support, endoscopic/surgical route when persistent; exact operation is source-gated.

Takehome: do not memorize eradication as a recipe; read resistance, prior exposure and source gate.

### 4. Complicaciones

- Hemorrhage:
  - Melena/hematemesis, anemia, shock.
  - Posterior duodenal bulb can injure the gastroduodenal artery.
- Perforation:
  - Acute abdomen, rigid abdomen, free air.
- Penetration:
  - Pain radiating to back, possible pancreatic involvement.
- Gastric outlet obstruction:
  - Vomiting, bloating, retained food, dehydration/alkalosis.
- Recurrence:
  - Persistent H. pylori, ongoing NSAID use, smoking or gastrinoma.
- Premalignant/malignant:
  - Atrophy, metaplasia, dysplasia, gastric cancer risk, MALT lymphoma association.

Takehome: complications are the exam's way of changing the first step.

### 5. Seguimiento

- Confirm H. pylori eradication after therapy with active tests.
- Reassess NSAID/aspirin exposure and recurrence risk.
- Gastric ulcer/suspicious lesion: biopsy and follow-up endoscopy logic.
- Premalignant histology:
  - Displasia is the direct ENAM high-risk finding.
  - Exact surveillance interval and biopsy protocol remain source-gated.
- Bleeding ulcer:
  - Watch for rebleeding and treat source/driver.
- Refractory ulcer:
  - Recheck adherence, H. pylori cure, NSAID use, malignancy and gastrinoma.

Takehome: follow-up is not symptom relief alone; it closes eradication, malignancy and recurrence risk.

### 6. Pronostico

- Good prognosis when H. pylori is eradicated, NSAIDs are stopped, malignancy is excluded and complications are controlled.
- Worse prognosis with prior complicated ulcer, ongoing NSAID/aspirin need, bleeding, perforation, obstruction, premalignant gastric change, malignancy or Z-E/MEN1.

Takehome: prognosis follows the driver that remains active.

## Product modifiers ENAM/RM

- ENAM direct:
  - Classic duodenal-type pain -> EUP.
  - Diclofenac + nocturnal epigastric pain -> EUP.
  - Clarithromycin resistance >15% -> bismuth quadruple components.
  - Z-E/MEN1 -> handle PPI interference and secretin test.
  - Dysplasia -> closer surveillance.
- RM:
  - H2 receptor mechanism -> cimetidine.
  - Low-risk bleeding stigmata/no hemostasis -> local answer flat pigmented spot, but do not hard-code Forrest number without source-lock.
  - Gastric atrophy -> B12 by intrinsic factor loss; note the clinical-histology tension.
  - Metronidazole + alcohol -> disulfiram-like symptoms.
  - Sucralfate -> polymer/barrier, not antisecretory.

units.title: Vigilancia epidemiologica
units.body:
# Vigilancia epidemiologica

## Exam identity

Vigilancia epidemiologica is the public-health system that collects, analyzes, interprets and disseminates health-event data so the system can detect risk, identify outbreaks, prioritize action and control harm.

Takehome: the exam does not want "data collection"; it wants the next sanitary decision.

## Guion

### 1. Por que existe / concepto

- Surveillance exists because cases seen one by one hide population patterns.
- The system makes individual events comparable by using case definitions, notification channels and analysis by person, place and time.
- It is continuous, systematic and timely.
- It includes collection, analysis, interpretation and dissemination.
- Its endpoint is action: prevention, control, resource mobilization, alert, feedback or policy decision.
- It is not the same as an isolated research project.
- It is not complete when the case is registered; it is complete when information returns to the system and guides intervention.

Takehome: surveillance turns signals into action.

### 2. A quien / donde aplica

- Applies to diseases, deaths, outbreaks and public-health events under surveillance.
- Includes communicable diseases, vaccine-preventable diseases, metaxenic diseases, zoonoses, maternal-perinatal events, environmental risks, NCD-related events and other priority events depending on the national norm.
- Operates from the establishment/community level to local, regional and national public-health levels.
- Uses clinical services, laboratories, field teams, records, community reports, media/event surveillance and situational analysis.
- In exams, it appears as:
  - A clinician or health center deciding whether to notify.
  - A cluster of cases suggesting brote.
  - A public-health team choosing active surveillance.
  - A dengue, measles, foodborne disease, yellow fever, TB-HIV or maternal death item.

Takehome: surveillance is territorial and operational; it is not only hospital reporting.

### 3. Como se reconoce en stems

- The stem gives:
  - Multiple cases in time/place.
  - A suspected case of a high-impact disease.
  - A case with travel/exposure history.
  - A laboratory result with public-health consequences.
  - A need to identify risk areas, contacts, vectors or exposed groups.
  - A question about immediate vs periodic notification.
  - A table, curve, map or trend.
- The answer often asks for:
  - Type of surveillance.
  - Case classification.
  - Notification action.
  - Outbreak interpretation.
  - Correct first public-health step.
  - Source or mode of transmission.

Takehome: when the stem asks what to do with a signal, think surveillance.

## Manejo / operacion

### 1. Diagnostico operacional

- Step 1: identify the event.
  - Disease, death, syndrome, lab result, outbreak, rumor, cluster or exposure.
- Step 2: apply a case definition.
  - Clinical criteria.
  - Epidemiologic criteria.
  - Laboratory criteria.
  - Person-place-time limits when relevant.
- Step 3: classify the case.
  - Suspected.
  - Probable.
  - Confirmed.
  - Discarded.
- Step 4: decide notification.
  - Obligatory or not.
  - Immediate or periodic.
  - Channel and level.
  - Exact list, deadline and platform are source-gated.
- Step 5: analyze and respond.
  - Person, place, time.
  - Observed vs expected.
  - Risk groups and territory.
  - Action and feedback.

Takehome: do not count before defining who counts.

### 2. Clasificacion

#### By capture method

- Passive surveillance:
  - Establishments routinely notify what they detect.
  - Efficient and broad.
  - Main weakness: underreporting and delay.
- Active surveillance:
  - The system deliberately searches for cases in community, records, labs or contacts.
  - Useful in outbreaks, elimination, high-priority events and underreporting.
  - ENCAPS lock: searching for people who did not attend services or reviewing records intentionally is active surveillance.
- Sentinel surveillance:
  - Selected sites collect higher-quality data.
  - Useful for trends, severity, quality and feasibility.
  - Trap: do not assume it estimates the whole country automatically.
- Syndromic surveillance:
  - Detects syndrome patterns before etiologic confirmation.
  - Early but less specific.
- Laboratory surveillance:
  - Confirms agents, typing, resistance, serotype or variant.
  - Does not replace clinical and epidemiologic criteria.
- Event-based/community surveillance:
  - Captures rumors, unusual events, community alerts, media signals or animal events.
  - Requires verification.

Takehome: surveillance type depends on how cases are captured, not on how important the disease sounds.

#### By urgency

- Immediate notification:
  - Used when delay can increase population harm or outbreak spread.
  - Examples tested locally include suspected foodborne outbreak and jungle yellow fever.
  - Exact current event list and deadline are source-gated.
- Periodic notification:
  - Used for routine surveillance events where consolidated monitoring is the key.
  - Weekly periodicity appears often in exams, but disease-specific deadlines are source-gated.

Takehome: urgency is event-specific; never invent the official deadline.

#### By event interpretation

- Endemia:
  - Expected occurrence in a population/territory.
- Conglomerado/cluster:
  - Grouping of cases in time/place/person; may be an early warning.
- Brote:
  - Cases above expected in a defined time/place or an event that, by its nature, triggers investigation and control.
- Epidemia:
  - Excess occurrence over a broader population or territory.
- Artifact:
  - Apparent increase caused by better detection, changed definition, new lab, duplicate reports or reporting delay.

Takehome: compare observed vs expected before calling everything a brote.

### 3. Manejo operativo

- Suspected high-risk event:
  - Notify according to current norm.
  - Begin verification and case investigation.
  - Do not wait for perfect confirmation when delay is dangerous.
- Suspected outbreak:
  - Notify.
  - Verify diagnosis.
  - Define case.
  - Build line list.
  - Search actively.
  - Describe by person, place and time.
  - Generate and test hypotheses.
  - Control early if the source or transmission route is plausible and active.
- Routine trend:
  - Consolidate data.
  - Analyze trend and geography.
  - Compare with expected levels.
  - Feed back to local teams.
  - Adjust interventions.
- Community/vector risk:
  - Use community surveillance and focal control when there is risk without established local transmission.
  - Direct ENAM lock: imported dengue with no local transmission and public spaces with vector risk -> activate community surveillance committee, not mass fumigation as the first reflex.

Takehome: notification and control can happen while investigation continues.

### 4. Direct exam locks

- Dengue imported cases, no local transmission, vector-risk public spaces:
  - Key: activate community surveillance committee.
  - Trap: mass fumigation or population ELISA without local transmission.
- Dengue symptoms, local Aedes area, no travel, lab positive:
  - Key: autochthonous case.
  - Trap: imported case.
- Suspected dengue outbreak with multiple cases in 48 hours:
  - Key: report to the national surveillance system and request serologic confirmation.
  - Trap: wait for lab before notifying.
- Fever-rash-IgM positive after travel to measles-transmission country:
  - Key: imported case.
  - Trap: autochthonous just because it was diagnosed locally.
- Hospital water supply with gram negative bacteria:
  - Key: common vehicle transmission.
  - Trap: person-to-person route.
- Maternal death after eclampsia then intracerebral hemorrhage:
  - Key: underlying cause is eclampsia.
  - Trap: confusing immediate mechanism with initiating cause.
- TB endemic zone with rising HIV and poor TB preventive therapy:
  - Key: TB-HIV coinfection incidence increases.
  - Trap: ignoring trend and prevention failure.

Takehome: exams like surveillance because it forces classification plus action.

### 5. Seguimiento

- Monitor completeness:
  - Are all expected units reporting?
- Monitor timeliness:
  - Are events being notified on time?
- Monitor data quality:
  - Are cases duplicated, incomplete or misclassified?
- Monitor trend:
  - Are incidence, positivity, mortality, lethality or attack rates changing?
- Monitor intervention:
  - Did cases decrease after control?
  - Did active search reveal hidden cases?
  - Did feedback improve reporting?
- Use situational rooms and bulletins to return information to decision-makers and notifying teams.

Takehome: follow-up asks whether surveillance changed action and outcomes.

### 6. Pronostico / system performance

- Strong surveillance:
  - Detects unusual events early.
  - Uses clear definitions.
  - Notifies on time.
  - Analyzes person-place-time.
  - Feeds back to teams.
  - Triggers proportionate action.
- Weak surveillance:
  - Underreports.
  - Delays notification.
  - Confuses suspected with confirmed.
  - Uses outdated lists.
  - Produces dashboards without decisions.
  - Fails to close the feedback loop.

Takehome: the prognosis of a surveillance system is its capacity to detect early and act proportionately.

## Product modifiers ENAM/RM/ENCAPS

- ENAM:
  - Emphasize classification and first action.
  - Common pattern: travel vs local exposure, autochthonous vs imported, outbreak notification, vehicle transmission.
  - If the item gives no current norm, choose the decision logic instead of memorized deadlines.
- RM:
  - Higher risk of normative traps: dengue scenario, event list, deadline, platform, situational room.
  - Do not publish scenario I-IV definitions until source-lock.
  - Safe local lock: sustained autochthonous dengue transmission in multiple districts without declared epidemic points to scenario III in the local RM key; scenario IV needs epidemic/outbreak/intensified transmission.
- ENCAPS:
  - Emphasize first-level action: detect, notify, search actively, mobilize community, request resources, interrupt transmission and feed back.
  - Common trap: staying in registration without action.
  - Active surveillance examples are high-yield.

## Checklist final

1. What event or case am I counting?
2. Does it meet a case definition?
3. Is it suspected, probable, confirmed or discarded?
4. Is notification obligatory?
5. Is it immediate or periodic? Source-gated.
6. Is there excess over expected, or only a cluster?
7. What do person-place-time show?
8. What action follows now?
9. How does information return to the team?

units.title: Demencia
units.body:
# Demencia

## Exam identity

Demencia is an acquired, chronic cognitive decline that interferes with daily function. Exams test it as a routing problem: distinguish delirium, depression, mild cognitive impairment and normal aging before naming Alzheimer or another subtype.

Takehome: no functional loss, no dementia diagnosis; no attention check, no safe dementia diagnosis.

## Guion

### 1. Por que da / fisiopatologia

- Dementia syndrome happens when cognitive networks fail enough to impair independence.
- Alzheimer:
  - Classic pattern: progressive episodic memory failure.
  - Local exam pathology: beta-amyloid plaques plus tau neurofibrillary tangles.
  - Acetylcholine deficit is clinically relevant for symptomatic treatment logic.
- Vascular dementia:
  - Cognitive impairment from cerebrovascular disease.
  - Lacunes, multi-infarct disease, strategic infarcts or white-matter small-vessel disease.
- Lewy body dementia:
  - Synucleinopathy with Lewy bodies.
  - Produces cognitive fluctuations, visual hallucinations and parkinsonism.
- Frontotemporal dementia:
  - Frontal/anterior temporal network degeneration.
  - Presents as behavior or language change before memory in many stems.
- Normal pressure hydrocephalus:
  - Treatable mimic with ventriculomegaly and triad: gait, urinary symptoms, cognitive decline.
- Secondary/reversible causes:
  - Drugs, alcohol, depression, thyroid disease, B12 deficiency, infection, metabolic disorder, subdural hematoma, tumor, HIV/syphilis in risk contexts and NPH.

Takehome: mechanism matters because some "dementias" are actually treatable mimics.

### 2. A quien / epidemiologia / factores de riesgo

- Alzheimer:
  - Older age is the major exam context.
  - Down syndrome, family history, APOE4 and traumatic brain injury appear in teaching sources, but genetic testing is not a routine exam-first move.
- Vascular:
  - Hypertension, diabetes, atherosclerosis, smoking, prior stroke or lacunar disease.
- Lewy body:
  - Older adult with dementia plus parkinsonism/hallucinations/fluctuation.
- Frontotemporal:
  - Often earlier onset, classically before 65.
  - Family reports personality, social conduct or language change.
- NPH:
  - Older adult with gait disorder, urinary urgency/incontinence and cognitive slowing.
- Delirium risk:
  - Older adult, hospitalization, infection, dehydration, hypoxia, pain, polypharmacy, anticholinergics, benzodiazepines.

Takehome: age tells context, but tempo and first domain tell diagnosis.

### 3. Como presenta

- Alzheimer:
  - Repeats questions.
  - Loses keys/documents.
  - Leaves stove on.
  - Gets lost outside.
  - Later fails to recognize relatives.
  - May develop theft delusions or behavioral symptoms.
- Lewy body:
  - Visual hallucinations, often vivid.
  - Cognitive/attention fluctuations.
  - Parkinsonism: facies, rigidity, bradykinesia, short gait.
  - REM sleep behavior can support diagnosis.
- Vascular:
  - Stepwise deterioration.
  - Executive dysfunction and psychomotor slowing.
  - Focal neurologic signs.
  - Pseudobulbar syndrome or gait difficulty in small-vessel disease.
- Frontotemporal/prefrontal:
  - Disinhibition, euphoria/irritability, socially inappropriate behavior, poor hygiene, apathy, loss of empathy, poor decisions.
  - Language variants: nonfluent/agrammatic, semantic or logopenic depending pattern.
- NPH:
  - Magnetic gait/gait apraxia, urinary urgency/incontinence, cognitive slowing.
- Delirium:
  - Acute/subacute onset, fluctuating course, inattention, altered alertness, medical/drug trigger.
- Depression/pseudodementia:
  - Mood symptoms dominate, intense complaint, "I do not know", lower effort, possible improvement after depression treatment.

Takehome: in dementia exams, the first symptom is the map.

## Manejo

### 1. Diagnostico

- First step:
  - Obtain collateral history from family/caregiver.
  - Define tempo: hours/days, weeks/months, years.
  - Test attention and level of consciousness.
  - Document functional impact: finances, cooking, medications, navigation, hygiene, work, safety.
- Cognitive assessment:
  - Use a brief validated tool as screening, not as diagnosis alone.
  - ENCAPS first-level older adult anchor: Pfeiffer can be used for cognitive impairment screening.
  - MMSE/Pfeiffer/MoCA cutoffs remain source-gated for public manual use.
- Lab and reversible screen:
  - Review medications, alcohol and sensory deficits.
  - Common exam screen: CBC, glucose/electrolytes/calcium, renal/hepatic, TSH, B12.
  - HIV/syphilis and other tests when risk, age, course or context supports.
- Imaging:
  - Structural brain imaging helps rule out subdural, tumor, NPH and vascular disease.
  - Stronger need when atypical, rapid, young, focal, traumatic, gait/urinary pattern or vascular signs.
  - Safety lock: anticoagulation or trauma plus subacute cognitive decline/headache/focality is a chronic subdural route, not an Alzheimer route.
- Alzheimer diagnosis:
  - Clinical syndrome plus exclusion of reversible causes and supportive imaging when indicated.
  - Biomarkers and PET are source-gated for publication.
- Vascular diagnosis:
  - Clinical vascular pattern plus compatible imaging.
  - Direct ENAM lock: Hachinski 5 and pseudobulbar/gait/swallowing picture -> CT with multiple lacunar microinfarcts in periventricular white matter and basal ganglia.

Takehome: a low test score starts evaluation; it does not finish it.

### 2. Clasificacion

- Dementia syndrome vs mimics:
  - Delirium.
  - Depression/pseudodementia.
  - Mild cognitive impairment.
  - Normal aging.
  - Sensory impairment or low education/language mismatch.
- Major dementia subtypes:
  - Alzheimer.
  - Vascular.
  - Lewy body.
  - Frontotemporal.
  - Parkinson disease dementia.
  - Normal pressure hydrocephalus.
  - Secondary/reversible.
- Mechanism/histology local locks:
  - Alzheimer: amyloid plaques and tau tangles.
  - Lewy body: alpha-synuclein/Lewy bodies.
  - FTD/Pick: frontal/anterior temporal pattern; Pick bodies/neurons in classic teaching.
  - Vascular: lacunes, infarcts, white-matter disease.
- Timing lock:
  - Lewy body dementia: dementia precedes or is simultaneous with parkinsonism.
  - Parkinson disease dementia: established Parkinsonism comes at least about a year before dementia in classic teaching.

Takehome: classify by syndrome first, pathology second, treatment third.

### 3. Manejo terapeutico

- General foundation:
  - Explain diagnosis and prognosis.
  - Identify caregiver and support network.
  - Review medications; reduce anticholinergic and sedative burden when possible.
  - Treat sensory deficits, sleep problems, pain, constipation and medical triggers.
  - Safety: stove, wandering, driving, finances, falls, medication administration.
  - Exercise, structured routine, cognitive/social stimulation and caregiver training.
- Alzheimer:
  - Acetylcholinesterase inhibitors are symptomatic options in mild to moderate contexts.
  - Memantine is used in moderate-severe or later-stage contexts depending guideline.
  - Exact drug, dose, stage and contraindications are source-gated.
  - Anti-amyloid monoclonal antibodies are not core ENAM therapy; eligibility, amyloid confirmation, ARIA risk, MRI monitoring, APOE counseling and anticoagulation cautions are source-gated and specialist-level.
- Lewy body:
  - Cholinesterase inhibitor logic may help cognition/behavior.
  - Avoid typical/high-potency antipsychotics when possible because of severe sensitivity risk.
  - If psychosis/agitation requires treatment, use specialist-informed cautious strategy.
- Vascular:
  - Control vascular risk: blood pressure, diabetes, smoking, lipids and stroke prevention as indicated.
  - Rehab, gait/fall prevention and caregiver support.
- Frontotemporal:
  - No routine disease-modifying/symptomatic cognitive drug claim for AChE/memantine in pure FTD.
  - Behavioral strategies; SSRIs can be used for disinhibition/compulsions in some contexts.
  - Antipsychotics only with caution and clear indication.
- NPH:
  - Image and refer; tap test/shunt evaluation when candidate.
- Advanced dementia:
  - Goals of care, nutrition, aspiration risk, pressure injury prevention, infection decisions, home care and caregiver burden.
  - ENCAPS lock: advanced dementia with severe immobility and acute symptoms in community -> program home care with the health team.

Takehome: treatment is not only a pill; safety and caregiver are part of the prescription.

### 4. Complicaciones

- Delirium superimposed on dementia.
- Falls, wandering and accidents.
- Malnutrition, dehydration and medication errors.
- Aspiration pneumonia and respiratory infections in advanced disease.
- Behavioral and psychological symptoms: agitation, hallucinations, sleep disruption, aggression, apathy, depression, delusions.
- Caregiver burnout.
- Loss of capacity and consent issues.
- Institutionalization risk.

Takehome: advanced dementia mortality often comes through immobility, infection, aspiration and frailty.

### 5. Seguimiento

- Track cognition, function and behavior over time.
- Reassess diagnosis if course is too fast, focal, fluctuating or inconsistent.
- Monitor caregiver burden and safety risks.
- Review medications regularly.
- Screen for depression, delirium triggers, pain, sleep and sensory impairment.
- Update care goals, legal/ethical planning and home support.
- Revisit treatable causes when a new decline appears.

Takehome: sudden worsening in known dementia is delirium or new disease until proven otherwise.

### 6. Pronostico

- Alzheimer:
  - Progressive; local card gives average 8-10 years but this should be source-checked before publication.
- Vascular:
  - Depends on vascular control and recurrent events; stepwise worsening can occur.
- Lewy body:
  - Sensitive to antipsychotics; parkinsonism, falls and hallucinations shape risk.
- Frontotemporal:
  - Earlier onset and behavior/language burden create family and safety stress.
- NPH and secondary causes:
  - Potentially treatable; outcome depends on timely recognition and candidate selection.

Takehome: prognosis changes most when you find the treatable mimic.

## Product modifiers ENAM/RM/ENCAPS

- ENAM:
  - High-yield: Alzheimer vs Lewy vs vascular vs prefrontal/FTD.
  - Read for tempo, attention, hallucinations, parkinsonism, focality, functional loss.
  - Direct locks include stove fires/wandering/recognition failure for Alzheimer/dementia, visual hallucinations + parkinsonism + fluctuations for Lewy, and Hachinski/lacunes for vascular.
  - Subacute decline after trauma/anticoagulation is a subdural trap, not "new Alzheimer".
- RM:
  - No formal RM count in `topics_current`; use as differential reasoning support, not closed GT.
  - Likely traps: delirium, pseudodementia, NPH, antipsychotic sensitivity in Lewy.
- ENCAPS:
  - Adult older-care context: Pfeiffer screening and home care for advanced dementia with immobility.
  - Primary-care product should emphasize screening, referral, caregiver, home visit and red flags.

## Checklist final

1. Is the onset acute/fluctuating?
2. Is attention impaired?
3. Is there functional loss?
4. Is mood/sleep/pain/medication explaining the picture?
5. What domain failed first?
6. Are there focal signs, gait/urinary symptoms or hallucinations?
7. Have reversible causes been screened?
8. What safety/caregiver action is needed today?

units.title: Abdomen agudo
units.body:
# Abdomen agudo

## Exam identity

Abdomen agudo is a syndrome of acute abdominal pain that may hide immediately surgical, vascular, infectious, hemorrhagic, gynecologic or extra-abdominal disease. The exam asks for the next decision, not a decorative differential list.

Takehome: stability and peritoneal danger decide the first move.

## Guion

### 1. Por que da / fisiopatologia

- Visceral pain:
  - Dull, deep, poorly localized.
  - Comes from distention, stretch or spasm.
  - Foregut -> epigastrium; midgut -> periumbilical; hindgut/pelvic -> lower abdomen.
- Parietal pain:
  - Sharp, localized, worsens with movement.
  - Means parietal peritoneum irritation.
  - Defense, rebound and board-like abdomen are danger signals.
- Referred pain:
  - Shoulder, scapula, groin or back can point to diaphragm, biliary, renal or vascular causes.
- Major mechanisms:
  - Inflammatory: appendicitis, cholecystitis, diverticulitis, pancreatitis.
  - Obstructive: small bowel obstruction, volvulus, hernia.
  - Perforative: perforated peptic ulcer, perforated diverticulitis, bowel perforation.
  - Vascular: mesenteric ischemia, ruptured aneurysm.
  - Hemorrhagic: trauma, ectopic pregnancy, ruptured spleen/aneurysm.
  - Gyneco-urologic: ectopic pregnancy, ovarian torsion, PID/abscess, renal colic, pyelonephritis.
  - Extra-abdominal: MI, pneumonia, DKA, porphyria, toxins.

Takehome: abdomen agudo is the body saying "find the mechanism before time runs out."

### 2. A quien / factores de riesgo

- Older adult:
  - Ischemia, aneurysm, malignancy, diverticulitis and muted peritonitis.
- Prior surgery:
  - Adhesive obstruction.
- NSAID or peptic ulcer history:
  - Perforated ulcer.
- Hypertension/atherosclerosis/atrial fibrillation:
  - Vascular abdomen and ischemia.
- Woman of childbearing age:
  - Ectopic pregnancy and torsion must compete with appendicitis.
- Immunosuppressed/steroid user:
  - Blunted signs of peritonitis.
- Recent operation:
  - Leak, bile peritonitis, abscess or hemorrhage.
- Trauma:
  - Hemorrhage or hollow viscus injury until excluded.

Takehome: the same pain means different risk depending on age, sex, drugs, surgery and vascular background.

### 3. Como presenta

- Peritonitis/perforation:
  - Sudden severe pain.
  - Board-like abdomen, rebound, involuntary guarding.
  - Free subdiaphragmatic air or neumoperitoneum.
  - Loss of liver dullness can support free air.
- Obstruction:
  - Colicky abdominal pain.
  - Distention.
  - Vomiting.
  - Constipation/obstipation.
  - Initially high-pitched sounds; late silent abdomen is danger.
- Ischemia:
  - Severe pain out of proportion to exam early.
  - Later peritonitis, acidosis/lactate, pneumatosis, shock.
  - ENAM lock: elderly hypertensive, melena, diffuse pain, distention, peritonitis, pneumatosis, high LDH -> acute mesenteric ischemia.
- Biliary/inflammatory:
  - RUQ + fever/Murphy -> biliary route.
  - RLQ migration -> appendicitis route.
  - LLQ -> diverticulitis or gynecology.
  - Epigastric radiating to back -> pancreatitis; epigastric sudden with free air -> ulcer perforation.
- Postoperative:
  - Fever, hypotension, peritonitis after cholecystectomy -> bile peritonitis.

Takehome: sudden and rigid is perforation; colicky and distended is obstruction; pain out of proportion is ischemia.

## Manejo

### 1. Diagnostico

- Immediate assessment:
  - ABC, perfusion, vitals, mental status, urine output.
  - Look for shock, sepsis, peritonitis, trauma and pregnancy.
- History:
  - Time of onset, exact sudden onset, migration, character, vomiting vs pain sequence, stool/flatus, bleeding, fever, urinary/gyne symptoms.
  - Previous surgery, NSAIDs, anticoagulants, vascular disease, pregnancy risk, immunosuppression.
- Exam:
  - Inspect, auscultate, percuss, palpate gently away from maximal pain.
  - Guarding, rebound and rigidity are peritoneal danger.
  - Check hernias, scars, groin, rectal/pelvic/testicular route when relevant.
- Labs:
  - CBC, electrolytes/renal, glucose, liver tests when indicated, coagulation, urinalysis.
  - hCG in woman of childbearing age.
  - Lipase for epigastric/pancreatitis route.
  - Lactate/ABG/VBG for shock/ischemia/sepsis.
  - Blood tests alone rarely diagnose the cause.
- Imaging:
  - Stable adult, unclear/nonlocalized or complicated abdomen: CT abdomen-pelvis with contrast is often the workhorse.
  - Suspected biliary disease: ultrasound.
  - Suspected gynecology/pregnancy: pelvic ultrasound route.
  - Suspected obstruction/perforation: X-ray can show air-fluid levels/free air, but CT defines cause if stable.
  - Do not delay surgery for imaging when instability or definitive perforation/peritonitis already declares the route.

Takehome: tests are chosen to change the next decision, not to postpone it.

### 2. Clasificacion

- By urgency:
  - Red: shock, diffuse peritonitis, free air, mesenteric ischemia, ruptured ectopic, ruptured AAA, strangulated hernia, trauma instability.
  - Orange: stable but complicated/unclear abdomen needing urgent imaging and surgical evaluation.
  - Yellow: localized inflammatory or medical abdomen after dangerous causes are excluded.
- By mechanism:
  - Inflammatory.
  - Obstructive.
  - Perforative.
  - Vascular.
  - Hemorrhagic.
  - Gyneco-urologic.
  - Extra-abdominal mimic.
- By management:
  - Immediate operation/control of focus.
  - Resuscitation plus urgent imaging.
  - Antibiotics plus drainage/source control.
  - Medical management/observation only after surgical emergencies are reasonably excluded.

Takehome: classify by what it can do to the patient in the next hours.

### 3. Manejo terapeutico

- First measures:
  - NPO.
  - Two IV lines if unstable.
  - Fluids and resuscitation.
  - Analgesia and antiemetic; analgesia is not forbidden.
  - Oxygen/monitoring when unstable.
  - NG tube when vomiting/obstruction risk is relevant.
  - Foley/urine output in shock or operative candidates.
- Antibiotics:
  - Indicated when intra-abdominal infection, sepsis, perforation, peritonitis, complicated appendicitis/cholecystitis/diverticulitis or surgical contamination is likely.
  - Cover gram-negative and anaerobic organisms by local protocol.
  - Exact regimen/dose/duration is source-gated.
- Source control:
  - Septic shock from approachable abdominal focus -> control/eradicate focus as soon as possible.
  - ENAM direct lock: do not wait until vasopressors stop or after arbitrary antibiotic doses if focus is surgically approachable.
- Perforation:
  - Free air plus acute abdomen/peritonitis -> urgent surgical route.
  - PPI/endoscopy is not definitive and can be dangerous/delaying in perforation.
- Stable unclear abdomen:
  - CT with contrast to define cause before operating.
  - RM/RM-GT lock: stable elderly with Blumberg and free Douglas fluid but no demonstrated perforation -> contrasted CT.

Takehome: resuscitation buys time; source control saves the patient.

### 4. Complicaciones

- Sepsis and septic shock.
- Peritonitis and abscess.
- Bowel necrosis/gangrene.
- Perforation and fecal/bile contamination.
- Hemorrhage and shock.
- Short bowel, fistula and postoperative leak when resection/anastomosis occurs.
- Missed ectopic pregnancy, torsion, MI, pneumonia or vascular catastrophe.

Takehome: late abdomen agudo becomes necrosis, leak, abscess or shock.

### 5. Seguimiento

- Reassess vitals, pain, abdominal exam and perfusion repeatedly.
- Watch lactate/acidosis, urine output, fever and mental status.
- If managed nonoperatively, define a clear failure threshold: worsening pain, peritonitis, fever, tachycardia, rising lactate, ileus, abscess, no improvement.
- After surgery/source control:
  - Monitor for abscess, leak, fistula, ileus and wound infection.
  - Adjust antibiotics to source control and culture/local protocol.
- If diagnosis remains unclear:
  - Repeat exam is a diagnostic tool, but not a substitute for urgent action when danger signs appear.

Takehome: observation is active reassessment, not passive waiting.

### 6. Pronostico

- Worse prognosis with:
  - Shock, delayed source control, advanced age, immunosuppression, mesenteric ischemia, perforation, lactate/acidosis, renal failure, diffuse peritonitis and postoperative leak.
- Better prognosis when:
  - Early danger recognition, resuscitation, correct imaging, antibiotics when indicated and timely source control occur.

Takehome: timing is prognosis in surgical abdomen.

## Product modifiers ENAM/RM/ENCAPS

- ENAM:
  - Direct locks: bile peritonitis post-cholecystectomy, mesenteric ischemia with pneumatosis/LDH, septic shock source control, neumoperitoneum -> laparotomy, NSAID ulcer perforation -> surgery.
  - Recurrent trap: asking for another test when free air already gives the answer.
- RM:
  - RM-GT-185 bifurcation:
    - Perforated duodenal ulcer with free subdiaphragmatic air -> suture/perforation control.
    - Stable unclear abdomen with peritoneal sign/liquid but no free air -> contrasted CT.
  - Colonoscopy is a dangerous distractor in acute abdomen/peritonitis.
- ENCAPS:
  - No direct package found.
  - If used for first-level products, emphasize recognition, stabilization, referral and not delaying surgical evaluation.
- EsSalud:
  - Although the master sequence labels this topic Plata, local EsSalud ledgers elevate abdomen agudo to high-priority operational content.
  - Teach it as guard/referral reasoning: stabilize, communicate, transfer safely and do not delay source control or specialty response.
  - Keep exact product rank source-gated until ledgers are reconciled.

## Checklist final

1. Is the patient unstable?
2. Is there peritonitis, free air or shock?
3. Is pain out of proportion?
4. Is there obstruction with strangulation signs?
5. Is the patient a woman of childbearing age?
6. Is this trauma?
7. Will imaging change management or delay control of focus?
8. What must happen now: fluids, antibiotics, CT, ultrasound, surgery, referral or observation?

units.title: Medicina ocupacional
units.body:
# Medicina ocupacional

## Exam identity

Medicina ocupacional is the discipline that protects health in people who work by identifying occupational hazards, assessing risk, controlling exposure, surveilling worker health and managing occupational events.

Takehome: exam questions usually ask which occupational system action prevents the next case.

## Guion

### 1. Por que da / concept

- The work environment can harm health through:
  - Physical agents: noise, vibration, radiation, heat/cold, pressure.
  - Chemical agents: solvents, vapors, gases, metals, pesticides, dusts.
  - Biological agents: blood, needles, TB, hepatitis, HIV, zoonoses.
  - Ergonomic agents: force, load, repetition, awkward posture, poorly designed tools.
  - Psychosocial agents: overload, low control, violence, harassment, night shifts, burnout risk.
- Hazard is the source of possible harm.
- Risk is probability/severity of harm in a specific exposure context.
- Occupational disease requires causal relation between work exposure and disease.
- Accident of work is an acute event linked to work that causes injury, disability or death.
- Incident/dangerous incident can have no injury but still reveal system failure.

Takehome: first name the exposure; then decide whether it is risk, accident, incident or disease.

### 2. A quien / exposure groups

- Health workers:
  - Needles, blood/body fluids, TB, hepatitis/HIV, shift work, violence, burnout and musculoskeletal overload.
- Miners/construction:
  - Silica, asbestos, dust, noise, falls and ergonomic burden.
- Food/chemical industry:
  - Vapors, formaldehyde, solvents, irritants, poor ventilation.
- Agriculture:
  - Pesticides, organophosphates, heat, zoonoses and musculoskeletal load.
- Office/service work:
  - Sick building syndrome, indoor air quality, screen/posture, psychosocial risk.
- High-risk workers:
  - Need job-specific surveillance and risk-based exams; exact legal periodicity is source-gated.

Takehome: the same symptom becomes occupational when task, agent, time and co-worker pattern fit.

### 3. Como presenta

- Acute event:
  - Cut, puncture, fall, splash, burn, acute poisoning.
  - Think accident route if harm occurred.
  - Think incident/dangerous incident if no harm but potential was serious.
- Chronic exposure:
  - Hipoacusia from noise, silicosis/asbestosis, dermatitis, occupational asthma, lead poisoning, repetitive strain.
  - Ask if symptoms worsen at work and improve away from work.
- Cluster/environment:
  - Multiple workers with similar symptoms point to workplace source.
  - RM lock: sick building syndrome asks for indoor air quality.
- Management/normative stems:
  - IPERC, training, EMO, registry, investigation, SAT/MTPE notification and committee/supervisor cues.

Takehome: occupational stems hide the answer in the job, exposure and temporal pattern.

## Manejo / Decision

### 1. Diagnostico and classification

- Define the occupational problem:
  - Hazard/risk without damage.
  - Incident/dangerous incident.
  - Accident of work.
  - Occupational disease.
  - Worker-health surveillance problem.
  - Environmental/engineering control problem.
- Build the exposure history:
  - Job title, task, agent, intensity, duration, PPE, ventilation, co-workers affected, timing with work/rest.
- Match agent to damage:
  - Noise -> audiometry/hipoacusia pattern.
  - Dusts -> pulmonary disease package.
  - Solvents/vapors -> mucosal/respiratory/neuro symptoms.
  - Blood/needle -> occupational biological exposure route.
  - Pesticides -> toxidrome route.
  - Ergonomic load -> musculoskeletal/nerve compression route.
- Do not call it occupational only because the patient works.

Takehome: the diagnosis needs a job-exposure-damage chain.

### 2. Clasificacion

- By risk factor:
  - Physical.
  - Chemical.
  - Biological.
  - Ergonomic.
  - Psychosocial.
- By event:
  - Incident/dangerous incident: no injury/disease, potential harm.
  - Accident: acute harm during work context.
  - Occupational disease: damage from work exposure/nexus.
- By prevention level:
  - Primary: eliminate/reduce exposure.
  - Secondary: surveillance, EMO, screening for early damage.
  - Tertiary: rehabilitation, adaptation and reintegration.
- By control hierarchy:
  - Elimination.
  - Substitution.
  - Engineering controls.
  - Administrative controls.
  - PPE.

Takehome: prevention hierarchy is more testable than memorizing isolated examples.

### 3. Manejo preventivo

- First decision:
  - Control the hazard at the source when possible.
- Hierarchy of controls:
  - Eliminate: remove the hazardous agent/process.
  - Substitute: replace with a less hazardous agent/process.
  - Engineering: ventilation, enclosure, barriers, guards, local extraction.
  - Administrative: rotation, training, signage, work-rest cycles, protocols.
  - PPE: respirators, gloves, eye protection, hearing protection.
- Surveillance:
  - Risk-based exams and monitoring detect early damage.
  - Surveillance does not replace hazard control.
- Incident/accident investigation:
  - Ask why the system allowed exposure.
  - Avoid blaming only worker behavior.
- SAT/notification:
  - Use source-locked MTPE/SAT exact pathway.
  - Compact gate allows exact distinction: mortal/dangerous incident vs nonfatal routes; do not simplify as grave/mild.

Takehome: EPP is useful, but it is rarely the best answer when source control is available.

### 4. Classic exam locks

- Formaldehyde vapor + inactive extraction + symptoms:
  - Eliminate/reduce source or contamination.
  - Do not choose only PPE if source/ventilation is available.
- Ergonomics:
  - Adapts work design, tools and tasks to worker physical/cognitive characteristics.
- Occupational HIV exposure:
  - Classify as occupational if it occurs during work activity.
  - Exact PEP/HBV/HCV steps are source-gated.
- Hospital new professionals:
  - Prioritize training on respiratory infection/TB control.
- Sick building syndrome:
  - Cause/problem: indoor air quality.
- Dangerous incident:
  - High-potential undesired event without injury/disease.

Takehome: many items are not treatment questions; they are system-prevention questions.

### 5. Complications / consequences

- Preventable recurrence if the hazard remains.
- Chronic irreversible disease: hipoacusia, pneumoconiosis, cancer, chronic dermatitis, chronic musculoskeletal disease.
- Biological infection after occupational exposure.
- Legal and institutional risk if event is not registered/investigated.
- Psychological harm and burnout when psychosocial risk is treated as personal weakness.
- False security when PPE is treated as full control.

Takehome: untreated exposure creates cases, not just symptoms.

### 6. Seguimiento

- Reassess exposure after intervention.
- Check whether co-workers are affected.
- Monitor environmental measurements when relevant.
- Monitor medical indicators by risk, not as generic checkups.
- Track recurrence, absenteeism, near-misses and accidents.
- Close the loop: finding -> control -> surveillance -> registry -> corrective action.

Takehome: occupational follow-up proves that the system changed, not only that one worker was seen.

## Product modifiers ENAM/RM/ENCAPS/EsSalud

- ENAM:
  - Use direct locks from BD_ENAM 2020-2026.
  - Treat COVID isolation as historical, not current guidance.
  - Strongest current patterns: source control, ergonomics, occupational exposure classification, TB training.
- RM:
  - Indoor air quality and incident peligroso are anchors.
  - Normative definitions need exact source if turned into public claims.
- ENCAPS/SERUMS:
  - SP-2.12 has no direct history; build from official norm and source-gated compact.
  - Use worker-health risk in first-level settings: puncture, TB, psychosocial risk, ergonomics.
  - Do not generate HIV/HBV/HCV exact PEP claims from memory.
- EsSalud:
  - No direct count in current ledger.
  - Potential angle: evaluation of incapacity, occupational disease and SCTR, but source-gated.

## Checklist final

1. What is the job/task?
2. What is the hazard?
3. Is this risk, incident, accident or occupational disease?
4. Is there a causal exposure-damage chain?
5. What is the highest feasible control in the hierarchy?
6. Does the worker need surveillance or urgent clinical care?
7. Is SAT/MTPE notification being asked exactly?
8. Is the claim historical, current, or source-gated?

units.title: Estadistica inferencial
units.body:
# Estadistica inferencial

## Exam identity

Estadistica inferencial uses sample data to decide whether an observed difference, association or effect is compatible with chance under a hypothesis model.

Takehome: exam stems usually give enough information to choose a test or interpret a statistical error.

## Guion

### 1. Por que existe / concepto

- Descriptive statistics summarizes what was observed.
- Inferential statistics asks what the observed sample suggests about the population.
- Hypothesis testing starts with:
  - H0: no difference, no association or no effect.
  - H1: there is difference, association or effect.
- The exam does not usually ask for calculation.
- The exam asks for:
  - Test choice.
  - Meaning of p or CI.
  - Error type.
  - Variable role.
  - Sampling or design clue.

Takehome: inferential statistics is not math decoration; it is decision-making under uncertainty.

### 2. A quien / when it appears

- Clinical trials:
  - Compare treatments, primary/secondary outcomes, p values and multiplicity.
- Cohorts/prospective studies:
  - Loss to follow-up reduces sample and power.
- Cross-sectional or observational studies:
  - Categorical association, correlation, regression.
- Surveys:
  - Sampling type and variable roles.
- Residentado:
  - Error alpha/beta and power.
- ENCAPS:
  - More likely adjacent to diagnostic tests, instrument validation or data analysis.

Takehome: read the research situation before memorizing the test name.

### 3. Como se reconoce

- Variable type clues:
  - Numeric outcome: mean, HbA1c, blood pressure, cholesterol, days.
  - Categorical outcome: yes/no, infected/not infected, clinical form, sex, exposed/non-exposed.
  - Ordinal outcome: Likert, pain score categories, severity ranks.
  - Time-to-event: survival, relapse time, death over follow-up.
- Group clues:
  - Two independent groups.
  - More than two independent groups.
  - Same patients before/after.
  - Matched pairs.
- Interpretation clues:
  - p < 0.05.
  - IC95 crosses 0 or 1.
  - H0 true/false.
  - Sample size decreases.
  - Multiple secondary outcomes.

Takehome: variables and structure choose the method.

## Manejo / Decision

### 1. Diagnostico estadistico

- If the stem asks association between two categorical variables:
  - Chi-square if expected counts are adequate.
  - Fisher exact test if expected counts are small.
- If the stem asks two independent numeric means:
  - t independent if assumptions are acceptable.
  - Mann-Whitney if non-normal/ordinal.
- If the stem asks before/after in same patients:
  - Paired t if numeric and assumptions acceptable.
  - Wilcoxon signed-rank if non-normal/ordinal.
- If the stem asks more than two independent means:
  - ANOVA.
  - Kruskal-Wallis if non-normal/ordinal.
- If the stem asks paired categorical before/after:
  - McNemar.
- If the stem asks numeric-numeric association:
  - Pearson if linear/normal.
  - Spearman if ordinal/non-normal/monotonic.
- If the stem asks binary outcome prediction/adjustment:
  - Logistic regression.
- If the stem asks numeric outcome prediction:
  - Linear regression.
- If the stem asks time-to-event comparison:
  - Kaplan-Meier describes curves; log-rank compares curves; Cox estimates hazard ratio.

Takehome: do not pick a test until outcome and grouping are clear.

### 2. Clasificacion

- By decision:
  - Difference.
  - Association.
  - Prediction/adjustment.
  - Estimation.
  - Error interpretation.
  - Sampling/design clue.
- By outcome:
  - Numeric.
  - Categorical.
  - Ordinal.
  - Binary.
  - Time-to-event.
- By data structure:
  - Independent.
  - Paired/repeated.
  - Matched.
  - More than two groups.
- By assumptions:
  - Parametric.
  - Nonparametric.
  - Exact/small-cell.

Takehome: classification prevents wrong-test reflexes.

### 3. Interpretation

- p value:
  - Probability of observing data this extreme or more if H0 were true.
  - p < alpha means reject H0.
  - p >= alpha means do not reject H0.
  - It is not the probability that H0 is true.
- IC95:
  - Range of values compatible with the data under the method.
  - Narrower IC means more precision.
  - If it crosses the null, usually no statistical significance in a two-sided 5% test.
  - Null is 0 for differences/correlation and 1 for ratios.
- Type I error:
  - False positive.
  - Reject true H0.
  - ENAM/RM lock: claiming difference when none exists.
- Type II error:
  - False negative.
  - Do not reject false H0.
  - ENAM/RM lock: failure to detect real association.
- Power:
  - 1 - beta.
  - Increases with sample size and larger true effects.
  - Falls with high variability and loss to follow-up.
- Multiple comparisons:
  - More unadjusted tests increase cumulative type I error.
  - ENAM lock: secondary endpoint p=0.04 after nonsignificant primary endpoint can be false positive.

Takehome: p, IC, alpha, beta and power answer different questions.

### 4. Direct exam locks

- Decreased sample due to losses:
  - Type II error increases.
  - Power decreases.
- Random first subject, then every k subjects:
  - Systematic sampling.
  - Neighbor topic: Muestreo.
- Two categorical variables:
  - Chi-square.
- H0 rejected even though no true difference:
  - Type I/alpha.
- H0 not rejected even though true effect exists:
  - Type II/beta.
- Independent variable:
  - Exposure/intervention/manipulated variable.
- Dependent variable:
  - Outcome/response.
- Correlation:
  - Association between variables, not causation.

Takehome: most ENAM items are one-step if you label the cue correctly.

### 5. Complications / common errors

- Equating statistical significance with clinical importance.
- Treating nonsignificance as proof of equality.
- Ignoring low power after loss to follow-up.
- Using chi-square for means.
- Using ANOVA for categorical outcomes.
- Using t independent instead of paired t.
- Treating one unadjusted secondary outcome as proof.
- Interpreting OR as RR when outcome is common.
- Assuming adjusted regression proves causality.

Takehome: the most dangerous statistical error is overclaiming.

### 6. Seguimiento / item-writing controls

- Every statistical item should state:
  - Outcome type.
  - Group structure.
  - Whether paired or independent.
  - If assumptions are normal/non-normal when needed.
  - What the question asks: test, interpretation, error or design clue.
- If two tests could be defensible, the stem is under-specified.
- If p and IC conflict, check whether they refer to same model/outcome.
- If many outcomes are tested, ask whether adjustment was performed.

Takehome: a good statistics question has one discriminating cue and one defensible answer.

## Product modifiers ENAM/RM/ENCAPS/EsSalud

- ENAM:
  - Direct locks: beta rises when sample shrinks; systematic sampling; chi-square; type I from multiplicity; independent/dependent variables; correlation as association.
- RM:
  - RM-GT-227 anchors alpha and beta errors.
  - Residentado can ask power, p value, CI and distractors such as `1-p`, `1-alpha`.
- ENCAPS:
  - Coverage routes through INV-2.2 Procesamiento y analisis de datos.
  - Use basic_only logic: descriptive vs inferential, simple variable/test interpretation, representativeness and basic data processing.
  - Do not import advanced Cox/Bonferroni/regression diagnostics into first-level products unless blueprint-approved.
- EsSalud:
  - Ledger tension: `topics_current` says 0 but curriculum/essalud frequency says n=6 and priority Plata.
  - Treat as Plata source-gated until reconciled.

## Checklist final

1. What is the outcome variable?
2. Is it numeric, categorical, ordinal, binary or time-to-event?
3. How many groups?
4. Are observations independent or paired?
5. Is the question about difference, association, prediction, estimation or error?
6. Does the CI cross the null?
7. Does the p value justify the claim?
8. Is there low power or multiple comparisons?
